Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), inherited from the cited Lebesgue, polar, Newtonian and distribution interfaces ([[def-countable-choice]]).
Work in $\mathbb R^3$ with its Euclidean structure ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]], [[def-metric-ball]]) and the constants of [[def-em-si-conventions]], $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}>0$.
Use one-based labels $v_i:=v(i-1)$ for vectors $v\in\mathbb R^3$, $i=1,2,3$; $\partial_i$ means the derivative in that coordinate (the supplier's $\partial_{i-1}$), and $e_i$ below is the standard unit vector in that direction. Divergence, curl and gradient are the cited operators with these labels, so relabelling does not change them.
Let $\Phi$ be the $n=3$ fundamental solution of $-\Delta$ of [[def-laplace-fundamental-solution-with-positive-minus-laplacian-sign]], normalised by $-\Delta T_\Phi=\delta_0$; then $\omega_2=4\pi$ and
$$\Phi(z)=\frac{1}{4\pi|z|}\qquad(z\ne0)$$
([[cor-volume-of-the-unit-n-ball]], [[lem-euclidean-chart-measure-agrees-with-polar-surface-measure]]).
Let $Nf$ be the Newtonian potential of [[def-newtonian-potential]].

(a) [Smooth compact sources] Let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^1$ with compact support contained in $\overline B_R$, $R>0$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[def-metric-ball]]), put $\varphi:=\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho$ and $E:=-\nabla\varphi$.
Then $\varphi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ ([[thm-newtonian-potential-for-holder-data-is-classical]]), and pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$
$$-\Delta\varphi=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E=0$$
with the operators of [[def-laplacian-of-a-c2-function]] and [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]].
Moreover, with $Q:=\int\rho\,d\lambda_3$, for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$ the absolutely convergent Coulomb integral representation holds, and its far-field bound holds for $|x|>2R$,
$$E(x)=\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{x-y}{|x-y|^3}\rho(y)\,d\lambda_3(y)\quad(x\in\mathbb R^3),\qquad |E(x)|\le\frac{\| \rho\|_1}{\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2}\quad(|x|>2R),$$
and for $|x|>2R$ the potential obeys the decay bound $|\varphi(x)|\le |Q|/(4\pi\varepsilon_0|x|)+R\|\rho\|_1/(\pi\varepsilon_0|x|^2)$ ([[lem-em-newtonian-far-field-gradient]], [[thm-decay-of-the-newtonian-potential-of-compactly-supported-data]]).
The pair $(E,0,\rho,0)$ therefore realises the pure electrostatic regime of [[def-em-electrostatic-regime]] with source $\rho$, and $E$ is the field of the localised Newtonian potential.

(b) [Uniqueness with vanishing at infinity] If $\psi\in C^2(\mathbb R^3)$ satisfies $-\Delta\psi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$ pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$ and $\lim_{|x|\to\infty}\psi(x)=0$, then $\psi=\varphi$ ([[thm-weak-maximum-principle-for-the-laplacian]]).
In particular, among $C^2$ solutions of the Poisson equation of a compactly supported $C^1$ source decaying at infinity, the localised Newtonian potential is the unique one.

(c) [Compactly supported $L^1$ sources] If instead $\rho\in L^1(\mathbb R^3)$ is real, measurable and compactly supported, then $N\rho$ is finite $\lambda_3$-almost everywhere, belongs to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, is $C^\infty$ and harmonic off the support of $\rho$, and its regular distribution satisfies
$$-\Delta T_{\varepsilon_0^{-1}N\rho}=T_{\rho/\varepsilon_0}\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-newtonian-potential-solves-poisson-distributionally]], scaled by $\varepsilon_0^{-1}$; [[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]], [[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(d) [Point charge] Let $q\in\mathbb R$ and $x_0\in\mathbb R^3$ and define, with arbitrary values at $x_0$,
$$\varphi_q(x):=\frac{q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|},\qquad E_q(x):=\frac{q\,(x-x_0)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0|x-x_0|^3}\qquad(x\ne x_0).$$
Then $\varphi_q\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $E_q$ is locally integrable and $C^\infty$ off $x_0$, $E_q=-\nabla\varphi_q$ on $\mathbb R^3\setminus\{x_0\}$, and, with $T_{\varphi_q}$ the regular distribution of $\varphi_q$ and $\operatorname{div}E_q:=\sum_i\partial_iT_{E_{q,i}}$, $\operatorname{curl}E_q:=(\partial_2T_{E_{q,3}}-\partial_3T_{E_{q,2}},\ \partial_3T_{E_{q,1}}-\partial_1T_{E_{q,3}},\ \partial_1T_{E_{q,2}}-\partial_2T_{E_{q,1}})$,
$$-\Delta T_{\varphi_q}=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{div}E_q=\frac{q}{\varepsilon_0}\delta_{x_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}E_q=0\qquad\text{in }\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^3)$$
([[thm-minus-laplacian-of-the-fundamental-solution-is-dirac]] for the first identity, [[lem-em-distributional-gradient-smooth-off-a-point]] for the passage from the potential to the field, [[def-distributional-derivative]], [[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]).
The distribution $q\delta_{x_0}$ is the fixed-time reading of the stationary point charge of [[def-em-weak-sources]](b) with charge parameter $q$ and constant trajectory $z\equiv x_0$ ([[def-em-electrostatic-regime]](e)); so the pair $(E_q,0)$ satisfies the distributional pure electrostatic equations with that point source.
This is an idealised point-source model: no claim of uniqueness for the point source, no self-force and no statement about the field at $x_0$ itself is made.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron in the laboratory frame. Its boundary $\Gamma=\partial\Omega$ has the outward unit normal $n$ on the relative interior of each planar face; edge and vertex values will be irrelevant under the face-area convention below. Use the SI conventions of this framework. In particular $E$ has units $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$, $H$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-1}}$, $D$ has units $\mathrm{C\,m^{-2}}$, $B$ has units $\mathrm T$, and a volume current density $J$ has units $\mathrm{A\,m^{-2}}$.

For the boundary integrals, let $\mathcal F$ be the finite family of relative interiors of the planar two-dimensional faces of $\Gamma$. Write $\lambda_2$ for Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R^2$, defined as the restriction of Lebesgue outer measure to its Carath\'eodory-measurable sets; under the assumed $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, this is a complete measure. For each face $F\in\mathcal F$, let $P_F$ be its supporting plane and fix a Euclidean isometry $\iota_F:\mathbb R^2\to P_F$. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\Gamma$ (a set in the sigma-algebra generated by the open subsets of $\Gamma$), define $dS_F(A):=\lambda_2\bigl(\iota_F^{-1}(A\cap F)\bigr)$. Any two choices of $\iota_F$ differ by an affine Euclidean isometry of $\mathbb R^2$ with absolute Jacobian determinant $1$, so the Borel change-of-variables formula makes $dS_F$ independent of that choice. Each face is bounded and lies in a finite rectangle in its plane, so $dS_F(F)<\infty$. Set $dS:=\sum_{F\in\mathcal F}dS_F$ on $\Gamma$. The edges and vertices have $dS$-measure zero and are omitted, so $n$ is the outward face normal $dS$-almost everywhere; its values on edges and vertices do not affect any boundary expression. Since $dS$ is finite and Lebesgue measure restricted to $I$ is sigma-finite, $dS\otimes d\lambda_1|_I$ is the unique sigma-finite product measure on $\Gamma\times I$, with rectangle values $dS(A)\lambda_1(J)$ for Borel $A\subseteq\Gamma$ and Lebesgue-measurable $J\subseteq I$. All boundary $L^p(\Gamma)$ and $L^p(\Gamma\times I)$ spaces and almost-everywhere statements use these measures.

Every cross product in the boundary formulas is the right-handed Euclidean cross product in the positively oriented orthonormal frame basis: for $u=(u_1,u_2,u_3)$ and $v=(v_1,v_2,v_3)$, $u\times v=(u_2v_3-u_3v_2,\,u_3v_1-u_1v_3,\,u_1v_2-u_2v_1)$, as in the cross-product definition of this library.

For a real vector field $u\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$, its distributional curl is the distribution defined by

$$\langle\operatorname{curl}u,\varphi\rangle=\int_\Omega u\cdot\operatorname{curl}\varphi\,d\lambda_3,\qquad \varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3).$$

As in the real graph space definition of the imported mathematical library, $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ consists of the $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional curl is represented by an $L^2$ vector field, with norm

$$\|u\|_{H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)}^2=\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2+\|\operatorname{curl}u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as carried by that imported weak-derivative convention. Let $\varepsilon,\mu:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$ be measurable, essentially bounded, real symmetric coefficient fields, independent of time. Require constants $0<a_\varepsilon\le b_\varepsilon<\infty$ and $0<a_\mu\le b_\mu<\infty$ such that, for almost every $x\in\Omega$ and every $v\in\mathbb R^3$,

$$a_\varepsilon |v|^2\le v\cdot\varepsilon(x)v\le b_\varepsilon |v|^2,\qquad a_\mu |v|^2\le v\cdot\mu(x)v\le b_\mu |v|^2.$$

The coefficient units are $\mathrm{F\,m^{-1}}$ and $\mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}$, respectively. They define bounded symmetric multiplication operators on $L^2$. Define $D(t)=\varepsilon E(t)$ and $B(t)=\mu H(t)$. The spatially varying coefficient fields are explicit local model data; they are not inferred from the homogeneous material-closure postulate. Its constant symmetric branch is a special case.

A field $E:I\to L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ is in $C^1(I;L^2)$ when it has a derivative in the $L^2$ norm at every $t\in I$ and that derivative is norm-continuous. $C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$ means norm-continuity into the graph space. A finite-energy model solution is a pair

$$E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)),$$

with $J\in C(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))$, satisfying the adopted evolution equations as $L^2$ identities for each $t\in I$,

$$\varepsilon\,\partial_t E=\operatorname{curl}H-J,\qquad \mu\,\partial_t H=-\operatorname{curl}E.$$

Its stored field energy is the finite real number

$$W(t):=\frac12\int_\Omega\bigl(E(x,t)\cdot\varepsilon(x)E(x,t)+H(x,t)\cdot\mu(x)H(x,t)\bigr)\,d\lambda_3(x).$$

There are two alternative boundary models.

**PEC.** Perfect electric conductor means $E(t)\in H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ for every $t$, where $H_0(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ is exactly the closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb R^3)$ in the displayed graph norm. This closure definition is used; it is not replaced by an unproved identification with every possible trace kernel.

**Impedance.** A Green-compatible tangential boundary pair consists of measurable fields $E_\tau,H_\tau\in L^2(\Gamma\times I;\mathbb R^3)$ with $n\cdot E_\tau=n\cdot H_\tau=0$ almost everywhere and, for almost every $t$,

$$\int_\Omega\bigl(\operatorname{curl}H\cdot E-H\cdot\operatorname{curl}E\bigr)\,d\lambda_3=-\int_\Gamma n\cdot(E_\tau\times H_\tau)\,dS.$$

This Green identity is part of impedance admissibility; membership in $H(\operatorname{curl})$ alone does not assert that such an $L^2$ pair exists. Let $Y\in L^\infty(\Gamma)$ be a time-independent scalar surface admittance, in siemens, with $Y\ge0$ almost everywhere. The impedance law is

$$H_\tau=Y(n\times E_\tau)\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Gamma\times I.$$

Then $Y|E_\tau|^2\in L^1(\Gamma\times I)$ and is the nonnegative outward boundary-power density in $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. No pointwise boundary trace of an arbitrary $H(\operatorname{curl})$ field is asserted.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) as carried by the declared
distributional and surface source objects of [[def-em-weak-sources]]. In the
flat classical laboratory model of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], with the positive
constants and SI conventions of [[def-em-si-conventions]], adopt the following
additional physical assumption for models using the declared point or
stationary-sheet sources: the locally integrable field pair and the
volume-plus-singular source pair of [[def-em-weak-sources]](a)-(d) must satisfy
its solution predicate (e). Explicitly,

$$\operatorname{div}E=\rho/\varepsilon_0,\qquad\operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad\operatorname{curl}B=\mu_0J+c^{-2}\partial_tE$$

are required in $\mathcal D'(U)$, meaning that all four residual pairings
defined there vanish for every compact smooth test. This is a physical adoption
of the classical vacuum idealisation in that source class, not a theorem about
sources and not a consequence of the original locally integrable source branch
of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. When the singular part vanishes, the adopted
identities coincide with that earlier weak branch.

Only source and field tuples satisfying these identities are models of this
postulate; the postulate does not assert existence for every prescribed source
pair, and compatibility conditions remain consequences to be checked. Sources
are the exact point and stationary-sheet types defined earlier, including their
properness or endpoint and tangential-current qualifications. No moving sheet,
line current, magnetic source, product of distributions, self-force,
regularisation, matter dynamics or material constitutive law is introduced.
This postulate reports no experiment or measurement and does not infer
empirical certainty from its mathematical formulation.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the convention of
the surface-measure interface inherited from [[def-em-surface-distribution]]
([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory
region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with the units and constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $\mathcal D'(U)$ be the space of
distributions on $U$ ([[def-distribution]],
[[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]]); recall that the pairing
$\langle T,\psi\rangle$ is bilinear with no conjugation and that the
distributional partial derivatives are
$\langle\partial_\mu T,\psi\rangle=-\langle T,\partial_\mu\psi\rangle$
([[def-distributional-derivative]]).

(a) [Fields as distributions] Locally integrable fields and source densities on
$U$ are identified with their regular distributions
([[def-regular-distribution-from-a-locally-integrable-function]],
[[thm-locally-integrable-functions-embed-in-distributions]]).

(b) [Point sources] Let $I_0\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval,
let $z:I_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be a $C^1$ trajectory whose graph map
$\gamma(t)=(z(t),t)$ is proper into the open set $U$, and let $q\in\mathbb R$
(coulombs). By [[lem-em-point-current-continuity]],

$$\langle\rho_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}\psi(z(t),t)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_{\mathrm{pt}},\psi\rangle:=q\int_{I_0}z'(t)\,\psi(z(t),t)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$ with
$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=0$. If instead
$I_0=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, $z$ extends continuously to $[a,b]$, the
absolute improper integral $\int_a^b|z'(t)|\,dt$ is finite and both endpoint
events lie in $U$, the same formulas define distributions with

$$\partial_t\rho_{\mathrm{pt}}+\operatorname{div}J_{\mathrm{pt}}=q\,\delta_{\gamma(a)}-q\,\delta_{\gamma(b)}$$

([[def-dirac-delta-and-its-derivatives]]); a finite-history point source
therefore contributes an endpoint term unless that term is included
explicitly, and the pairings above exclude it only by the stated properness or
endpoint hypotheses.

(c) [Stationary-sheet sources] Let $S\subset\Omega$ be a fixed compact embedded
$C^2$ hypersurface with a chosen unit normal $n$ pointing from the side
$\Omega_-$ to the side $\Omega_+$ ([[def-em-surface-distribution]],
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]]), and let
$\sigma:S\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $K:S\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous
with $K(x,t)\cdot n(x)=0$ for all $(x,t)$; $\sigma$ carries C m$^{-2}$ and $K$ carries A m$^{-1}$ (a tangential surface current
density; the sheet is stationary). Then

$$\langle\rho_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_S\sigma(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt,\qquad \langle J_S,\psi\rangle:=\int_I\int_SK(x,t)\psi(x,t)\,dS(x)\,dt$$

define distributions on $U$: for $\psi$ with compact support the inner
integrals are continuous in $t$ on a compact parameter interval and the
functionals are bounded by
$(\sup|\sigma\psi|)\,\mathrm{area}(S)\,\mathrm{length}$ of the time projection
of the support, and likewise in the vector case. A normal sheet current (one
with $K\cdot n\ne0$), a line current and a moving sheet are not source types of
this definition.

(d) [Unrestricted weak fields and optional interface branches] The general
field class for the solution predicate (e) consists of all locally integrable
pairs $(E,B)$ on $U$, also when the source has a stationary-sheet part. No
classical one-sided trace or off-sheet $C^1$ regularity is required to define
those four distributional pairings. Additional trace hypotheses are optional
hypotheses of interface and jump results, not admission requirements of the
general weak model.

For a pointwise classical jump branch, one may additionally assume that $E,B$
are $C^1$ off $S\times I$ and, around every $(x_0,t_0)\in S\times I$, each side
is the restriction of a $C^1$ function on an open spacetime neighbourhood of
the corresponding closed side of a smaller stationary graph cylinder. These
joint one-sided extensions make the field traces and first spatial and
temporal derivatives continuous up to that side, locally uniformly on compact
cylinders.

For the broader weak-trace branch, retain spacetime $C^1$ regularity on
$(\Omega\setminus S)\times I$ and assume the original one-sided spatial
$C^1$ extensions at each time, with the explicit additional
conditions that the piecewise first spatial and temporal derivatives are in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(U)$ and the field traces are measurable and locally
integrable on $S\times I$ for $dS\,dt$. This branch supports sheet-distribution
and almost-everywhere jump identities; spatial continuity at each time gives
pointwise spatial identities for almost every time, and joint continuity of
the jump densities gives the further all-time upgrade. Separate spatial $C^1$
traces at each time alone do not imply that joint regularity or upgrade.
Whenever such traces exist, $[F]:=F_+-F_-$ denotes their jump in the chosen
normal convention.

(e) [Weak Maxwell equations with a distributional source pair] Let $E,B$ be a
field pair of class (d), let $\rho=\rho_v+\rho_s$ and $J=J_v+J_s$ be source
distributions on $U$ whose volume parts $\rho_v,J_v$ are locally integrable
volume densities with the charge and current quantity types of
[[def-em-sources]] (the weak predicate requires this stated
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ regularity, not the classical continuous-source
regularity) and whose singular parts $(\rho_s,J_s)$ are point sources as in (b)
or stationary-sheet sources as in (c), and let
$\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ with the constants of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]. Say that $E,B$ satisfy the weak Maxwell equations
with the source pair $(\rho,J)$ when, for every
$\psi\in C_c^\infty(U)$, the four pairings

$$\langle\operatorname{div}E-\rho/\varepsilon_0,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{div}B,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}E+\partial_tB,\psi\rangle,\quad \langle\operatorname{curl}B-\mu_0J-c^{-2}\partial_tE,\psi\rangle$$

all vanish, all derivatives being distributional derivatives of the regular
distributions of the fields and the source pairings being those of (b) and (c).
This clause defines a solution predicate. When the singular parts vanish, its
four identities are the same as the locally integrable weak branch of
[[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]. That earlier postulate explicitly excludes point
and sheet distributions and does not imply their physical adoption here;
adoption for the declared singular-source models is made separately, after
this definition. No physical field equation is deduced merely from defining
this predicate.

(f) [Scope] No product of two distributions is formed anywhere: the fields
occur only through their distributional derivatives paired with a test
function, and the source densities $\sigma,K$ occur only inside the ordinary
surface and time integrals of (b) and (c); products such as $\rho_sE$ or
$J_s\times B$ are not defined by this item. The definition asserts no existence
theorem for fields with singular sources, no conservation law (continuity for
these sources is proved separately where used) and no regularisation. Sources
that are not locally integrable and are not point or stationary-sheet sources,
moving sheets, line currents, and arbitrary products of distributions are
outside the definition.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
charge density $\rho$ of the framework's source definition carries C m$^{-3}$
and the current density $J$ carries A m$^{-2}$, so that the four-current
components $(c\rho,J)$ carry A m$^{-2}$; the electric field $E$ carries
V m$^{-1}$; the magnetic field $B$ carries the tesla (T), where
$1\ \mathrm{T}=1\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-1}\,m^{-1}}$; the scalar potential $\varphi$
carries V and the vector potential $A$ carries T m, so that the four-potential
components $(\varphi/c,A)$ carry T m; the components of the electromagnetic
two-form of the framework's tensor definition carry T; a force carries the
newton (N), $1\ \mathrm{N}=1\ \mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-2}}$.

(c) [Mechanical quantities] A rest mass parameter $m$ carries the kilogram
(kg) and a four-momentum $P=mU$ of the relativistic particle model carries
kg m s$^{-1}$; field energy density carries J m$^{-3}$, energy flux
W m$^{-2}$, so that $1\ \mathrm{W}=1\ \mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}=1\ \mathrm{V\,A}$.

(d) [Bookkeeping only] The unit of a quantity records the adopted system of
units; it does not show that a quantity is primitive in this or any other
framework, it contains no measurement, and it does not identify a quantity
with a similarly named quantity of another framework. The exact defining
values of $c$ and $e$ fix numerical conventions of the SI; they do not by
themselves identify $c$ with the vacuum propagation constant of ideal light,
which is the physical adoption of the framework's Minkowski postulate.

derivations.claim: Set $E(x,t)=E_q(x)$ time-independently and put $B=0$, $J=0$. The field convention is [F5], and by [F4] the source is $\rho=q\delta_{x_0}$; [F1] gives local integrability, $\operatorname{div}E_q=(q/\varepsilon_0)\delta_{x_0}$, and $\operatorname{curl}E_q=0$. Since $\partial_tE=\partial_tB=0$, the other three equations listed in [A1] hold with both sides zero. This is a distributional vacuum Maxwell solution with the stated stationary point source.

The shell in [F2] with outer radius $R/2$ lies inside $B_R(x_0)$. Nonnegativity of $|E_q|^2$ gives $ \frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\int_{B_R(x_0)}|E_q|^2\,d\lambda_3\ \ge\ \frac{q^2}{8\pi\varepsilon_0}\left(\frac1\delta-\frac2R\right) $ for every $0<\delta<R/2$. This lower bound is unbounded as $\delta\downarrow0$ because $q^2/\varepsilon_0>0$; thus each ball around $x_0$ has infinite ordinary electric energy and $u_E\notin L^1$ near the charge.

By [F3], a field with nonintegrable ordinary quadratic energy is outside the finite-energy boundary model, even though step 1.1 supplies its distributional Maxwell identities. This contradicts the refuted claim and proves the counterexample.

Work in a material rest frame: an inertial frame in whose coordinates each modelled material element has fixed spatial position $x$ and history $t\mapsto(ct,x)$, as defined by the framework's earlier material-closure formulation. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be the material region in that frame and $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ a nonempty open time interval. The electric field $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization fields $P_\ell:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and magnetic fields $B,H:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial-vector fields in that frame. At every fixed $x\in\Omega$, require $E(x,\cdot)\in C^0(I;\mathbb R^3)$ and $P_\ell(x,\cdot)\in C^2(I;\mathbb R^3)$ for each $1\le\ell\le N$, so the displayed time derivatives are classical. These are time-regularity conditions only; this postulate imposes no spatial regularity, which must be stated separately wherever a consuming field-equation result requires it. In SI, $E$ is in V m$^{-1}$, $P_\ell$ in C m$^{-2}$, $B$ in T and $H$ in A m$^{-1}$.

For a fixed finite integer $N\ge1$, adopt at every material point $x$ the constitutive equations

$$D(x,t)=\varepsilon_\infty E(x,t)+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell(x,t),\qquad B(x,t)=\mu H(x,t),$$

$$\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,t)+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell(x,t)=a_\ell E(x,t)\qquad (1\le\ell\le N).$$

Here $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ is a constant scalar with units F m$^{-1}$, $\mu>0$ is a constant scalar with units H m$^{-1}$, $a_\ell>0$ are constant parameters with units F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ are constant angular frequencies with units s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ are constant damping rates with units s$^{-1}$. The parameters are independent of position and time; this is the meaning of homogeneous in this model. The model is linear because all displayed field and oscillator relations are linear with fixed coefficients, and spatially local because the oscillator equation at $x$ uses only the field and oscillator state at that same $x$. The magnetic law has only the constant scalar coefficient $\mu$ and no independent magnetic polarization variable; this is the nonmagnetic oscillator model adopted here.

The word nonmagnetic here means that the oscillator sector has no dynamic magnetic response; the fixed scalar coefficient $\mu$ can still encode a separate static constitutive response. To identify the displayed quantities with the framework's macroscopic definitions, stipulate $P_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\varepsilon_\infty-\varepsilon_0)E+\sum_{\ell=1}^N P_\ell$ and $M_{\mathrm{tot}}=(\mu_0^{-1}-\mu^{-1})B$. Then $D=\varepsilon_0E+P_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum P_\ell$ and $H=\mu_0^{-1}B-M_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mu^{-1}B$. This is a constitutive identification in the model, not a microscopic decomposition.

At an initial time $t_0\in I$, the oscillator state consists of $P_\ell(x,t_0)$ and $\partial_tP_\ell(x,t_0)$. For a selected causal zero-past branch, choose an onset $\tau\in I$ and require $E(x,t)=0$ and $P_\ell(x,t)=\partial_tP_\ell(x,t)=0$ for every $t\in I$ with $t\le\tau$. Continuity gives $E(x,\tau)=0$, and the equation gives $\partial_t^2P_\ell(x,\tau)=0$, consistent with the $C^2$ zero extension through onset. For $t\ge\tau$ this branch is the retarded initial-value equation with those data, so its value at time $t$ uses the applied field only on $[\tau,t]$. If $\gamma_\ell=0$, no decaying stationary impulse response is assumed; in particular, this is not an absolutely integrable convolution for arbitrary bounded histories. This postulate does not assert that any actual material realizes the equations.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a nonempty bounded Lipschitz polyhedron in one material rest frame. Use real SI fields: $E,H,D,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, a free current density $J_f:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, polarization $P:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$, and, when present, carrier current $V:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$. Their units are V m$^{-1}$, A m$^{-1}$, C m$^{-2}$, T, A m$^{-2}$, C m$^{-2}$ and A m$^{-2}$, respectively. Let $\varepsilon_\infty>0$ and $\mu>0$ be constant scalar coefficients in F m$^{-1}$ and H m$^{-1}$. Each $u_L,u_D$ is in J m$^{-3}$ and the flux $E\times H$ is in W m$^{-2}$.

Assume Countable Choice, the smooth macroscopic Maxwell material model, and its curl equations

$$\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB,\qquad \operatorname{curl}H=J_f+\partial_tD$$

hold pointwise. The smooth macroscopic material model includes continuous free sources and the total polarization/magnetization identifications specified by the Lorentz or Drude closure. Assume $E,H$ are jointly $C^\infty$ pointwise and satisfy $E,H\in C^1(I;L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R^3))\cap C(I;H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega))$; $J_f$ and each material-current term belong to $C(I;L^2)$. Here $H(\operatorname{curl};\Omega)$ is the real $L^2$ vector fields whose distributional curl is represented by an $L^2$ vector field, with the graph norm. Take Lorentz fields $P_\ell$ jointly $C^\infty$ and in $C^2(I;L^2)$, or Drude fields $P,V$ jointly $C^\infty$ with $V\in C^1(I;L^2)$, so that the stored energies and current terms are finite. Take either one of the following constitutive branches:

1. **Finite Lorentz branch.** For some finite $N\ge1$, $D=\varepsilon_\infty E+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}P_\ell$, $B=\mu H$, and
   $$\partial_t^2P_\ell+\gamma_\ell\partial_tP_\ell+\omega_\ell^2P_\ell=a_\ell E,$$
   where $P_\ell$ is jointly $C^2$, $a_\ell>0$ in F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, $\omega_\ell>0$ in s$^{-1}$, and $\gamma_\ell\ge0$ in s$^{-1}$.
2. **Drude branch.** $D=\varepsilon_\infty E+P$, $B=\mu H$, $\partial_tP=V$, and $\partial_tV+\gamma V=aE$, where $P,V$ are jointly $C^1$, $a>0$ in F m$^{-1}$ s$^{-2}$, and $\gamma\ge0$ in s$^{-1}$.

For the Lorentz branch define

$$u_L:=\frac{\varepsilon_\infty|E|^2+\mu|H|^2}{2}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\frac{|\partial_tP_\ell|^2+\omega_\ell^2|P_\ell|^2}{2a_\ell}.$$

For the Drude branch define

$$u_D:=\frac{\varepsilon_\infty|E|^2+\mu|H|^2}{2}+\frac{|V|^2}{2a}.$$

The Lorentz density is positive definite in $(E,H,(P_\ell,\partial_tP_\ell)_{\ell=1}^N)$. The Drude density is positive definite in $(E,H,V)$; a constant polarization offset is not part of this energy.

Then the respective local identities hold pointwise:

$$\partial_tu_L+\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=-E\cdot J_f-\sum_{\ell=1}^{N}\frac{\gamma_\ell}{a_\ell}|\partial_tP_\ell|^2,$$

$$\partial_tu_D+\operatorname{div}(E\times H)=-E\cdot J_f-\frac{\gamma}{a}|V|^2.$$

If, in addition, the fields satisfy the exact closure-defined PEC branch of the finite-energy boundary model and $J_f=0$, then the total stored energy $U(t)=\int_\Omega u_L(x,t)\,dx$ or $U(t)=\int_\Omega u_D(x,t)\,dx$ is nonnegative and nonincreasing. More generally the corresponding fixed-volume balance includes the work $-\int E\cdot J_f$ and the displayed nonnegative material-loss terms; no claim of conservation without these terms is made.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ (The natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ (von Neumann),
On $\mathbb{N}$ the order is membership: $m < n \iff m \in n$), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of The vector space $F^{X}$ of all functions $X \to F$ with pointwise operations, and $F^{n}$ as the case $X = n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
(Vector space over a field). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4 and
Squares of nonzero elements are positive, the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
Integer powers $a^m$) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root (Square roots exist: a unique $\sqrt{a} \ge 0$ with $(\sqrt{a})^2 = a$; the positives are $\{x^2 : x \neq 0\}$).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space (The standard list $e : n \to F^{n}$ with $e_i(i) = 1_F$ and $e_i(j) = 0_F$ for $j \ne i$ is an ordered basis of $F^{n}$; hence $\dim_F F^{n} = n$, and $F^{0}$ is the zero space with basis $\varnothing$ and dimension $0$ clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
$\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and Conventions of this page, the standing $n \ge 1$ hypothesis, and what is taken up elsewhere in the reading order lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ (Laws of finite sums and finite products clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   (Squares of nonzero elements are positive), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of A norm on a real vector space, the induced metric, and the dictionary with the metric axioms
is proved in Cauchy-Schwarz $\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \le \lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2$ with its equality case, the triangle inequality for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$, the parallelogram law and polarisation, where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $a,c,\mu_0>0$, let $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, and let $\rho:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ and $J:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be jointly $C^\infty$. Suppose $\rho(y,t)=J(y,t)=0$ whenever $|y|>a$ and suppose the continuity equation $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_yJ=0$ holds everywhere.

Adopt the smooth vacuum Maxwell equations and the retarded, no-free-addition selection as the physical model assumptions. In the SI laboratory convention, define

$$\varphi(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0c^2}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\rho(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy,\qquad A(x,t):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{J(y,t-|x-y|/c)}{|x-y|}\,dy.$$

The integrals converge absolutely at every $(x,t)$. The resulting potentials are jointly $C^\infty$ and satisfy $W\varphi=\rho/\varepsilon_0$, $WA=\mu_0J$, and $\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ on $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, where $W=c^{-2}\partial_t^2-\Delta$. Consequently $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ are jointly smooth and satisfy the smooth vacuum Maxwell equations for $(\rho,J)$ everywhere. This is the selected retarded solution, with no independent homogeneous field added. No compact support in time is assumed.

Assume Countable Choice. Use the SI laboratory chart and source conventions: $\rho:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ has units $\mathrm C\,\mathrm m^{-3}$ and $J:\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ has units $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{-2}$. Let $a,c,\mu_0>0$, $\varepsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$, and let $\rho,J$ be jointly $C^\infty$, vanish for $|y|>a$, and satisfy $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}_yJ=0$. Let $K=[u_-,u_+]\subset\mathbb R$ be a nondegenerate compact interval, $u_-<u_+$, and put $K^\sharp=[u_--2a/c,u_++2a/c]$. For $j=0,1,2$, define

$$M_{\rho,j}:=\sup_{\overline B_a\times K^\sharp}|\partial_t^j\rho|,\qquad M_{J,j}:=\sup_{\overline B_a\times K^\sharp}|\partial_t^jJ|.$$

For $n\in S^2$ and $u\in K$, define the retarded current moment and its derivative by

$$I(n,u):=\int_{B_a}J(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy,\qquad V(n,u):=\partial_u I(n,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+n\cdot y/c)\,dy.$$

Let $E,B$ be the selected retarded fields of the preceding theorem, set $S=E\times B/\mu_0$, and define

$$\Gamma_E:=\frac{\mu_0\lambda_3(B_a)}{4\pi}\left(4c^2M_{\rho,0}+13caM_{\rho,1}+a^2M_{\rho,2}+3aM_{J,1}+\frac{a^2}{c}M_{J,2}\right),$$

$$\Gamma_B:=\frac{\mu_0\lambda_3(B_a)}{4\pi}\left(4M_{J,0}+\frac{13a}{c}M_{J,1}+\frac{a^2}{c^2}M_{J,2}\right).$$

Then for every $n\in S^2$, $u\in K$ and $r\ge2a$, with $E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r):=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi r}n\times(n\times V(n,u))$,

$$\left|E(rn,u+r/c)-E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)\right|\le\frac{\Gamma_E}{r^2},\qquad \left|B(rn,u+r/c)-\frac{n\times E_{\mathrm{lead}}(n,u,r)}{c}\right|\le\frac{\Gamma_B}{r^2}.$$

Consequently the radiation data of the preceding definition exist uniformly on $S^2\times K$ and equal

$$E_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)=\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}n\times(n\times V(n,u)),\qquad B_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)=\frac{n\times E_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)}{c}.$$

For each fixed retarded time $u$, the outward retarded-time flux has the exact limit

$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S^2}r^2n\cdot S(rn,u+r/c)\,d\Omega(n)=\frac{\mu_0}{16\pi^2c}\int_{S^2}|n\times V(n,u)|^2\,d\Omega(n).$$

Let the laboratory frame and SI conventions be those of the framework, and let $\rho,J$ be a jointly smooth conserved volume source supported in $\overline B_a(0)$ in space at every time, for some $a>0$. Let $E,B$ be the retarded fields generated by that source. Write $S^2=\{n\in\mathbb R^3:|n|=1\}$, $r=|x|$, and $t=u+r/c$. If maps $E_{\mathrm{rad}},B_{\mathrm{rad}}:S^2\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ satisfy

$$rE(rn,u+r/c)\longrightarrow E_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u),\qquad rB(rn,u+r/c)\longrightarrow B_{\mathrm{rad}}(n,u)$$

uniformly in $n\in S^2$ and $u$ in every compact interval as $r\to\infty$, then $E_{\mathrm{rad}}$ and $B_{\mathrm{rad}}$ are the electric and magnetic radiation data at fixed retarded time. The scaled fields carry units $\mathrm V$ and $\mathrm T\,\mathrm m$, respectively. This definition by itself does not assert that the limits exist.
If $f$ is $C^2$ on an open subset of $\mathbb R^m$, then $\partial_i\partial_j f=\partial_j\partial_i f$ for every pair of coordinate indices.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

derivations.claim: By [F1] choose $f\in C_c^\infty(B_a(0))$ with $0\le f\le1$ and $f=1$ on some ball $B_{r_0}(0)$ with $0<r_0<a$. Then $F:=\int f\,dy\ge\lambda_3(B_{r_0})>0$ by [F3]. Choose $G$ by applying the smooth cutoff supplier to a compact interval slightly larger than $[u-a/c,u+a/c]$ and multiply that cutoff by $(t-u)^2$. The resulting $G$ is compactly supported, equals $(t-u)^2$ on a neighborhood of the delay interval, and satisfies $G''(u)=2$.

The maps $\rho,J$ in the Example are jointly smooth and compactly supported in $B_a$ in space and in $\operatorname{supp}G\cup\operatorname{supp}G'$ in time. Their derivatives obey $\rho_t=-G'\partial_3f$ and $\operatorname{div}J=G'\partial_3f$, so $\rho_t+\operatorname{div}J=0$. Thus the retarded-history theorem applies.

For $n=e_1$, every source point in $B_a$ has $|y_1|<a$, so $G''(u+y_1/c)=2$. The shifted-current moment of [F2] is therefore $\displaystyle V(e_1,u)=\int_{B_a}J_t(y,u+y_1/c)\,dy=G''(u)\left(\int_{B_a}f(y)\,dy\right)e_3=2F e_3.$ Since $e_1\cdot e_3=0$, $e_1\times(e_1\times V(e_1,u))=-2F e_3\ne0$. The radiation-data formula [F2] now gives $\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{rad}}(e_1,u)=-\frac{\mu_0F}{2\pi}e_3\ne0,$ so $rE(re_1,u+r/c)$ converges to a nonzero vector.

Let $t_f\in\mathbb R$ be a fixed observation time and choose $t_-<\inf(\operatorname{supp}G\cup\operatorname{supp}G')$. For $y\in B_a$ and $x=rn$, $|x-y|\ge r-a$, so the source retarded time satisfies $t_f-|x-y|/c\le t_f-(r-a)/c$. If $r>a+c(t_f-t_-)$, this is less than $t_-$ for every $y\in B_a$, with a uniform strict margin. The source and all its derivatives vanish on a time neighborhood of every such argument; because the inequalities remain strict on a neighborhood of $(x,t_f)$, the retarded potentials are identically zero there and their derivatives vanish. Hence $E(rn,t_f)=B(rn,t_f)=0$ for all such $r$. This fixed-time limit and the nonzero scaled retarded-time limit of step 3.1 are different paths to infinity, not contradictory field values.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 proves F>0, so the constructed pulse is nonzero; zero source would not satisfy the conclusion.
Step 3.1 proves a nonzero radiation limit; the example excludes zero radiative amplitude.
Step 3.1 uses the unit direction n=e1.

Example and steps 1.1 and 3.1: a,c>0, the bump integral F>0 and G is quadratic throughout the closed delay window. Thus the selected radiation moment is 2F e3, nonzero; no nondegenerate K assumption is imposed.
Step 1.1 makes G quadratic throughout the closed delay interval, including endpoints.

citations.quote:
Fix an integer $n\ge1$. With the complex smooth-function convention of [[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]] and multi-indices of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], define
$$p_{\alpha\beta}(f)=\sup_{x\in\mathbb R^n}|x^\alpha\partial^\beta f(x)|,\qquad \mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)=\{f\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C):p_{\alpha\beta}(f)<\infty\text{ for all }\alpha,\beta\}.$$
The zero multi-index gives $x^0=1$ and $\partial^0f=f$. These are actual smooth functions, not equivalence classes. The notation $C_c^\infty$ uses the support convention in [[def-c-c-and-c-c-infinity-on-rn]].

Pointwise differentiation is linear; thus $p_{\alpha\beta}(f+g)\le p_{\alpha\beta}(f)+p_{\alpha\beta}(g)$ and $p_{\alpha\beta}(cf)=|c|p_{\alpha\beta}(f)$. In particular this set is a complex vector space and each $p_{\alpha\beta}$ is a seminorm. The zero function belongs to it. Since $p_{00}(f)=0$ forces $f(x)=0$ for every $x$, the family separates functions. No choice principle is needed.

Let $c>0$, let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] with its restricted inertial chart, let fields and units be those of [[def-em-fields]] and [[def-em-si-conventions]], and let the scalar-vector potential vocabulary on that region be that of [[def-em-potential-gauge-and-field-conventions]]: a **potential pair** $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ consists of $\varphi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $A:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^k$ jointly in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], and for a non-open time interval $I$ the joint classes in this item are read in the open-neighbourhood restriction convention of [[lem-em-joint-smooth-potentials]] (for open $I$ this is the ordinary class of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); for $k\ge1$ the **field pair** is

$$E(\varphi,A):=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA,\qquad B(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{curl}A,$$

where $\nabla$ is the gradient, $\operatorname{div}$ and $\operatorname{curl}$ are those of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]], and $\partial_t$ is the partial derivative at fixed position of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. For $k\ge1$ the **Lorenz divergence** of the pair is $G(\varphi,A):=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi$. The definitions in this item are stated on the laboratory region; the framework's fields are those of [[def-em-fields]]. No field equation is required to define the vocabulary; the existence theorem recalled in (a) has the additional hypotheses stated there.

(a) [Representations] Let $k\ge2$ be an integer and let $(E,B)$ be a field pair of class $C^{k-1}$ on $\Omega\times I$, meaning $E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of class $C^{k-1}$ jointly as in [[def-em-fields]]. A **potential representation of class $C^k$** of $(E,B)$ is a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^k$ on $\Omega\times I$ whose field pair is $(E,B)$, that is, $E=-\nabla\varphi-\partial_tA$ and $B=\operatorname{curl}A$ on $\Omega\times I$. More generally, a potential pair of class $C^1$ represents a specified field pair whenever these two identities hold, even if the fields have greater regularity than the defining derivatives alone guarantee. This definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. When $\Omega$ is open and star-shaped, $I$ is an interval with at least two elements, and the jointly $C^r$ field data, $r\ge2$, satisfy $\operatorname{div}B=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}E=-\partial_tB$ pointwise on $\Omega\times I$, [[pthm-em-spacetime-potentials]] supplies $\varphi\in C^{r-1}$ and $A\in C^r$ in the stated restriction convention, and smooth potentials for smooth data satisfying the same equations; it does not assert a $C^r$ scalar potential for merely $C^r$ data. Equality of field pairs does not by itself assert gauge relatedness on an arbitrary region; a converse needs its own domain and regularity hypotheses.

(b) [Gauge functions and gauge equivalence] A **gauge function** of class $C^m$, $m\ge2$, on $\Omega\times I$ is a function $\chi:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ of class $C^m$ jointly; its **gauge transformation** sends a potential pair $(\varphi,A)$ of class $C^m$ to

$$T_\chi(\varphi,A):=(\varphi-\partial_t\chi,\ A+\nabla\chi),$$

a potential pair of class $C^{m-1}$. Two potential pairs are **gauge related** when one is the gauge transform of the other by some gauge function. On pairs and generators of class $C^\infty$, $T_0$ is the identity and $T_{\chi_1}\bigl(T_{\chi_2}(\varphi,A)\bigr)=T_{\chi_1+\chi_2}(\varphi,A)$ for all $C^\infty$ generators $\chi_1,\chi_2$; hence gauge relatedness is an equivalence relation on the $C^\infty$ potential pairs, the inverse of $T_\chi$ being $T_{-\chi}$. For a fixed finite class the transform drops one order, and relatedness is used only through the transform it records.

(c) [Conditions] A potential pair is **in Lorenz gauge** on $\Omega\times I$ when $G(\varphi,A)=\operatorname{div}A+c^{-2}\partial_t\varphi=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$, and **in Coulomb gauge** in the chosen spatial chart when $\operatorname{div}A=0$ throughout $\Omega\times I$. These are properties of a pair in the stated conventions. The existence of a gauge function achieving either condition, with or without prescribed initial or boundary data, is a separate PDE conclusion with its own hypotheses and is not asserted by this definition.

(d) [Physical status] The physical content of a representation is its field pair $(E,B)$ of [[def-em-fields]]; the values of $\varphi$, of $A$ and of any gauge function are convention dependent and are auxiliary, and gauge related representations have the same field pair. The scalar potential $\varphi$ carries the volt, the vector potential $A$ carries the tesla metre, and a gauge function carries V s $=$ T m$^2$, so its time derivative and gradient have the units of $\varphi$ and $A$, respectively, consistently with [[def-em-si-conventions]]. No value of $\varphi$ or $A$ is by itself an observable or evidence for a field.

Fix a vector $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, a parameter $\omega>0$ and amplitudes $\mathbf e,\mathbf b\in\mathbb C^3$. Here $\mathbb C^3$ is the set of functions $\{0,1,2\}\to\mathbb C$ under componentwise operations, the complex analogue of the convention for $\mathbb R^n$ in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; we relabel the function values at $0,1,2$ by $1,2,3$ and write the coordinates of $\mathbf e$ as $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ and those of $\mathbf b$ as $(b_1,b_2,b_3)$. For $\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$, $\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle$ is the Euclidean inner product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], the real number $\sum_{j=1}^3k_jx_j$; for $t\in\mathbb R$ put

$$\theta(\mathbf x,t):=\langle\mathbf k,\mathbf x\rangle-\omega t\in\mathbb R .$$

Let $\exp$ be the complex exponential of [[def-complex-exponential]] (the power series $\sum_{n\ge0}z^n/n!$, convergent for every $z\in\mathbb C$), let $\operatorname{Re}$ be the real part of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]], and let $i$ be the imaginary unit of [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]].

For each $t\in\mathbb R$ define maps $\mathbf E(\cdot,t),\mathbf B(\cdot,t):\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ componentwise by

$$E_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(e_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad B_j(\mathbf x,t):=\operatorname{Re}\bigl(b_j\exp\bigl(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)\bigr)\bigr),\qquad j\in\{1,2,3\}.$$

Equivalently, $\mathbf E(\cdot,t)$ is the real part, taken componentwise, of the complex vector $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$, and likewise for $\mathbf B(\cdot,t)$ with $\mathbf b$ in place of $\mathbf e$.

### Well-definedness and conventions

For every $(\mathbf x,t)\in\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$ the number $\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is real, so $i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t)$ is a complex number and $\exp(i\,\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is defined by the everywhere-convergent exponential series; multiplying by the complex number $e_j$ or $b_j$ and taking real parts is likewise defined. Both amplitudes may be zero, in which case the corresponding field vanishes identically. The joint map $(\mathbf x,t)\mapsto(\mathbf E(\mathbf x,t),\mathbf B(\mathbf x,t))$ has $\mathbb R^3\times\mathbb R$, an open subset of $\mathbb R^4$, as its domain, so the $C^k$ conventions of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]] apply to any regularity statement made about it; this definition asserts no regularity of its own beyond well-definedness. The exponential is entire with $\exp'=\exp$ ([[thm-complex-exponential-is-entire-with-derivative-itself]]), which is what makes the encoded expressions differentiable in the plane-wave form; derivations that differentiate them use [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]] and the chain rule for holomorphic maps where they are applied.

Complex notation here is an encoding of real fields and of real linear equations, not a complex physical field. The symbols $\mathbf e$ and $\mathbf b$ are constant complex amplitudes, not fields; the complex quantity $\mathbf e\exp(i\theta(\mathbf x,t))$ is an auxiliary object whose real part is the field. Real parts, imaginary parts and complex conjugation are the explicit operations of [[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]. Since $\operatorname{Re}$ is additive and commutes with real scalar multiples, any identity obtained from the encoded expressions by sums, real scalar multiples, partial differentiation or integration may be projected by $\operatorname{Re}$ term by term; identities that multiply two encoded real fields may not be read off from a product of complex expressions without conjugation, and the correct second-order average rule is proved separately. No electromagnetic interpretation, equation of motion or physical identification is part of this definition.

Every $z\in\mathbb C$ has unique coordinates $z=a+bi$
([[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]]). Define
$$\operatorname{Re}z=a,\qquad \operatorname{Im}z=b,\qquad \overline z=a-bi,$$
and define its **modulus** by
$$|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}.$$
The real numbers are least-upper-bound complete
([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]), so the nonnegative square root exists and
is unique by [[thm-of-square-roots]].

$\mathbb C=\mathbb R[x]/(x^2+1)$ is a field containing the embedded copy of
$\mathbb R$. Every complex number has a unique form $a+bi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb R$,
and
$$ (a+bi)+(u+vi)=(a+u)+(b+v)i, $$
$$ (a+bi)(u+vi)=(au-bv)+(av+bu)i. $$
If $a+bi\ne0$, then
$$ (a+bi)^{-1}=\frac{a-bi}{a^2+b^2}. $$

The complex exponential is entire, and

$$ \exp'(z)=\exp z $$

for every $z\in\mathbb C$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb C$ be open, let $a\in U$, and write $f=u+iv:U\to\mathbb C$. The following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is complex differentiable at $a$.
2. Under $\mathbb C\cong\mathbb R^2$, the map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $Df(a)$ is multiplication by a complex number.
3. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f(a)=0$.
4. The map $f$ is real totally differentiable at $a$ and satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations

$$ u_x(a)=v_y(a),\qquad u_y(a)=-v_x(a). $$

When these conditions hold,

$$ f'(a)=u_x(a)+iv_x(a)=v_y(a)-iu_y(a)=\partial_zf(a). $$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $U\cong I\times\Omega$ be the laboratory region of [[def-em-lab-geometry]], so
that $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nonempty open interval, $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$
is nonempty open, $x=(x^1,x^2,x^3)$ is the position in the spatial chart,
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the frame basis of the spatial slice, and the spatial inner
product is the Euclidean form $\delta$; let the units and the constants $c>0$,
$\mu_0>0$ and $\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$ be those of
[[def-em-si-conventions]]; let $k\ge1$, and let
$E,B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ be an electric and a magnetic field of class
$C^k$ of [[def-em-fields]]. Write $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ and $|\cdot|$ for
the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
$\times$ for the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]].

(a) [Energy density and flux] The **electromagnetic energy density**
$u:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R$ and the **energy flux density** (the **Poynting
vector**) $S:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ are defined by

$$u(x,t):=\frac{\varepsilon_0}{2}\,\langle E(x,t),E(x,t)\rangle+\frac{1}{2\mu_0}\,\langle B(x,t),B(x,t)\rangle,\qquad S(x,t):=\frac{1}{\mu_0}\,E(x,t)\times B(x,t).$$

At fixed $t\in I$ the map $u(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R$ is a real-valued
function on $\Omega$ and $S(\cdot,t):\Omega\to\mathbb R^3$ is a spatial vector
field on $\Omega$, read in the basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$. The energy density
carries $\mathrm J\,\mathrm m^{-3}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{-1}\mathrm s^{-2}$ and
the energy flux density carries $\mathrm W\,\mathrm m^{-2}=\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm s^{-3}$.

(b) [Regularity] If $E,B$ are of class $C^k$, then $u$ and $S$ are of class
$C^k$: they are the components of a polynomial expression in the components of
$E,B$, and the verification below exhibits the composite map. In particular $u$
and $S$ are continuous, and the definitions use no derivative of the fields.

(c) [Pointwise reading, quadratic character] The definitions use only the values
of $E$ and $B$ at the same point $(x,t)$, and they are quadratic in the fields:
for every real $\lambda$ one has $u(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2u(E,B)$ and
$S(\lambda E,\lambda B)=\lambda^2S(E,B)$, and $u\ge0$. Consequently
decompositions of the fields do not make $u$ or $S$ additive; cross terms
generally contribute. No convention beyond the fixed laboratory frame enters
the definitions.

(d) [Products and singular support] If $E,B$ are only locally integrable (the
weak branch of [[post-em-vacuum-maxwell]]), the products $E_iE_j$, $B_iB_j$ and
the components of $E\times B$ need not be locally integrable, and no product of
distributions is defined. The displayed formulas then define $u$ and $S$
pointwise almost everywhere, and the framework uses them only where the local
integrability of the products, respectively of the component being integrated,
is separately established. No value of $u$ or $S$ is assigned at a point of
singular source support.

(e) [Status] This item defines quantities only. The interpretation of $u$ as an
energy density and of $S$ as an energy flux density, and every balance identity
involving them, is the content of [[pthm-em-poynting-balance]] and of the other
balance items of this page; no identification of $(u,S)$ with components of a
covariant tensor is made here, and the relation $S=c^2g$ to the momentum density
$g$ of [[def-em-vacuum-stress-momentum]] is a consequence of those definitions,
not an identification made at this point.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

Let $(A,V,\eta,C^+)$ be an oriented time-oriented affine Minkowski space
([[def-sr-affine-minkowski-model]]), let $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ be an inertial
frame with inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$
([[def-inertial-frame-and-inertial-chart]]), let $c>0$ be the framework's
conversion constant, and let $\delta$ be the Euclidean spatial form of that
frame on $n^\perp$, $n:=e_0$, with norm $|\cdot|$ and positive spatial
orientation ([[def-spatial-euclidean-structure-of-an-inertial-frame]]). Fix a
nonempty open interval $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ ([[def-interval]]) and a nonempty
open set $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$, and put

$$U:=\{p\in A:\ \text{there are }t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\text{ with }x^0(p)=ct,\ (x^1,x^2,x^3)(p)=y\}.$$

Then:

(a) [Chart restriction] $x(U)=\{(ct,y):t\in I,\ y\in\Omega\}$ and
$\Phi:U\to I\times\Omega$, $\Phi(p):=(x^0(p)/c,(x^1,x^2,x^3)(p))$, is a
bijection, because the inertial chart $x:A\to\mathbb R^4$ is a bijection and
$c>0$; its components are the **laboratory time coordinate**
$t(p):=x^0(p)/c$ and the **laboratory position**
$r(p):=(x^1(p),x^2(p),x^3(p))$. In the chart coordinates the pair
$(t(p),r(p))$ is the reading of the laboratory decomposition of $p$. Writing
$r(p)=(r^1(p),r^2(p),r^3(p))\in\mathbb R^3$, the standard basis of
$\mathbb R^3$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) labels the three coordinate
directions, and the identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ is the linear
map $\sum_{i=1}^3 r^i e_i$ into the three-dimensional real vector space
$n^\perp$ ([[def-vector-space]], [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

(b) [Slices and spatial structure] For each $t\in I$ the slice
$U_t:=\{p\in U:t(p)=t\}$ is carried bijectively onto $\Omega$ by $r$; the
constant vector $n=e_0$ is future unit timelike, and $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ is the
$\delta$-orthonormal positively oriented basis of $n^\perp$ in which the
coordinates of $r$ are expressed.

(c) [Laboratory fields] For a nonnegative integer $m$, a **laboratory field of rank $m$** is a map
$F:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^m$; it is identified with the map $U\to\mathbb R^m$,
$p\mapsto F(r(p),t(p))$, and with the family $(F(\cdot,t))_{t\in I}$ of maps
$\Omega\to\mathbb R^m$, its values at fixed time. Such a field is of class
$C^k$, for $m\ge1$, when the map $(y,t)\mapsto F(y,t)$ is $C^k$ in the sense of
[[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]. For $m=0$, set $\mathbb R^0:=\{()\}$;
the unique field into this singleton is declared $C^\infty$ (and $C^k$ for every
finite $k$), and each of its partial derivatives is the same singleton-valued
zero map. For $m\ge1$ and $k\ge1$, $\partial_{y_i}F$ (at fixed
$t$) and $\partial_tF$ (at fixed $y$) are the partial derivatives of
[[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. No regularity of a field is
asserted beyond the class stated for it.

(d) [Conventions] The product decomposition is a coordinate identification
inside the single inertial frame $(o;e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$; it is not a Galilean
transformation, it does not compare two inertial frames, and it does not
assert absolute simultaneity. The objects $I,\Omega,t,r,\delta$ and the
identification $\mathbb R^3\cong n^\perp$ belong to the named frame; changes
of inertial description are the proper orthochronous maps adopted in
[[post-sr-inertial-covariance]]. The frame is an origin together with an
ordered basis; it is not a congruence of observers, and no moving observer
field is defined here.

Let the laboratory region $U\cong I\times\Omega$, its spatial Euclidean structure
and its units be those of [[def-em-lab-geometry]] and
[[def-em-si-conventions]], and let $k\ge1$. An **electric field of class
$C^k$** on the region is a map $E:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ that is of class
$C^k$ in the sense of [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]; a
**magnetic field of class $C^k$** is a map $B:\Omega\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ of
the same class. At fixed $t\in I$ the maps $E(\cdot,t),B(\cdot,t):\Omega\to
\mathbb R^3$ are real spatial vector fields on the region $\Omega$, read in the
$\delta$-orthonormal basis $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of the frame. The framework uses:
$C^1$ fields in the classical Maxwell branch, $C^2$ fields where second or
mixed time-space derivatives of the fields appear, and $C^\infty$ fields in
the smooth existence branches; every statement carries its own regularity and
no regularity beyond it is asserted.

Conventions:

(a) The **polar-vector** and **axial-vector** conventions mean the following
component rules under a spatial orthogonal coordinate change $y'=Qy$, where
$Q$ is a real $3\times3$ matrix with $Q^{\mathsf T}Q=I_3$. Transpose,
matrix product and identity are those of [[def-transpose-of-a-matrix]] and
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]], and $\det Q$ is the determinant
of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]. At corresponding
points $E'(y',t)=QE(y,t)$ and $B'(y',t)=(\det Q)QB(y,t)$. Thus polar and axial
components agree in their transformation rule when $\det Q=1$ and differ by
a sign when $\det Q=-1$. These rules specify the orientation convention;
the adopted inertial descriptions have positive orientation, and no physical
orientation-reversing change of description is adopted here.

(b) The fields are defined by their values on $\Omega\times I$, and no value at
a point of singular source support is asserted.

(c) $E$ carries V m$^{-1}$ and $B$ carries T.

(d) The identification of the pair $(E,B)$ with the components of an
alternating two-form, including its transformation behaviour, is made in the
framework's electromagnetic two-form definition on this page and is not
presupposed here.

Adopt the SI system of units for this framework, with the following quantity
table and conventions; every symbol is a quantity of this framework and the
laboratory structure is that of [[def-em-lab-geometry]].

(a) [Coordinates and constants] $x^0=ct$ and each spatial coordinate $x^i$
carries the metre (m); the time coordinate $t$ carries the second (s); the
conversion constant $c>0$ carries m s$^{-1}$ and has the exact SI defining
value $c=299\,792\,458\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$; the elementary charge $e$ has the
exact SI defining value $e=1.602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, and this
item does not assert that physical charge is quantised; the magnetic constant
$\mu_0>0$ carries N A$^{-2}$ and is measured, so no exact numerical value of
$\mu_0$ is asserted. The pre-2019 SI fixed the historical nominal
$\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}:=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{H\,m^{-1}}
=4\pi\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{N\,A^{-2}}$ exactly; since the revised SI took
effect on 20 May 2019, $\mu_0$ is experimentally determined. The SI brochure
quotes the nominal $\mu_{0,\mathrm{nom}}$ as the estimate at the 2019 adoption
with relative standard uncertainty $2.3\times10^{-10}$; this is historical
estimate and uncertainty context, not an exact equality for the actual $\mu_0$
or a current measured value. The electric constant is defined within the
framework by

$$\varepsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$$

in F m$^{-1}$, consistent with the exact SI relation $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,
so that $c^2\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1$ and $\varepsilon_0$ inherits the relative
standard uncertainty of $\mu_0$.

(b) [Electromagnetic quantities] Charge $q$ carries the coulomb (C); the
