citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Fourier transformation on Schwartz space extends uniquely to a surjective complex-linear isometry $\mathcal F_2:L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)\to L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$. It preserves the first-variable-linear inner product, and hence is unitary.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$

   and the latter is also equivalent to

$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(V,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_V)$ and $(H,\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_H)$ be
complex Hilbert spaces ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-inner-product-space]]) and let $i:V\to H$ be a linear map with dense
image.

**Symmetric forms.** A *sesquilinear form on $V$* is a map
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb C$ that is linear in its first argument and
conjugate-linear in its second; it is *symmetric* if
$a(u,v)=\overline{a(v,u)}$ for all $u,v\in V$, in which case $a(u,u)\in\mathbb R$
and $\operatorname{Re}a(u,v)=\operatorname{Re}\overline{a(v,u)}$.

**Bounded and semibounded.** Such a form is *bounded* if there is $C>0$ with
$|a(u,v)|\le C\|u\|_V\|v\|_V$ for all $u,v\in V$, and *semibounded below with
bound $M\ge0$* if $a(u,u)\ge-M\|i(u)\|_H^2$ for every $u\in V$.

**Form seminorm and closedness.** Let $M\ge0$ be a bound as above and define the
*form seminorm*
$$\|u\|_{a,M}:=\Bigl(\operatorname{Re}a(u,u)+(M+1)\|i(u)\|_H^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\qquad(u\in V).$$
It is a seminorm because $a(u,v)+(M+1)\langle i(u),i(v)\rangle_H$ is a positive semidefinite Hermitian form; its Cauchy–Schwarz inequality follows by expanding its value on $u+tv$ and minimizing over the scalar $t$, and gives the triangle inequality. It need not separate points for a general dense-image map $i$. The form $a$ is *closed* if there are such an $M$ and constants $c,C>0$ with
$c\|u\|_V\le\|u\|_{a,M}\le C\|u\|_V$ for every $u\in V$; then
the form seminorm is a norm, and $(V,\|\cdot\|_{a,M})$ is complete because $V$ is. If $i$ is injective, it is already a norm before closedness, since its square is at least $\|i(u)\|_H^2$.

**Associated operator.** With $a$ and $i$ as above, define
$$D(A):=\Bigl\{u\in V:\ \text{there is }f\in H\text{ with }a(u,v)=\langle f,i(v)\rangle_H\text{ for every }v\in V\Bigr\},\qquad Au:=f .$$
The element $f$ is unique when it exists, because two candidates differ by an
element of $H$ orthogonal to the dense subspace $i(V)$, hence coincide;
$A$ is called the *operator associated with $a$*. This definition asserts
neither that $A$ is densely defined, nor that $A$ is symmetric, nor that $A$ is
self-adjoint or bounded below; the specific closed semibounded form of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-transported-radial-endpoint-realization]] establishes those
properties for its own associated operator by a direct computation. When $V$
is a subspace of $H$ and $i$ is the inclusion, $\|i(u)\|_H$ is written
$\|u\|_H$ and the pairing $\langle f,i(v)\rangle_H$ is written
$\langle f,v\rangle$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space, let $Q\subseteq H$ be a dense linear subspace, and let
$q:Q\times Q\to\mathbb C$ be a symmetric sesquilinear form, linear in its
first variable. Write $q[u]=q(u,u)$. Suppose that for some $c\ge0$,
$q[u]\ge-c\|u\|^2$ for every $u\in Q$, and that $Q$ is complete in the form
norm $\|u\|_{q,c}^2=q[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$. Then there is a unique self-adjoint
operator $H_q\ge-cI$ such that
$$D((H_q+cI)^{1/2})=Q,\qquad q(u,v)=\langle H_qu,v\rangle\quad(u\in D(H_q),\ v\in Q).$$
Equivalently, $D(H_q)$ consists exactly of those $u\in Q$ for which there is
$f\in H$ satisfying $q(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for all $v\in Q$, and then
$H_qu=f$. Under the $e^{tA}$ generator convention for associated forms, the
associated operator is $A=-H_q$. If $q_0$ is a densely defined closed symmetric
form with $q_0[u]\ge0$ and $v$ is a symmetric sesquilinear form on $Q(q_0)$
satisfying
$$|v[u,u]|\le a q_0[u]+b\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(q_0)),\qquad 0\le a<1,\ b\ge0,$$
then $q_0+v$ is closed and bounded below by $-b$ on the same domain. It has a
unique self-adjoint representing operator there. The form bound is not an
operator-relative bound.
Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Every Schwartz function belongs to complex $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, and the classes represented by $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ are dense there.

Assume Countable Choice, let $n\ge1$ and $k\in\mathbb N_0$, and use complex
scalars. Write $W^{k,2}=W^{k,2}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for the weak-derivative
Sobolev space of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], whose classes carry
the weak derivatives $D^\alpha f\in L^2(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ for
$|\alpha|\le k$ and the norm
$$\|f\|_{W^{k,2}}=\Bigl(\sum_{|\alpha|\le k}\|D^\alpha f\|_2^2\Bigr)^{1/2},$$
and let $H^k=H^k(\mathbb R^n)$ be the real-order Bessel-potential completion
of [[def-real-order-bessel-potential-sobolev-space]] with its canonical
embedding $E_k:H^k\to\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$
([[thm-bessel-potential-completions-embed-in-tempered-distributions]]). Let
$u_f\in\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$ denote the regular tempered distribution of
an $L^2$ class $f$. Then:

1. $E_k[H^k]=\{u_f:f\in W^{k,2}\}$, and
   $\Phi(f):=E_k^{-1}(u_f)$ is a bijection
   $\Phi:W^{k,2}\to H^k$. Thus, under the regular-distribution embedding,
   $W^{k,2}$ and $H^k$ are the same subspace of $\mathcal S'(\mathbb R^n)$.
2. There are constants $0<c_k\le C_k<\infty$, depending only on $n$ and $k$,
   with
$$c_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2\le\|f\|_{W^{k,2}} \le C_k^{1/2}\,\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2,$$
   and $\|\langle\xi\rangle^k\mathcal F_2f\|_2=\|\Phi(f)\|_{H^k}$. Hence the
   weak-derivative norm and the bracket-weighted $L^2$ norm are equivalent,
   and the latter is also equivalent to
   $\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}\mathcal F_2f\|_2$, by
$$\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2\le\|(1+4\pi^2|\xi|^2)^{k/2}h\|_2 \le(2\pi)^k\|\langle\xi\rangle^k h\|_2,\qquad h\in L^2 .$$
3. The three norm expressions are **not** identical in general: the
   bracket-weighted norm differs from both the weak-derivative norm and the
   Laplacian-weighted norm, as the Gaussian computation in the proof shows.
Assume countable choice. The Fourier transform is a topological automorphism of $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$, with $\mathcal F^2=R$ and $\mathcal F^{-1}=R\mathcal F$, where $Rf(x)=f(-x)$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. The map $f\mapsto u_f$, $u_f(\varphi)=\int_\Omega f\varphi$, is a complex-linear injection from $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ modulo almost-everywhere equality into $\mathcal D'(\Omega)$. It is continuous from the local $L^1$ topology, generated by $f\mapsto\int_K|f|$ for compact $K\subseteq\Omega$, to the strong distribution topology. In particular local $L^1$ convergence implies strong distribution convergence. The continuity estimate itself is choice-free; Countable Choice is used in the cited $L^1$ approximate-identity theorem proving injectivity.

derivations.claim: Define $q_0$ on $Q_0=W^{1,2}$ by the displayed weak-derivative pairing. By [F2], for $u,v\in Q_0$, $$q_0(u,v)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u(\xi)\overline{\widehat v(\xi)}\,d\xi.$$ Thus $q_0$ is sesquilinear, symmetric and nonnegative. Moreover $q_0[u]+\|u\|_2^2=\|u\|_{W^{1,2}}^2$, which is complete by [F3], so $q_0$ is closed by [F4]. Since Schwartz functions lie in $Q_0$ and are dense in $L^2$ by [F5], $Q_0$ is dense.

If $u\in D(H_0)=W^{2,2}$ and $v\in Q_0$, Plancherel [F2] and Cauchy–Schwarz [F6] give $q_0(u,v)=\int4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u\,\overline{\widehat v} =\langle H_0u,v\rangle$; both factors in this pairing are in $L^2$ by the $W^{2,2}$ and $W^{1,2}$ hypotheses.

Conversely, suppose $u\in Q_0$ and $f\in H$ satisfy $q_0(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for every $v\in Q_0$. Testing with Schwartz $v$ and using Plancherel gives $\int(4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u(\xi)-\widehat f(\xi))\overline{\widehat v(\xi)}\,d\xi=0$. The Fourier transform maps Schwartz space onto itself by [F5], and complex conjugation preserves Schwartz space, so the locally integrable function $4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u-\widehat f$ pairs to zero with every compactly supported smooth test function. It is locally integrable because $\widehat u,\widehat f\in L^2$ and the polynomial weight is bounded on compact sets. Injectivity of the regular-distribution map [F7] gives $4\pi^2|\xi|^2\widehat u=\widehat f$ almost everywhere; hence $|\xi|^2\widehat u\in L^2$. By [F3], $u\in W^{2,2}=D(H_0)$, and [F1] then gives $H_0u=f$. Thus the form-associated operator domain and action are exactly those of $H_0$.

Steps 1.2-1.3 show that the nonnegative self-adjoint operator $H_0$ is the operator represented by the dense closed form $q_0$. Uniqueness in [F4] therefore gives $Q(H_0)=D(H_0^{1/2})=Q_0$, completing the Statement.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]), let $d\ge1$ and work on the complex Hilbert space $H=L^2(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$, whose completeness follows from [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]] and whose Hilbert-space structure is defined in [[def-hilbert-space]].

(a) For a real measurable finite-valued function $a:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ define $M_af:=af$ on $D(M_a):=\{f\in H: af\in H\}$. Then $M_a$ is a densely defined self-adjoint operator on $H$ ([[def-adjoint-of-a-densely-defined-unbounded-operator]], [[def-symmetric-self-adjoint-and-essentially-self-adjoint]]).

(b) Let $c>0$, $b\in\mathbb R$, and let $\mathcal F_2$ be the unitary Plancherel transform with the convention $\widehat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}dx$ on $L^1$ ([[def-fourier-transform-on-l-one-of-rn]], [[thm-plancherel]]). Define

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $V\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ be real with $\operatorname{supp}V\subseteq B_R$, let $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, let $H_0=-\Delta$ and $H=H_0+M_V$ on $D(H)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and define

$$\Omega_\pm=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH}e^{-itH_0}.$$

These wave operators exist by the concrete Cook construction. Write $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)$ for the closed span of the eigenspaces, $\mathcal H_{\mathrm c}(H)=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)^\perp$, and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H),\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(H)$ for the absolutely continuous and singular continuous spectral subspaces: locally define $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}=\{u:\mu_u\ll dE\}$ and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}=\{u:\mu_u\text{ is atomless and singular to }dE\}$ for the PVM constructed by [[lem-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-cc-separable-spectral-calculus]]. Then:

(a) $\operatorname{ran}\Omega_\pm\subseteq\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$ and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(H)=\{0\}$;

(b) each wave operator individually is asymptotically complete:

$$\operatorname{ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{ran}\Omega_-=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)=\mathcal H_{\mathrm c}(H);$$

(c) $S=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-$ is unitary on $\mathcal H$ and commutes with $e^{-itH_0}$ for every real $t$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal H_0,\mathcal H$ be separable complex Hilbert spaces, $H_0$ and $H$ self-adjoint operators on them, and $J:\mathcal H_0\to\mathcal H$ a bounded linear map. Write $E_{H_0}$ and $E_H$ for their spectral projection valued measures. The absolutely continuous subspace $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ consists of vectors $u$ for which the scalar measure $B\mapsto\|E_{H_0}(B)u\|^2$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure; $P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$ is its orthogonal projection. Define the two-space wave operators, when the pointwise strong limits exist on $\mathcal H_0$, by

$$\Omega_\pm(H,H_0;J):=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty} e^{itH}J e^{-itH_0}P_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0),$$

where a strong limit means that for every $u\in\mathcal H_0$ the vector-valued expression converges in $\mathcal H$. The two signs are separate limits. When $J=I$ and $\mathcal H_0=\mathcal H$, write $\Omega_\pm(H,H_0)$. A wave operator is complete when its range is all of $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$. When both wave operators exist and are isometries on $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H_0)$, the scattering operator on that subspace is

$$S(H,H_0;J):=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-.$$

When both are complete with common range $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$, $S$ is unitary. For a fixed finite number $r\ge1$ of channels on an open energy interval $I\subset\mathbb R$, finite-channel data additionally consists of the standard space $\mathbb C^r$ and a matrix field $S:I\to U(r)$, where

$$U(r):=\{U\in M_r(\mathbb C):U^*U=UU^*=I_r\}.$$

Here $U^*$ is conjugate transpose, $\operatorname{tr}U=\sum_{j=1}^r U_{jj}$, and $\det U$ is the usual alternating determinant. The fixed channel number means that $I$ contains no channel threshold. This finite-channel data is an explicit on-shell input; the abstract wave-operator definition alone does not assert that a given pair has finite-dimensional energy fibers.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ and let $H_{\mathrm{pp}}$,
$H_{\mathrm{ac}}$, $H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ be the subspaces of
[[def-pure-point-absolutely-continuous-and-singular-continuous-spectral-subspaces]].
Then $H_{\mathrm{pp}},H_{\mathrm{ac}},H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ are closed, mutually
orthogonal, $T$-reducing subspaces with
$$H=H_{\mathrm{pp}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{ac}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{sc}},$$
canonically determined by $T$; the restrictions of $T$ to them are
self-adjoint and their spectral measures are respectively purely atomic,
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and atomless and
singular. If $H$ is separable and $\mu$ is a maximal scalar spectral measure
with disjoint Borel supports $B_{\mathrm{pp}},B_{\mathrm{ac}},B_{\mathrm{sc}}$
of its discrete, absolutely continuous and singular continuous parts, then
$H_{\mathrm{type}}=\operatorname{ran}E(B_{\mathrm{type}})$.

Here a support means a Borel carrier (zero mass off the set), not necessarily topological support. A maximal scalar spectral measure is a finite positive Borel measure mu with $E_x\ll\mu$ for every x (in particular a scalar spectral measure with this domination property qualifies). The last assertion is conditional on the supplied mu. On the zero Hilbert space use the unique PVM and full-domain zero operator directly.

derivations.claim: The Fourier convention in [F1] is $\widehat f_{2\pi}(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx$; with $p=2\pi\xi$, its multiplier $4\pi^2|\xi|^2$ is exactly $|p|^2$, and the unitary momentum transform is $(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int e^{-ip\cdot x}f(x)\,dx$. Thus the $H_0$ and domain $H^2$ in [F2] agree with those in the Statement. Since the potential is the same real bounded compactly supported multiplication operator, [F1] also gives the self-adjoint realization required by [F2].

By [F2], the two stated pointwise strong limits exist with the exact sign convention $e^{itH}e^{-itH_0}$, are isometries, and have the stated individual ranges. That same supplier proves the absent singular-continuous subspace; [F5] fixes the PVM meaning of these spectral subspaces. In the degenerate case $V=0$, the approximants are $e^{itH_0}e^{-itH_0}=I$, so $\Omega_\pm=I$ and $S=I$. By [F4], the supplier's scattering operator is exactly the $S$ defined in the Statement, so its unitarity and free-group commutation give (b).

The Fourier scaling and energy change of variables in [F3] use the same momentum transform and $d\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$ as in the Statement. Hence the local $F_0$, $Z_0(E)$, resolvent boundary value, and compact-region generalized adjoint agree term-for-term with [F3]; no independent normalization or sign change is introduced.

Applying [F3] with the identical $H_0,H,V$ now proves that $F_0$ is unitary, that $F_0SF_0^*$ is multiplication by $S_{\mathrm{stat}}(E)$, and that the displayed stationary formula is unitary for every $E>0$. The result is conditional on AC, CC and the compact-support model and makes no threshold or Coulomb assertion. This proves (a)–(c).

$$H_0:=\mathcal F_2^*\,M_{c|\xi|^2+b}\,\mathcal F_2,\qquad D(H_0):=\{f\in H:|\xi|^2\mathcal F_2f\in H\}.$$

Then $H_0$ is self-adjoint, $D(H_0)$ coincides with the Sobolev space $W^{2,2}(\mathbb R^d;\mathbb C)$ as a set (with equivalent norms, [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], [[thm-fourier-characterisation-of-integer-order-hilbert-sobolev-spaces]]), $H_0\ge b$ in the quadratic-form sense, and for every Schwartz function $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, $H_0f=-(c/4\pi^2)\Delta f+bf$.

(c) If $V:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ is measurable with $\|V\|_\infty<\infty$ and $H:=H_0+M_V$ with domain $D(H_0)$, then $H$ is self-adjoint on $D(H_0)$, is bounded below, and the assignment $t\mapsto e^{itH}$ is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group whose generator is $iH$: the limit $\lim_{t\to0}\frac1t(e^{itH}\psi-\psi)$ exists exactly for $\psi\in D(H)$ and equals $iH\psi$ ([[lem-self-adjoint-operator-generates-a-strongly-continuous-unitary-group]]).

(d) *Scope*: the argument uses only boundedness and measurability of $V$; it proves nothing for $V\propto-1/|x|$, $V\propto|x|^2$ or the delta interaction, does not identify $H_0$ with any measured free-particle Hamiltonian, and asserts no physical interpretation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $V\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ be real with $\operatorname{supp}V\subseteq B_R$, let $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$, let $H_0=-\Delta$ and $H=H_0+M_V$ on $D(H)=H^2(\mathbb R^3)$, and define

$$\Omega_\pm=\operatorname*{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH}e^{-itH_0}.$$

These wave operators exist by the concrete Cook construction. Write $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)$ for the closed span of the eigenspaces, $\mathcal H_{\mathrm c}(H)=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{pp}}(H)^\perp$, and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H),\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(H)$ for the absolutely continuous and singular continuous spectral subspaces: locally define $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}=\{u:\mu_u\ll dE\}$ and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}=\{u:\mu_u\text{ is atomless and singular to }dE\}$ for the PVM constructed by [[lem-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-cc-separable-spectral-calculus]]. Then:

(a) $\operatorname{ran}\Omega_\pm\subseteq\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$ and $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{sc}}(H)=\{0\}$;

(b) each wave operator individually is asymptotically complete:

$$\operatorname{ran}\Omega_+=\operatorname{ran}\Omega_-=\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)=\mathcal H_{\mathrm c}(H);$$

(c) $S=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-$ is unitary on $\mathcal H$ and commutes with $e^{-itH_0}$ for every real $t$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$V\in L^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R)$ be real and compactly supported, and set
$H_0=-\Delta$, $H=H_0+M_V$ on $H^2(\mathbb R^3)$. Use the independently
constructed complete wave operators

$$\Omega_\pm=\operatorname{s-lim}_{t\to\pm\infty}e^{itH}e^{-itH_0},\qquad S=\Omega_+^*\Omega_-,$$

whose individual ranges equal $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)=\mathcal H_c(H)$,
as in [[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-compact-support-asymptotic-completeness]].
The local positive-energy resolvent and outgoing solution are those of
[[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-outgoing-fredholm-invertibility]] and
[[thm-nrqm-controlled-dynamics-stationary-outgoing-integral-and-flux]].
These named supplier inputs must be proved independently; this item does not
establish completeness by assuming its own stationary identification.

Write $\sigma$ for surface measure on $S^2$, normalized by $\sigma(S^2)=4\pi$,
$\mathfrak h=L^2(S^2,d\sigma)$, and

$$\widehat g(p)=(2\pi)^{-3/2}\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-ip\cdot x}g(x)\,dx,\qquad (F_0g)(E,\omega)=\frac{E^{1/4}}{\sqrt2}\widehat g(\sqrt E\,\omega).$$

For a compactly supported $g\in L^2$ and $E=k^2>0$, let $R_H(E\pm i0)g$
denote the local resolvent limits, and define the free trace on compact sources
and the two stationary transforms by

$$Z_0(E)g=\frac{\sqrt k}{4\pi^{3/2}}\int e^{-ik\omega\cdot x}g(x)\,dx,\qquad Z_\pm(E)g=Z_0(E)\bigl[g-VR_H(E\pm i0)g\bigr].$$

Then:

(a) $F_0$ is a unitary from $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$ onto
$\mathcal K=L^2((0,\infty),dE;\mathfrak h)$. The initially defined stationary
transforms extend to $Z_\pm=F_0\Omega_\pm^*$ on $L^2(\mathbb R^3)$; their
restrictions to $\mathcal H_{\mathrm{ac}}(H)$ are unitary onto $\mathcal K$,
they vanish on the pure point subspace, and they diagonalize $H$ as
multiplication by $E$ on its absolutely continuous subspace.

(b) There is a measurable operator-valued unitary $S(E)$ on $\mathfrak h$
such that $F_0SF_0^*=M_{S(E)}$. No generic nonradial potential is assumed to
preserve individual spherical harmonic channels. For $R\in SO(3)$ set
$V_R(x)=V(R^{-1}x)$ and $(U_Ra)(\omega)=a(R^{-1}\omega)$. The covariance is
$S[V_R](E)=U_RS[V](E)U_R^{-1}$, not commutation with $U_R$ for a fixed
nonradial $V$.

(c) Let $u_{k,d}$ be the outgoing stationary solution restricted to a ball
$B$ containing the support of $V$:

$$u_{k,d}=(I+\chi_BR_0(k^2+i0)V)^{-1}\bigl(e^{ikd\cdot x}|_B\bigr),\qquad f_k(\omega,d)=-\frac1{4\pi}\int_Be^{-ik\omega\cdot x}V(x)u_{k,d}(x)\,dx.$$

Here $R_0(z)=(H_0-z)^{-1}$ and $\chi_B$ denotes restriction/localization;
the inverse is the inverse of **$I+K$**, not of $K$. Define
$(\mathcal A_ka)(\omega)=\int_{S^2}f_k(\omega,d)a(d)\,d\sigma(d)$. Then

$$S(E)=I-2\pi i\,Z_0(E)\bigl[V-VR_H(E+i0)V\bigr]Z_0(E)^*=I+\frac{ik}{2\pi}\mathcal A_k.$$

Adjoints $Z_0(E)^*$ and products in this formula are understood on the
compact interaction region, not as bounded maps into global $L^2$ plane waves.
The right side is norm-continuous on compact positive-energy intervals and
gives a unitary representative for every $E>0$.

(d) If in addition $V$ is radial, the energy-angular fiber decomposes in the
fixed countable spherical harmonic basis as
$S(E)Y_{lm}=S_l(E)Y_{lm}$. For the reduced radial equation

$$-\varphi_l''+\left(\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}+V(r)\right)\varphi_l=k^2\varphi_l,\qquad \varphi_l(r)/r^{l+1}\longrightarrow1,$$

let $f_l$ be the outgoing solution with
$f_l(r)=e^{i(kr-l\pi/2)}(1+O(r^{-1}))$ outside the interaction region and set
$W_l=W(\varphi_l,f_l)=\varphi_lf_l'-\varphi_l'f_l$. Then

$$S_l(E)=\frac{\overline{W_l(E)}}{W_l(E)},\qquad |S_l(E)|=1.$$

Equivalently, for the real normalized regular solution
$a_l=\sqrt{\rho_l}\,\varphi_l=c_lf_l+d_l\overline f_l$,
$\rho_l=k/(\pi|W_l|^2)$, the multiplier is
$(c_l/d_l)/(c_l^0/d_l^0)$, where the superscript $0$ denotes the corresponding
free normalization. The real regular transforms
$(T_lg)(E)=\int_0^\infty a_l(E,r)g(r)\,dr$ extend to unitaries from the
absolutely continuous reduced radial subspace onto $L^2((0,\infty),dE)$.
They implement the scalar channel statement with the incoming/outgoing phase
factors specified in the proof. No Coulomb continuum transform is used for a
compact potential.

No zero-energy nonresonance, absence of a zero eigenvalue, positivity of the
whole spectrum, finite bound-spectrum assumption, or radiality is imposed on
(a)-(c). The negative and any zero point spectrum are omitted by the
absolutely continuous restriction, rather than falsely declared nonexistent.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space H with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ and let $H_{\mathrm{pp}}$,
$H_{\mathrm{ac}}$, $H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ be the subspaces of
[[def-pure-point-absolutely-continuous-and-singular-continuous-spectral-subspaces]].
Then $H_{\mathrm{pp}},H_{\mathrm{ac}},H_{\mathrm{sc}}$ are closed, mutually
orthogonal, $T$-reducing subspaces with
$$H=H_{\mathrm{pp}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{ac}}\oplus H_{\mathrm{sc}},$$
canonically determined by $T$; the restrictions of $T$ to them are
self-adjoint and their spectral measures are respectively purely atomic,
absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure, and atomless and
singular. If $H$ is separable and $\mu$ is a maximal scalar spectral measure
with disjoint Borel supports $B_{\mathrm{pp}},B_{\mathrm{ac}},B_{\mathrm{sc}}$
of its discrete, absolutely continuous and singular continuous parts, then
$H_{\mathrm{type}}=\operatorname{ran}E(B_{\mathrm{type}})$.

Here a support means a Borel carrier (zero mass off the set), not necessarily topological support. A maximal scalar spectral measure is a finite positive Borel measure mu with $E_x\ll\mu$ for every x (in particular a scalar spectral measure with this domination property qualifies). The last assertion is conditional on the supplied mu. On the zero Hilbert space use the unique PVM and full-domain zero operator directly.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $d\geq1$, $\epsilon>0$, and $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$. The kernel of $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)$ is

$$ K_\epsilon(x,y):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)\,d\xi . $$

It belongs to $L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})$ and satisfies

$$ \|K_\epsilon\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})}=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\|a\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^{2d})}. $$

The kernel integral defines a bounded operator on $L^2(\mathbb R^d)$ that agrees with the Schwartz-space definition of $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)$, and its operator norm is at most the displayed kernel norm. This estimate is finite for each $\epsilon>0$ but is not uniform as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

Assume countable choice. The negative-sign, $2\pi$-normalized Fourier transform is continuous $\mathcal F:\mathcal S\to\mathcal S$, and
$$\mathcal F(\partial^\alpha f)(\xi)=(2\pi i\xi)^\alpha\widehat f(\xi),\qquad \partial^\beta\widehat f=\mathcal F((-2\pi ix)^\beta f).$$

Assume countable choice. For every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ and every $x\in\mathbb R^n$,
$$f(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}\widehat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi.$$
The integral is absolutely convergent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice (The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$
Assume countable choice and let $n\ge1$. Every Schwartz function belongs to complex $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$, and the classes represented by $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^n)$ are dense there.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. If $f : V \to \mathbb C$ belongs to $L^1(\lambda_n)$,
then
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Assume countable choice. For complex $C^1$ functions $u,v$ on $[a,b]$, $a<b$, Lebesgue integration gives $\int_a^b u'v=u(b)v(b)-u(a)v(a)-\int_a^b uv'$ and $\int_a^b u'=u(b)-u(a)$. If instead $u,v\in C^1(\mathbb R;\mathbb C)$, $u'v,uv'\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ and $u(x)v(x)\to0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$, then $\int_{\mathbb R}u'v=-\int_{\mathbb R}uv'$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ (The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ (The lower and upper Darboux integrals of a bounded $f$ on $[a,b]$ as $\sup_P L(f,P)$ and $\inf_P U(f,P)$, Darboux integrability as their equality, and the notation $\int_a^b f$). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$L^2(\mu)$ be the quotient of $\mathcal L^2(\mu)$ by the almost-everywhere zero
functions ([[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]), with the quotient
norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]).

1. On **real** $L^2(\mu)$ the formula
   $$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int fg\,d\mu$$is a well-defined inner product, linear in both variables, positive definite, with $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu)$ is a real Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). 2. On **complex** $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ the formula$$\langle f,g\rangle:=\int f\overline g\,d\mu$$
   is a well-defined inner product, linear in the first variable and
   conjugate-linear in the second, positive definite, with
   $\langle f,f\rangle=\|f\|_2^2$; with it $L^2(\mu;\mathbb C)$ is a complex
   Hilbert space ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]).

In both cases the inner product induces exactly the established quotient
$L^2$ norm.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: Let $\widehat a(\lambda)=\int e^{-i\lambda\cdot z}a(z)\,dz$, and similarly for $b$. These are rescaled versions of the negative-sign $2\pi$ Fourier transform; [F3], [F4], and the linear frequency scaling in [F8] imply they are Schwartz, integrable, and have inverse $a(z)=(2\pi)^{-2d}\int e^{i\lambda\cdot z}\widehat a(\lambda)\,d\lambda$. For $\lambda=(q,p)$, define the unitary map $$ (T^\epsilon_{q,p}u)(x)=e^{iq\cdot(x+\epsilon p/2)}u(x+\epsilon p). $$ The phase has modulus one and [F6] preserves the norm under translation, so $T^\epsilon_{q,p}$ is unitary, with inverse given by reversing the translation and phase. Fourier inversion [F4], this formula, Fubini [F5], and [F8] applied to the complex $L^1$ integrands under $x\mapsto y=x+\epsilon p$ give the scalar form representation $$ \mathcal B_a(u,v):=(2\pi)^{-2d}\int\widehat a(\lambda)\langle T^\epsilon_\lambda u,v\rangle\,d\lambda . $$ For $u,v\in L^2$, this scalar integral is absolutely convergent and bounded by $(2\pi)^{-2d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$. For Schwartz $u,v$, use $T^\epsilon_{q,p}u(x)=e^{iq\cdot(x+\epsilon p/2)}u(x+\epsilon p)$, change variables by [F8] to $y=x+\epsilon p$, and then apply Fourier inversion in $q$: $\int e^{iq\cdot(x+y)/2}\widehat a(q,(y-x)/\epsilon)\,dq=(2\pi)^d\int e^{-i(y-x)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a((x+y)/2,\xi)\,d\xi$. This gives $\mathcal B_a(u,v)=\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u,v\rangle$. Both forms are bounded on $L^2\times L^2$, so [F7] extends their equality from the dense Schwartz subspace to all $L^2$ pairs; [F2] supplies the bounded Weyl extension.

Direct substitution in $T^\epsilon_{q,p}T^\epsilon_{q',p'}u$ gives the Weyl relation $$ T^\epsilon_\lambda T^\epsilon_\mu=e^{-i\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}T^\epsilon_{\lambda+\mu}. $$ For $u,v\in L^2$, first apply [step 1.1] with $w=\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u$; then $$ \langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u,v\rangle =(2\pi)^{-2d}\int\widehat a(\lambda)\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v\rangle\,d\lambda. $$ Apply [step 1.1] for $b$ to each pair $(u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v)$. Since $T_\lambda^\epsilon$ is unitary, $\langle T_\mu^\epsilon u,T_\lambda^{\epsilon *}v\rangle=\langle T_\lambda^\epsilon T_\mu^\epsilon u,v\rangle$; the double integral is absolutely convergent with majorant $(2\pi)^{-4d}\|\widehat a\|_1\|\widehat b\|_1\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$, so Fubini and the Weyl relation give $$ c_\epsilon(z)=(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}e^{-i\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,d\lambda\,d\mu . $$ The phase-space Fourier coefficient of $\{a,b\}$ is $-\sigma(\lambda,\mu)\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)$; this follows by differentiating the Fourier modes in the explicitly fixed Poisson convention.

Fix $\lambda,\mu$ and write $f(s)=e^{-is\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}$, a $C^2$ complex function on $[0,1]$. Applying [F10] to the real and imaginary parts twice gives $f(1)-f(0)=\int_0^1f'(r)\,dr=f'(0)+\int_0^1\int_0^r f''(s)\,ds\,dr=f'(0)+\int_0^1(1-s)f''(s)\,ds$; the last equality is Fubini [F5] on the continuous integrand over the triangle. Since $f'(0)=-i\epsilon\sigma/2$ and $f''(s)=-\epsilon^2\sigma^2e^{-is\epsilon\sigma/2}/4$, this derives $$ e^{-i\epsilon\sigma/2}=1-\frac{i\epsilon\sigma}{2} -\frac{\epsilon^2\sigma^2}{4}\int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma/2}\,ds. $$ Set $$ R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu):=\frac{\sigma(\lambda,\mu)^2}{4} \int_0^1(1-s)e^{-is\epsilon\sigma(\lambda,\mu)/2}\,ds . $$ Consequently the symbol remainder is $$ r_\epsilon(z)=-(2\pi)^{-4d}\iint\widehat a(\lambda)\widehat b(\mu)e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)\,d\lambda\,d\mu. $$ For multi-indices $\alpha,\beta$ with $|\alpha|,|\beta|\le K:=4d+4$, differentiate $|\alpha|$ times in $z$ and integrate by parts $|\beta|$ times in $\lambda$ using [F9] coordinatewise to estimate $z^\beta\partial_z^\alpha r_\epsilon(z)$. Each integration is justified because the Fourier factors and all their derivatives have rapid decay and every differentiated factor has at most polynomial growth; thus the derivative products are integrable and boundary products vanish. Each $\lambda$-derivative of the remainder factor is bounded by $$ |\partial_\lambda^\gamma R_\epsilon(\lambda,\mu)|\le C_\gamma\langle\lambda\rangle^2\langle\mu\rangle^{|\gamma|+2} \quad (|\gamma|\le K), $$ because $\sigma$ is bilinear, $\partial_\lambda\sigma$ is linear in $\mu$, and $0<\epsilon\le1$. Derivatives of $e^{i(\lambda+\mu)\cdot z}$ contribute powers of $\lambda+\mu$. Thus the absolute integrand is bounded by a finite sum of $$ |\partial_\lambda^\gamma\widehat a(\lambda)|\,\langle\lambda\rangle^{K+2}\, |\widehat b(\mu)|\,\langle\mu\rangle^{2K+2}. $$ For completeness, in Fourier dimension $n=2d$, if $2k>L+n$, then $$ \int\langle\lambda\rangle^L|\partial^\gamma\widehat f(\lambda)|\,d\lambda \le C\sum_{|\delta|\le2k}\|\partial^\delta(z^\gamma f)\|_{L^1} \le C p_M(f) $$ whenever $M\ge2k$ and $M>|\gamma|+n$: apply $(1-\Delta_z)^k$ to $z^\gamma f$, use its Fourier multiplier $\langle\lambda\rangle^{2k}$, and integrate the resulting $\langle z\rangle^{-M+|\gamma|}$ bound. Taking $K=4d+4$, $L_a=K+2$, $L_b=2K+2$, choose $k_a=3d+4$ for $a$ and $k_b=5d+6$ for $b$. Then $2k_a>L_a+2d$, $2k_b>L_b+2d$, and $M=12d+16$ exceeds both $2k_b$ and $K+2d$, so the weighted estimates hold for all indicated derivatives. This proves $p_K(r_\epsilon)\le C_dp_M(a)p_M(b)$, uniformly in $\epsilon$. The same argument with any fixed larger $K$ proves every Schwartz seminorm of $r_\epsilon$ is finite, so $r_\epsilon\in\mathcal S$. Hence $c_\epsilon=ab+\frac{i\epsilon}{2}\{a,b\}+\epsilon^2r_\epsilon$ is Schwartz, and the weak Fourier representation from step 1.1 identifies the product in step 2.1 with $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(c_\epsilon)$.

The kernel of $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_\epsilon)$, in $q=(x+y)/2$, $s=x-y$, is $$ K_\epsilon(q,s)=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int e^{is\cdot\xi/\epsilon}r_\epsilon(q,\xi)\,d\xi. $$ The affine map $(x,y)\mapsto(q,s)$ has absolute determinant $1$, and the kernel integrands are Schwartz and hence complex $L^1$, so [F8] justifies this kernel-coordinate substitution. Since $K=4d+4\ge2d+2$, $\langle(q,\xi)\rangle^K\ge\langle q\rangle^{d+1}\langle\xi\rangle^{d+1}$ and $\int_{\mathbb R^d}\langle\xi\rangle^{-d-1}d\xi<\infty$ imply $\int|\partial_\xi^\gamma r_\epsilon(q,\xi)|\,d\xi\le C_dp_K(r_\epsilon)\langle q\rangle^{-d-1}$ for $|\gamma|\le2d+2$. Integrating by parts with $(1-\Delta_\xi)^{d+1}$ is justified coordinatewise by [F9], because $r_\epsilon$ is Schwartz; using this bound gives $$ |K_\epsilon(q,s)|\leq C_dp_{12d+16}(a)p_{12d+16}(b)\epsilon^{-d} \langle q\rangle^{-d-1}(1+|s|/\epsilon)^{-2d-2}. $$ For fixed $x$, $dy=2^d\,dq$ and $s=2(x-q)$; [F8] applies to these affine changes in the absolutely integrable row integrals, and integrating this bound in $y$ is at most a constant times $\epsilon^{-d}\int(1+|x-q|/\epsilon)^{-2d-2}\,dq\leq C_d$; the same bound holds with $x,y$ interchanged. Let $R$ and $C$ be the resulting uniform row and column $L^1$ bounds for the actual kernel $K_\epsilon(x,y)=K_\epsilon((x+y)/2,x-y)$. For $u\in L^2(\mathbb R^d)$, Tonelli [F13] and the column bound make $\int|K_\epsilon(x,y)||u(y)|^2dy$ finite for almost every $x$. At such $x$, factor the integrand as $\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(x,y)|}\,[(K_\epsilon/|K_\epsilon|)(x,y)\sqrt{|K_\epsilon(x,y)|}u(y)]$, with quotient $0$ where the kernel vanishes. Cauchy–Schwarz [F12] in $L^2(dy)$ gives $$ |\int K_\epsilon(x,y)u(y)\,dy|^2\le R\int|K_\epsilon(x,y)||u(y)|^2\,dy. $$ Tonelli [F13] and the column bound then give $\|\int K_\epsilon(\cdot,y)u(y)\,dy\|_2^2\le RC\|u\|_2^2$. This proves the integral-kernel Schur estimate with norm at most $\sqrt{RC}$ and hence $\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_\epsilon)\|\le C_dp_{12d+16}(a)p_{12d+16}(b)$. Combining steps 2.1–4.1 proves the asserted Weyl composition formula with the plus sign fixed by $[Q_j,P_k]=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $d\geq1$, let $0<\epsilon$ be a dimensionless parameter, and use the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ of [[def-schwartz-space-and-its-seminorms]]. For $a\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^{2d})$, define the Weyl quantization on $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a)u)(x):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\int_{\mathbb R^d} e^{i(x-y)\cdot\xi/\epsilon}a\!\left(\frac{x+y}{2},\xi\right)u(y)\,d\xi\,dy . $$

The integral is absolutely convergent for each fixed $x$, since its integrand is Schwartz in $(y,\xi)$. The Wigner integral below is absolutely convergent for each $(x,\xi)$ for the same reason.

For a normalized $u\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$, define its Wigner distribution by

$$ W_\epsilon[u](x,\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-iy\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x+y/2)\overline{u(x-y/2)}\,dy . $$

Use the inner product $\langle f,g\rangle=\int f(x)\overline{g(x)}\,dx$, linear in its first argument ([[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]). Define the scaled Fourier transform on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$ by

$$ (\mathcal F_\epsilon u)(\xi):=(2\pi\epsilon)^{-d/2}\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-ix\cdot\xi/\epsilon}u(x)\,dx . $$

For the coordinate and momentum observables define $Q_j u=x_j u$ and $P_j u=-i\epsilon\partial_{x_j}u$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^d)$. The product rule ([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]) gives
$$ [Q_j,P_k]u:=Q_jP_ku-P_kQ_ju=i\epsilon\delta_{jk}u. $$
This fixes the Poisson and Moyal signs used on this page.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

citations.quote:
Let $M$ be a finite-dimensional smooth manifold, let $d\geq1$ be an integer, and give $\mathbb C^d$ its standard Hermitian inner product. Let $P:M\to\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^d)$ be a $C^2$ map such that $P(x)^2=P(x)=P(x)^*$ and $\operatorname{rank}P(x)=r$ is constant. Define
$$E_P=\{(x,v)\in M\times\mathbb C^d:P(x)v=v\},\qquad \pi(x,v)=x.$$
Its fiber at $x$ is $\operatorname{ran}P(x)$ with the inner product inherited from $\mathbb C^d$. For a $C^1$ section $s:U\to\mathbb C^d$ over an open $U\subseteq M$ satisfying $P s=s$, define the projected connection by $\nabla s=P\,ds$, where $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative. For a $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, put $P_\gamma(t)=P(\gamma(t))$ and $K_\gamma(t)=[P_\gamma'(t),P_\gamma(t)]$. Kato transport along $\gamma$ is the matrix solution $W_\gamma'(t)=K_\gamma(t)W_\gamma(t)$, $W_\gamma(0)=I_d$.

The connection and Kato transport are defined from the projector family itself; no Schrödinger Hamiltonian or physical time evolution is needed. A coherent uniformly gapped spectral projection of a $C^2$ finite Hermitian family is one source of such a $C^2$ family: under Countable Choice, an earlier finite-dimensional adiabatic result supplies that regularity.

Let $M$, $d$, and $P$ satisfy [[def-nrqmx-smooth-projector-bundle]], and write $E_P$ for its range family. Then $E_P\to M$ is a rank-$r$ $C^2$ complex vector bundle, and $\nabla s=P\,ds$ is a Hermitian connection on it. For every $C^2$ path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$, the Kato equation $W'=[P_\gamma',P_\gamma]W$, $W(0)=I_d$, has a unique $C^2$ solution. That solution is unitary and satisfies $P_\gamma(t)W(t)=W(t)P_\gamma(0)$ for every $t\in[0,1]$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector
space, and let $k\geq0$. A **smooth $V$-valued differential $k$-form** on
$M$ is a family of alternating $k$-linear maps

$$\alpha_p:(T_pM)^k\longrightarrow V$$

such that $\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a scalar smooth $k$-form in the sense of
[[def-smooth-differential-k-form]] for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Equivalently,
for one (and hence every) basis $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)$ of $V$, the unique
components in $\alpha=\sum_i v_i\alpha^i$ all belong to $\Omega^k(M)$.

For such an $\alpha$, its **componentwise exterior derivative** is the unique
$V$-valued $(k+1)$-form $d_V\alpha$ characterized by

$$\lambda\circ d_V\alpha=d(\lambda\circ\alpha)$$

for every $\lambda\in V^*$. Indeed, in a basis with dual basis
$(\lambda^1,\ldots,\lambda^r)$, set

$$d_V\alpha=\sum_i v_i\,d\alpha^i,\qquad \alpha^i=\lambda^i\circ\alpha.$$

The scalar formula defining $d$ is real-linear term by term
[[def-exterior-derivative-by-the-invariant-vector-field-formula]], and its
output is a smooth form
[[lem-the-invariant-exterior-derivative-formula-is-c-infinity-multilinear]].
Thus the displayed construction has the stated characterization. It is
independent of the chosen basis because linear functionals separate points of
$V$, and the characterization also proves uniqueness.

The two smoothness descriptions are equivalent in both directions: testing
all $\lambda$ includes the dual basis components, while every
$\lambda\circ\alpha$ is a fixed real linear combination of the components in
one basis. If $M$ is empty, these assignments and identities are vacuous. If
$V=0$, there is only the zero-valued form and its derivative is zero; if
$\dim V=1$, the definition is exactly the scalar definition after choosing
one nonzero basis vector. No metric, nondegeneracy, manifold boundary, or
endpoint is involved. A single finite basis exists by finite-dimensionality;
the definition is basis-independent and chooses no basis or family, so no
choice axiom is used.

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.

derivations.claim: Differentiate $P^2=P$ in a tangent direction $X$ to obtain $(dP)(X)P+P(dP)(X)=(dP)(X)$. Multiplying on both sides by $P$ gives $P(dP)(X)P=0$. For a $C^1$ section $s$ with $Ps=s$, the curvature is $\nabla^2s(X,Y)=P(dP(X)\,ds(Y)-dP(Y)\,ds(X))$. Substituting $ds(X)=dP(X)s+P\,ds(X)$ and using $P(dP)P=0$ leaves $P(dP(X)dP(Y)-dP(Y)dP(X))Ps$. This is $P(dP\wedge dP)P\,s$, proving the projector formula.

In a local frame write a section as $s=Va$. Then $\nabla(Va)=P\,d(Va)=V(V^*dV\,a+da)=V(da+A a)$, where $A=V^*dV$. Differentiating $V^*V=I_r$ gives $(dV)^*V+V^*dV=0$, so $A^*=-A$. Applying $d+A$ twice gives $dA+A\wedge A$; expressing the already computed curvature in this frame gives $F_{\mathrm{fr}}=V^*FV=dA+A\wedge A$.

For $V'=Vg$, direct differentiation gives $A'=V'^*dV'=g^{-1}Ag+g^{-1}dg$, since $g^*=g^{-1}$. The frame-coordinate covariant derivative changes from $d+A$ to $g^{-1}(d+A)g$ on coefficient sections. Squaring this identity gives $dA'+A'\wedge A'=g^{-1}(dA+A\wedge A)g$, which is the claimed curvature covariance.

For a path the definitions give $W'=[P',P]W$; [F2] proves that its unique solution is unitary and satisfies $P(t)W(t)=W(t)P(0)$. This is projector parallel transport and uses no Schrödinger evolution.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
For an integer $d\ge1$, let $\mathsf H_d=\{A\in M_d(\mathbb C):A=A^*\}$, regarded as a real vector space. For $A,B\in\mathsf H_d$, define the trace pairing $\langle A,B\rangle_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(AB)$ and write $\|A\|_{\mathrm{HS}}:=\sqrt{\operatorname{Tr}(A^2)}$. The following A-page lemma verifies that the pairing is a real inner product and that this expression is its norm.

Let $m\ge1$ and let $F=(F_a)_{a=1}^m$ be a finite family in $\mathsf H_d$. It is informationally complete when its real linear span is all of $\mathsf H_d$. Its synthesis map is $S:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $S c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aF_a$. Define the Gram matrix by $G_{ab}:=\operatorname{Tr}(F_aF_b)$; the following well-definedness lemma establishes that the trace pairing makes $S^*$ well-defined and that $G=S^*S$ is real symmetric positive semidefinite.

For this positive semidefinite real matrix $G$, let $G^+$ be its unique Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse in $M_m(\mathbb R)$, defined by the four Penrose equations over $\mathbb R$. Define the canonical dual operators $D_a=\sum_{b=1}^m(G^+)_{ba}F_b$ and the reconstruction map $D:\mathbb R^m\to\mathsf H_d$, $D c=\sum_{a=1}^m c_aD_a$. A later A-page lemma identifies this finite pseudoinverse with its spectral formula.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $H$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space of dimension $d\ge1$ ([[def-hilbert-space]]), with adjoints as in [[def-adjoint-of-a-linear-map-between-inner-product-spaces]] and the finite trace as in [[def-trace-of-an-endomorphism]]. Recall that an endomorphism $F$ is an **effect** when $F\ge0$ and $I-F\ge0$, i.e. $0\le F\le I$ in the quadratic-form order ([[def-non-negative-and-positive-operator]]).

(a) *Definitions.* A finite POVM is a finite family $(F_a)_{a=1}^p$, $p\ge1$, of effects with $\sum_aF_a=I$. An **instrument** here is a finite family $(M_{a,r})_{1\le a\le p,\,1\le r\le q_a}$ of endomorphisms of $H$, where each $q_a$ is a non-negative integer; its outcome operators and update maps are $F_a:=\sum_rM_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}$ and $I_a:\operatorname{End}(H)\to\operatorname{End}(H)$, $I_a(R):=\sum_rM_{a,r}RM_{a,r}^*$, with empty sums equal to zero. It is **normalized** when $\sum_{a,r}M_{a,r}^*M_{a,r}=I$. For a normalized instrument the $F_a$ are its **outcome effects**, as proved in (b); without normalization they need not be effects.

(b) If $(F_a)$ is a finite POVM and $\rho$ a density operator ([[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]]) then $p_a:=\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)\ge0$ and $\sum_ap_a=1$. If $(M_{a,r})$ is a normalized instrument then the $F_a$ form a finite POVM, $\operatorname{tr}I_a(\rho)=p_a$, each $I_a(\rho)$ is non-negative, and whenever $p_a>0$ the normalized update $I_a(\rho)/p_a$ is a density operator.

(c) *Ideal Lüders case.* For an orthogonal projection $P$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]) put $M_0=P$, $M_1=I-P$. Then $\sum_jM_j^*M_j=P+(I-P)=I$, the effects are $F_0=P$, $F_1=I-P$, and $I_j(\rho)=P\rho P$ or $(I-P)\rho(I-P)$.

(d) *Non-determination.* Effects alone do not determine the update: there are two normalized instruments on $\mathbb C^2$ with the same outcome effects $F_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$, $F_1=\operatorname{diag}(0,1)$ whose updates differ on the same input.

Work with finite-dimensional system and environment spaces $H_S=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_E=\mathbb C^m$, where $d,m\geq1$, using the ordered tensor product $H_S\otimes H_E$ with the system factor first. A system or environment state is a positive semidefinite Hermitian matrix of trace one; these state matrices are dimensionless. At the initial time, for every allowed system state $\rho$, adopt the joint preparation $\rho\otimes\eta$, where the fixed environment state $\eta$ does not depend on $\rho$. For each $t\geq0$, choose a declared unitary $U_t$ on $H_S\otimes H_E$, meaning $U_t^*U_t=U_tU_t^*=I$, with $U_0=I$. The reduced system dynamics is the map $\Phi_t(\rho)=\operatorname{Tr}_E\!\left(U_t(\rho\otimes\eta)U_t^*\right)$, where for the fixed product basis the finite partial trace has entries $(\operatorname{Tr}_E R)_{\alpha\beta}=\sum_{j=1}^mR_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,j)}$. This assignment excludes initially correlated joint states. It imposes no one-parameter group, continuity, or semigroup law on $U_t$.

A time-homogeneous finite GKSL model may instead be selected as a separate approximation: choose a fixed finite-dimensional Hamiltonian matrix $H=H^*$ in joules, a constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, and finitely many jump matrices $L_a$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1/2}$, and use $T_t=e^{t\mathcal L}$ for $t\geq0$ with $\mathcal L(X)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}[H,X]+\sum_a\left(L_aXL_a^*-\frac12\{L_a^*L_a,X\}\right)$. Each application must state its rates and physical regime. Selecting this approximation is not a consequence of the finite unitary reduction, and this postulate claims no weak-coupling or reservoir limit.

For a complex vector space $H$, write $\operatorname{End}(H)$ for the set of
linear maps $H\to H$ ([[def-linear-map]]).

Let $H_A,H_B$ be finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces with fixed
ordered orthonormal bases $(e_i)_{i<a}$ and $(f_j)_{j<b}$, respectively. The
ordered product basis of $H_A\otimes H_B$ has the $A$ index first. For
$R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)$ define
$\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\in\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ by

$$\bigl(\operatorname{Tr}_B(R)\bigr)_{i i'}:=\sum_{j<b}R_{(i,j),(i',j)}.$$

Rows are output coordinates and columns are input coordinates, as in
[[def-coordinate-column-and-matrix-of-a-linear-map]]. If $b=0$, the sum is
empty and equals $0$. The notation $\operatorname{Tr}_B$ means that the second
factor is contracted; the first factor and its order are retained.

For finite-dimensional complex inner-product spaces $H_A,H_B$, the partial
trace $\operatorname{Tr}_B:\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\to
\operatorname{End}(H_A)$ is the unique linear map satisfying

$$\operatorname{tr}\bigl((\operatorname{Tr}_B R)\circ T\bigr)=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(R\circ(T\otimes I_{H_B})\bigr)\quad\text{for every }R\in\operatorname{End}(H_A\otimes H_B)\text{ and }T\in\operatorname{End}(H_A).$$

Here $I_{H_B}$ is the identity map $y\mapsto y$ on $H_B$; $\operatorname{End}$
is the notation defined in [[def-qc-partial-trace]].

Its coordinate formula is independent of the chosen ordered orthonormal basis
of $H_B$. The assertion includes zero-dimensional factors.

Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.

Let $d\geq1$ and let $\Phi_t:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be a family of finite quantum channels indexed by $t\geq0$, where “finite quantum channel” has the meaning in [[def-qsm-dt-channel-definition]]. The family obeys the **semigroup law** when $\Phi_0=\operatorname{id}_{M_d(\mathbb C)}$ and $\Phi_{t+s}=\Phi_t\circ\Phi_s$ for every $s,t\geq0$.

The family is **CP-divisible** when for every $0\leq s\leq t$ there exists a finite quantum channel $V_{t,s}:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi_t=V_{t,s}\circ\Phi_s$. CP-divisibility is this specified factorization property; the definition does not assert that it is a universal meaning of “Markovian”.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

For real $x,y$, $\exp(x+iy)=e^x(\cos y+i\sin y)$ and $|\exp(x+iy)|=e^x$. In particular $e^{i\pi}+1=0$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[thm-complex-exponential-addition-and-real-extension]], [[thm-eulers-formula]], [[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]], [[thm-pythagorean-and-parity-identities-for-all-six-trigonometric-functions]], [[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], [[thm-quarter-turn-values-and-shift-formulas]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[cor-trigonometric-parity-and-pythagorean-identity]], [[thm-sine-cosine-signs-monotonicity-and-ranges]], [[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]], [[def-pi-via-first-positive-cosine-zero]].

derivations.claim: By [F3], choose an orthonormal environment eigenbasis $(|k\rangle)_{k=1}^m$ with $\eta=\sum_{k=1}^mp_k|k\rangle\langle k|$, $p_k\geq0$, and $\sum_kp_k=1$. Choose any system orthonormal basis $(|\alpha\rangle)_{\alpha=1}^d$ and use their ordered product basis. By [F2], this basis change leaves the finite partial trace in [F1] unchanged. For environment indices $j,k$ define the system matrix $K_{jk}$ by $(K_{jk})_{\alpha\beta}:=\sqrt{p_k}(U_t)_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,k)}$. Expanding $X\otimes\eta$, conjugating by $U_t$, and applying the coordinate formula [F1] gives, entry by entry, $\Phi_t(X)=\sum_{j,k=1}^mK_{jk}XK_{jk}^*$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$.

For a two-qubit instance take $Z=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$, $g>0$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, $H_{\mathrm{tot}}=\hbar g\,Z\otimes Z$ with $\hbar$ in joule-seconds, and $\eta=|+\rangle\langle+|$ where $|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$ in the chosen environment $Z$ eigenbasis. By [F3], the finite spectral exponential gives $U_t=e^{-igtZ\otimes Z}=\sum_{b=\pm1}V_b(t)\otimes|b\rangle\langle b|$, with $V_b(t)=\operatorname{diag}(e^{-ibgt},e^{ibgt})$. The partial trace in [F1] therefore gives $\Phi_t(X)=\frac12(V_{+1}(t)XV_{+1}(t)^*+V_{-1}(t)XV_{-1}(t)^*)$, so for $X=\begin{pmatrix}a&z\\w&c\end{pmatrix}$ the diagonal entries are unchanged and the off-diagonal entries are multiplied by $\kappa(t)=\frac12(e^{-2igt}+e^{2igt})=\cos(2gt)$, using [F7], [F8], and [F9].

By [F10], choose $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$ with $\cos\theta=0$ and $\sin\theta=1$; hence $\theta>0$. Set $s=\theta/(2g)>0$. Euler's identity [F9] gives $e^{i\theta}=i$, and [F7]–[F8] give $e^{-i\theta}=(e^{i\theta})^{-1}=-i$. Applying [F8] again yields $\kappa(s)=0$ and $\kappa(2s)=\frac12(e^{-2i\theta}+e^{2i\theta})=-1$.

For system basis indices $\beta,\delta$, unitarity of $U_t$ gives $(\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}^*K_{jk})_{\beta\delta}=\sum_{k=1}^mp_k\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{\alpha=1}^d\overline{(U_t)_{(\alpha,j),(\beta,k)}}(U_t)_{(\alpha,j),(\delta,k)}=\sum_kp_k\delta_{\beta\delta}=\delta_{\beta\delta}$. Thus $\sum_{j,k}K_{jk}^*K_{jk}=I_d$, so [F5] makes the Kraus map in step 1.1 completely positive and trace-preserving; by [F4], $\Phi_t$ is a finite channel.

Let $X_{\!P}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\rho_\pm=(I\pm X_{\!P})/2$. Since $X_{\!P}=X_{\!P}^*$ and $X_{\!P}^2=I$, each $\rho_\pm$ is a projection; since $\operatorname{Tr}X_{\!P}=0$, each has trace one. Steps 1.2 and 1.3 give $\Phi_s(\rho_+)=\Phi_s(\rho_-)=I/2$, while $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_+)=\rho_-$ and $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_-)=\rho_+$. Consequently $\Phi_{2s}(\rho_+)\ne\Phi_s(\Phi_s(\rho_+))=I/2$, so the semigroup law in [F6] fails. If a channel $V_{2s,s}$ satisfied $\Phi_{2s}=V_{2s,s}\circ\Phi_s$, it would send the equal matrices $\Phi_s(\rho_+)$ and $\Phi_s(\rho_-)$ to equal outputs, contradicting the two distinct outputs at $2s$. By step 2.1, the family consists of channels, so this contradiction proves it is not CP-divisible by [F6].

The family is **CP-divisible** when for every $0\leq s\leq t$ there exists a finite quantum channel $V_{t,s}:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi_t=V_{t,s}\circ\Phi_s$. CP-divisibility is this specified factorization property; the definition does not assert that it is a universal meaning of “Markovian”.

Let $d,e\geq1$ be integers, let $H_{\mathrm{in}}=\mathbb C^d$ and $H_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb C^e$ with their standard inner products, and write $M_d(\mathbb C)$ and $M_e(\mathbb C)$ for the complex linear maps on these spaces. A matrix $X$ is **positive semidefinite**, written $X\geq0$, when it is Hermitian and $\langle Xv,v\rangle\geq0$ for every vector $v$. The finite spectral convention in [[lem-qsm-matrix-state-calculus]] gives positive matrices their orthonormal eigenbases and positive square roots.

A **positive map** is a complex-linear map $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ such that $\Phi(X)\geq0$ whenever $X\geq0$. For each integer $r\geq1$, identify $M_r(\mathbb C)\otimes M_d(\mathbb C)$ with matrices on $\mathbb C^r\otimes\mathbb C^d$ in the ordered product basis. The map $\Phi$ is **completely positive** when $\operatorname{id}_r\otimes\Phi$ is positive for every such $r$, where $\operatorname{id}_r$ is the identity map on $M_r(\mathbb C)$.

The map $\Phi$ is **trace-preserving** when $\operatorname{Tr}(\Phi(X))=\operatorname{Tr}(X)$ for every $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$. A **finite quantum channel** is a complex-linear map that is both completely positive and trace-preserving, abbreviated CPTP. Unitality, $\Phi(I_d)=I_e$, is a separate condition and is not part of this definition.

This is a mathematical definition. A physical preparation, measurement, or open-system model must separately identify when one of these maps represents a physical transformation.

Let $d,e\geq1$ and let $\Phi:M_d(\mathbb C)\to M_e(\mathbb C)$ be complex-linear. Choose the standard input basis $(|i\rangle)_{i=1}^d$, let $E_{ij}=|i\rangle\langle j|$, and use the ordered tensor convention input-reference $\otimes$ output. Define the (unnormalized) Choi matrix

$$J(\Phi):=\sum_{i,j=1}^{d}E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_d(\mathbb C)\otimes M_e(\mathbb C).$$ Then $\Phi$ is completely positive if and only if $J(\Phi)\geq0$, and this holds if and only if there are $q\leq de$ matrices $K_1,\ldots,K_q:\mathbb C^d\to\mathbb C^e$ such that $$\Phi(X)=\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_aXK_a^*\qquad(X\in M_d(\mathbb C)).$$

The empty sum is allowed when $\Phi=0$. For any such Kraus representation, $\Phi$ is trace-preserving if and only if $\sum_{a=1}^{q}K_a^*K_a=I_d$.
