supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Use the following conventions on a complex inner-product space $H$ of dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. For an endomorphism $A$, define $\operatorname{Tr}A:=\sum_{j=1}^D\langle Ae_j,e_j\rangle$ in an orthonormal basis; step 3.1 proves basis independence. For any Hermitian $M$, its **positive spectral subspace** (called its positive support here) is $S_M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda>0}\ker(M-\lambda I)$; when $M\geq0$ this equals $(\ker M)^\perp$. Its support logarithm is $\log(M|_{S_M}):=\sum_{\lambda>0}(\log\lambda)P_\lambda|_{S_M}$, where $P_\lambda$ is the orthogonal projection onto that eigenspace. No value $\log0$ is assigned; for $M=0$ this is the unique endomorphism of the zero space. For the set $\mathcal D(H)$ of positive semidefinite Hermitian endomorphisms with trace one, a point $\rho$ is **extreme** if every equality $\rho=t\sigma+(1-t)\tau$ with $\sigma,\tau\in\mathcal D(H)$ and $0<t<1$ implies $\sigma=\tau=\rho$.

Let $H$ be a complex inner-product space of finite dimension $D\geq1$, with inner product linear in its first argument. Every Hermitian endomorphism $M$ has an orthonormal eigenbasis with real eigenvalues. For a real function $f$ on its finite spectrum, define $f(M)$ by its spectral projections; this definition is independent of the choice of eigenbasis. In particular positive square roots, exponentials, and logarithms on positive supports are well defined.

For a density matrix $\rho$ on $H$, meaning a Hermitian positive semidefinite operator with $\operatorname{Tr}\rho=1$, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho A)=\sum_jp_j\langle Au_j,u_j\rangle$ for bounded $A$, where $\rho=\sum_jp_j|u_j\rangle\langle u_j|$. The weighted form $(X,Y)_\rho=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho X^*Y)$ satisfies Cauchy–Schwarz, $|(X,Y)_\rho|^2\leq(X,X)_\rho(Y,Y)_\rho$. Finally, $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^2)\leq1$, with equality exactly for rank-one densities, and those are exactly the extreme points of the finite density-matrix set.

citations.quote: The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$.

(b) Let $E$ be a projection-valued measure on a measurable space $(X,\Sigma)$ acting on $H$ ([[def-projection-valued-measure]]). Then $\mu_\rho(B):=\operatorname{tr}(\rho E(B))$ is a well-defined probability measure on $(X,\Sigma)$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-probability-measure]]); it is given by the absolutely convergent series $\mu_\rho(B)=\sum_nw_n\|E(B)u_n\|^2$ in every expansion of (a), and reduces to $\mu_\rho(B)=\|E(B)u\|^2$ for a pure density operator $\rho=T_{u,u}$ with $\|u\|=1$.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad
V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n
\langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))=
\exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Assume Countable Choice, let $r\ge1$ and $\hbar>0$, and use the
Schrödinger quadratures of [[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. Put
$$D=\{f\in L^2(\mathbb R^r):x_jf\in L^2(\mathbb R^r),\ \partial_jf\in L^2(\mathbb R^r)\text{ for every }j\}.$$
For
$$\|f\|_{\mathrm{quad}}:=\|f\|_2+\sum_{j=1}^r(\|x_jf\|_2+\|\partial_jf\|_2),$$
the Schwartz space $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ is dense in $D$. The weak
derivatives in this definition are taken in the distributional sense and
agree with the Fourier-defined momentum
domains in the cited quadrature definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice, an integer $r\ge1$, and an action scale
$\hbar>0$. Inner products are linear in the first argument
([[def-inner-product-space]]). Use the Fock-to-Schrödinger unitary
$\mathcal U:\mathcal F_s(\mathbb C^r)\to L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ of
[[lem-nrqmx-finite-mode-fock-schr-identification]]. In Schrödinger coordinates
define the self-adjoint quadratures
$$Q_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(\sqrt\hbar\,x_j)\mathcal U,\qquad P_j=\mathcal U^{-1}(-i\sqrt\hbar\,\partial_{x_j})\mathcal U,$$
where $x_j$ is the real multiplication operator on its maximal domain. Fix the
angular-frequency Fourier unitary by
$$[\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}f](k)=(2\pi)^{-r/2}\int_{\mathbb R^r}e^{-ik\cdot x}f(x)\,dx\quad(f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)),$$
and define $-i\partial_{x_j}:=\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}^{-1}M_{k_j}\mathcal F_{\mathrm{ang}}$, where $M_{k_j}$ is multiplication by $k_j$ on its maximal domain. Their common Schwartz core satisfies
$$[Q_j,Q_k]=[P_j,P_k]=0,\qquad [Q_j,P_k]=i\hbar\delta_{jk}I.$$
Write $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$ and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
The Weyl unitary labelled by $z=(q_1,p_1,\ldots,q_r,p_r)$ is the unitary
whose grouped-coordinate formula, with $q=(q_1,\ldots,q_r)$ and
$p=(p_1,\ldots,p_r)$, is
$$[W(z)f](x)=e^{i\sqrt\hbar\,q\cdot(x+\sqrt\hbar p/2)}f(x+\sqrt\hbar p).$$
It obeys $W(z)W(z')=e^{-i\hbar z^TJz'/2}W(z+z')$ and is regular and
irreducible. By the finite-dimensional Stone–von Neumann theorem, every
nonzero irreducible regular Weyl system with this finite phase space and this
same nonzero central parameter is unitarily equivalent to it.

A density operator is a positive trace-class operator $\rho$ with
$\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$. Its quadrature second moments are finite when, for
one (equivalently every) spectral expansion
$\rho=\sum_n w_n|\psi_n\rangle\langle\psi_n|$ with $w_n>0$,
$\sum_nw_n\|R_j\psi_n\|^2<\infty$ for every $j$. For such a state define
$$d_j=\sum_nw_n\langle R_j\psi_n,\psi_n\rangle,\qquad V_{jk}=\operatorname{Re}\sum_nw_n \langle(R_j-d_jI)\psi_n,(R_k-d_kI)\psi_n\rangle.$$
These quantities are independent of the chosen orthonormal eigenbasis in
each eigenspace. The state is Gaussian when its Weyl characteristic function
has the form
$$\operatorname{tr}(\rho W(z))= \exp\!\left(i z^Td-\tfrac12z^TVz\right)\quad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r}),$$
with real $d$ and real symmetric $V$. Here $R_j$ has units
$\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, each Weyl label has units
$1/\sqrt{\mathrm{action}}$, and $V$ has units of action. No finite particle
number truncation is used.

Assume AC, $r\ge1$, and $\hbar>0$. Let $R=(Q_1,P_1,\ldots,Q_r,P_r)^T$,
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$,
and let $W(z)$ be the regular irreducible Weyl system of
[[def-nrqmx-finite-mode-symplectic-data]]. For every real
$S\in\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$, there is a unitary $M_S$ on
$L^2(\mathbb R^r)$ such that
$$M_S^*W(z)M_S=W(S^Tz)\qquad(z\in\mathbb R^{2r});$$
equivalently, $M_S^*RM_S=SR$ on the common transported Schwartz core.
Any two such implementers differ by a scalar of modulus one. The same
construction applies in every nonzero irreducible regular representation
with this finite phase space and fixed central parameter $\hbar$, after the
unitary equivalence of
[[thm-nrqmx-finite-weyl-uniqueness-interface]].

There is also a connected topological group
$\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ of normalized propagators of real
homogeneous quadratic Hamiltonians on this finite-mode Schrödinger space.
Here a unitary Schwartz automorphism means a unitary on $L^2(\mathbb R^r)$
whose restriction is a continuous linear bijection of the Schwartz space
$\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ with continuous inverse. A normalized propagator is defined on a compact interval $[0,T]$ with $0<T<\infty$. Its coefficient path $K:[0,T]\to M_{2r}(\mathbb R)$ has Lebesgue-integrable entries and is symmetric, $K(t)=K(t)^T$ for every $t$; an almost-everywhere symmetric integrable path is understood through a symmetric representative. In the displayed interleaved quadrature order put
$$H_t=\frac14\sum_{a,b=1}^{2r}K_{ab}(t)(R_aR_b+R_bR_a)\quad\text{on }\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r),$$
with no linear or scalar term. The path $U:[0,T]\to\mathcal U(L^2(\mathbb R^r))$ consists of unitary Schwartz automorphisms, has $U(0)=I$, and for every $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ its trajectory $U(t)f$ is absolutely continuous in each Schwartz seminorm $p_{\alpha,\beta}(g)=\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta g(x)|$ and satisfies $i\hbar\,\partial_tU(t)f=H_tU(t)f$ almost everywhere. Absolute continuity in a seminorm means the finite disjoint-interval condition for the seminorms of the increments. The construction below proves existence, uniqueness and continuity of the inverse path in the same pointwise Schwartz topology. Precisely, $\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ is the set of all endpoint operators $U(T)$ for this integrable-coefficient class, over all such $T$ and $K$. Piecewise-smooth coefficient paths are included and yield the same endpoint set, as proved below; the definition does not restrict the admissible propagators to that subclass.
Give $\operatorname{Mp}$ the topology of pointwise convergence of $U$ and
$U^{-1}$ on $\mathcal S(\mathbb R^r)$ in its Schwartz topology; give
$\operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R)$ its usual matrix topology.
The map
$$\pi:\operatorname{Mp}(2r,\mathbb R)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Sp}(2r,\mathbb R),\qquad M\longmapsto S \quad\text{when }M^*W(z)M=W(S^Tz),$$
is a two-fold covering homomorphism. Its two points over $S$ act by $M_S$
and $-M_S$ when $M_S$ denotes either normalized lift; an arbitrary Weyl
implementer may differ from them by any scalar phase. This connected double
cover and its unitary action are the metaplectic group and metaplectic
representation. All mode counts here are finite; no infinite-mode
implementation claim is part of the statement.

There is a unitary $M$ on finite-mode Fock, obtained by transporting an
individual finite symplectic implementer through the Fock–Schrödinger
unitary, such that $M^*aM=a'$ on the transported Schwartz core and
$M^*W(z)M=W(S_g^Tz)$ in grouped Weyl-label order.

Let $r\ge1$, $\hbar>0$, and
$J=\bigoplus_{j=1}^r\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$.
For every real symmetric positive definite $2r\times2r$ matrix $V$, there
are an interleaved symplectic matrix $S$ ($S^TJS=J$) and positive numbers
$\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_r$ such that
$$V=S D S^T,\qquad D=\operatorname{diag}(\nu_1,\nu_1,\ldots,\nu_r,\nu_r).$$
Moreover,
$$V+i\hbar J/2\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \nu_j\ge\hbar/2\ \text{for every }j.$$
Here $A\succeq0$ means the Hermitian matrix $A$ has nonnegative quadratic
form on every complex vector.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. The map $T\mapsto U(t)=e^{itT}$, computed by the
Borel functional calculus of $T$
([[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]]), is a bijection from the set of
self-adjoint operators on $H$ onto the set of strongly continuous

derivations.claim: For finitely supported $\psi$, each shift $\psi_n\mapsto\psi_{n-\delta}$ preserves the $\ell^2$ norm, so the triangle inequality gives $\|H_0\psi\|_2\le(\sum_{\delta\in S}\|T_\delta\|)\|\psi\|_2$. Hence $H_0$ extends uniquely to a bounded operator $H$. For finitely supported $\psi,\phi$, reindexing the finite sum gives $\langle H_0\psi,\phi\rangle=\sum_{m,\delta}\langle T_\delta\psi_m,\phi_{m+\delta}\rangle=\sum_{m,\delta}\langle\psi_m,T_\delta^*\phi_{m+\delta}\rangle=\langle\psi,H_0\phi\rangle$, because $T_\delta^*=T_{-\delta}$ and $S=-S$. Density and boundedness extend symmetry to all of $\mathcal H$, so $H=H^*$.

Under $k=2\pi x$, the functions $e^{-ik\cdot n}$ are the characters $e_{-n}(x)$. For each internal coordinate $a$, the corresponding scalar character family is complete and Parseval by [F1] and [F2]; summing the $r$ coordinate norm identities proves $\|\mathcal F_0\psi\|_{\mathcal K}=\|\psi\|_{\mathcal H}$. This norm identity agrees with the conjugate-linear-first pairings fixed in the Definition. The range contains every vector-valued trigonometric polynomial, a dense subspace of $\mathcal K$ by [F1] coordinatewise. Hence $\mathcal F_0$ extends uniquely to an isometry $\mathcal F:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$. Its range is closed because $\mathcal H$ is complete, and contains a dense subspace, so it is all of $\mathcal K$. Therefore $\mathcal F$ is unitary.

Direct substitution and the change of index $m=n-\delta$ give, for finitely supported $\psi$, $\mathcal F_0(H_0\psi)(k)=\sum_{\delta\in S}T_\delta e^{-ik\cdot\delta}\sum_m\psi_m e^{-ik\cdot m}=h(k)\mathcal F_0\psi(k)$. The finite sum defining $h$ is continuous and satisfies $\sup_k\|h(k)\|\le\sum_{\delta\in S}\|T_\delta\|$, so multiplication by $h$ is bounded on $L^2$. Extending the identity from the dense finitely supported sequences proves the claimed unitary equivalence. Also, $h(k)^*=\sum_\delta T_\delta^*e^{ik\cdot\delta}=\sum_\delta T_{-\delta}e^{-ik\cdot(-\delta)}=h(k)$, and its entries are trigonometric polynomials, hence smooth.

Write the eigenvalues of $h(k)$ in nondecreasing order as $\lambda_1(k)\le\cdots\le\lambda_r(k)$. For a Hermitian matrix $A$ with eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_r$, its $j$th eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda_j(A)=\max_{\dim L=r-j+1}\min_{\|v\|=1,\,v\in L}\langle Av,v\rangle$: every such $L$ intersects $\operatorname{span}(e_1,\ldots,e_j)$ nontrivially, while $L=\operatorname{span}(e_j,\ldots,e_r)$ attains the value. Since every unit-vector Rayleigh quotient changes by at most $\|A-B\|$ when $A$ is replaced by $B$, this formula gives $|\lambda_j(A)-\lambda_j(B)|\le\|A-B\|$. Thus each $\lambda_j(k)$ is continuous.

Fix $k_0$. The gap and continuity in step 1.4 let us choose disjoint small circles around the distinct eigenvalues in the selected block at $k_0$ so that, on some neighborhood of $k_0$, all selected eigenvalues stay inside their union and all complementary eigenvalues stay outside. The inverse matrix $(zI-h(k))^{-1}$ is $C^\infty$ in $k$ on this fixed contour: differentiating the inverse gives $\partial_j(zI-h)^{-1}=(zI-h)^{-1}(\partial_jh)(zI-h)^{-1}$, and repeated differentiation gives finite sums of products of smooth matrices. Therefore its contour integral is $C^\infty$. At each $k$, [F3] diagonalizes $h(k)$ and [F4] gives $2\pi i$ for an eigenvalue inside a component circle. For an exterior eigenvalue $\lambda$, write that circle as $z=c+Re^{it}$ and put $q=R/|\lambda-c|<1$. The finite geometric identity gives $(z-\lambda)^{-1}=-\sum_{j=0}^N(z-c)^j/(\lambda-c)^{j+1}+r_N(z)$ with $\sup|r_N|\le q^{N+1}/(|\lambda-c|(1-q))$. Each polynomial term integrates to zero because $\oint(z-c)^jdz=iR^{j+1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(j+1)t}dt=0$, and the remainder integral is bounded by $2\pi R\sup|r_N|\to0$. Thus the scalar exterior integral is zero. Summing the component circles gives coefficient $1$ on the selected eigenvalues and $0$ on their complement, proving that the matrix contour integral is exactly the selected orthogonal projector. On overlaps the local definitions project onto the same selected eigenspaces, so they agree and define the asserted global projector.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator on a complex Hilbert space $H$ with
spectral projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]). The **discrete
spectrum** $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ is the set of eigenvalues of $A$ that are
isolated points of $\sigma(A)$ and whose eigenspace is finite dimensional; the
**essential spectrum** is
$$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A):=\sigma(A)\setminus\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A),$$
with $\sigma(A)$ as in [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]].

For $H=\{0\}$ use its unique PVM directly: the spectrum and both parts
are empty and every projection has rank zero. Below suppose $H\ne\{0\}$,
as required by the cited spectral theorem.

**Spectral-projection description, with proofs.** Fix $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ and write
$P_\varepsilon:=E((\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon))$ for
$\varepsilon>0$.

Here rank means the algebraic dimension of the range when finite; rank
$=\infty$ means the range is not finite dimensional. The calculus
[[thm-unbounded-borel-functional-calculus]] gives the support facts:
$E(\mathbb R\setminus\sigma(A))=0$, and every open interval about a
spectral point has nonzero projection. Projections on disjoint sets have
orthogonal ranges, and $E(B)E(C)=E(B\cap C)$
[[def-projection-valued-measure]].

1. *$E(\{\lambda\})$ is the projection onto $\ker(A-\lambda)$.* If
   $x=E(\{\lambda\})x$, its scalar measure $E_x$ is supported on
   $\{\lambda\}$ by the projection identity. Thus
   $\int\mu^2dE_x=\lambda^2\|x\|^2<\infty$, so $x\in D(A)$, and
   $$\|(A-\lambda)x\|^2=\int|\mu-\lambda|^2dE_x=0.$$
   The domain and norm identities are supplied by the unbounded calculus and
   [[lem-unbounded-pvm-integral-is-well-defined-and-closed]]. Hence $Ax=\lambda x$.
   Conversely, for an eigenvector (or the zero vector) the same norm identity
   gives zero integral. On $\{|\mu-\lambda|\ge1/n\}$ this bounds the measure
   by $n^2$ times that zero integral; taking the countable union shows
   $E_x(\mathbb R\setminus\{\lambda\})=0$.
   Since $\|(I-E(\{\lambda\}))x\|^2$ equals this scalar measure,
   $E(\{\lambda\})x=x$.
2. *A finite-rank interval contains only finitely many spectral points.*
   If $P_\varepsilon$ has rank $r<\infty$ and its interval contained $r+1$
   distinct spectral points, choose disjoint small open intervals about those
   finitely many points, all contained in the given interval. Each has a
   nonzero projection by support. Choose one unit vector in each range.
   They are orthonormal vectors in $\operatorname{ran}P_\varepsilon$, hence
   linearly independent (take inner products with each vector), contradicting
   its dimension $r$. Thus there are at most $r$ spectral points there.
   In particular any $\lambda\in\sigma(A)$ with such a finite-rank
   $P_\varepsilon$ is isolated: take a smaller interval around $\lambda$
   excluding the other finitely many points. For that interval the projection
   is $E(\{\lambda\})$ by support, is nonzero by support, and has finite rank
   since its range lies in $\operatorname{ran}P_\varepsilon$. By item 1,
   $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of finite multiplicity.
3. *The two rank characterizations.* If $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$,
   an isolating interval has projection $E(\{\lambda\})$, of finite rank
   by item 1. Conversely, if $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue and some
   $P_\varepsilon$ has finite rank, item 2 proves it discrete. Hence
   $$\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue and some }P_\varepsilon\text{ has finite rank}.$$
   If $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, item 2 excludes every finite-rank
   interval. Conversely, if every $P_\varepsilon$ has infinite rank, each is
   nonzero, so support puts $\lambda$ in $\sigma(A)$, and the just-proved
   discrete characterization excludes it from $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$.
   Therefore
   $$\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{rank}P_\varepsilon=\infty\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0.$$
4. *$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ is closed.* If $\lambda_n\in
   \sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ and $\lambda_n\to\lambda$, then for every
   $\varepsilon>0$ some $n$ has $(\lambda_n-\varepsilon/2, \lambda_n+
   \varepsilon/2)\subseteq(\lambda-\varepsilon,\lambda+\varepsilon)$, so
   $\operatorname{rank}P_\varepsilon\ge\operatorname{rank}P_{\varepsilon/2}^{(n)}
   =\infty$ and $\lambda\in\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$ by item 3.

The closure conclusion is in $\mathbb R$, and also in $\mathbb C$ since
$\mathbb R$ is closed there. A spectral accumulation point has infinitely
many spectral points in every surrounding interval, so item 2 forces infinite
rank. An isolated eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity has its infinite-dimensional
eigenspace inside every interval range by item 1. Consequently an accumulation point of $\sigma(A)$ and an isolated eigenvalue of
infinite multiplicity both lie in $\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, and $\sigma(A)$
is the disjoint union of $\sigma_{\mathrm d}(A)$ and
$\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $H\ne\{0\}$ be a complex Hilbert space and
let $A$ be a self-adjoint operator with $A\ge-cI$ for some $c\ge0$. Let
$E_A$ be its spectral projection-valued measure, let
$Q(A)=D((A+cI)^{1/2})$, and define the associated form by
$$q_A[u]=\|(A+cI)^{1/2}u\|^2-c\|u\|^2\quad(u\in Q(A)).$$
Set $\alpha=\inf\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(A)$, with $\alpha=+\infty$ when the
essential spectrum is empty. For each integer $k\ge1$, put
$$\lambda_k(A)=\inf_{\substack{L\subseteq Q(A)\text{ linear},\ \dim L=k}}\ \sup_{\substack{u\in L\\\|u\|=1}}q_A[u],$$
where the infimum of an empty family is $+\infty$. Then $\lambda_k(A)$ is the
$k$th eigenvalue below $\alpha$, counted with multiplicity, when at least $k$
such eigenvalues exist; otherwise $\lambda_k(A)=\alpha$. If the inclusion
$Q(A)\hookrightarrow H$ is compact in the form norm
$\|u\|_{Q(A)}^2=q_A[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$, then $A$ has a complete orthonormal
eigenbasis; every eigenvalue has finite multiplicity, and the only possible
accumulation is at $+\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator on the nonzero
complex Hilbert space $H$. Then there is a unique regular projection valued
measure $E$ on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of $\mathbb R$ such that
$$
D(T)=\Bigl\{x\in H:\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda^2\,dE_x(\lambda)<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad Tx=\int_{\mathbb R}\lambda\,dE(\lambda)x\quad(x\in D(T)).
$$
Conversely, if $E$ is a regular projection valued measure on $\mathbb R$, then
the operator $\int\lambda\,dE$ with that domain is self-adjoint and its
spectral projection valued measure is $E$ again.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $T$ be a self-adjoint operator with spectral
projection valued measure $E$ on $\mathbb R$ acting on a complex Hilbert space $H$
([[thm-spectral-theorem-for-unbounded-self-adjoint-operators]]) and let
$f,g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be Borel. Write $u(T)=u(E)$, with the truncation definition below. If $H=\{0\}$, use its unique PVM and unique full-domain operator directly. Then:

1. $f(T)^*=\overline f(T)$;
2. $f(T)g(T)$ has domain $D(g(T))\cap D((fg)(T))$ and equals the restriction of
   $(fg)(T)$ to that domain, and its closure is $(fg)(T)$;
3. on $D(f(T))\cap D(g(T))$ the sum $f(T)+g(T)$ equals the restriction of
   $(f+g)(T)$, and the closure of $f(T)+g(T)$ is $(f+g)(T)$;
4. the spectrum of $f(T)$ is the essential range
   $\{z\in\mathbb C:E(f^{-1}(B_\varepsilon(z)))\ne0$ for every
   $\varepsilon>0\}$ of $f$ with respect to $E$;
5. if $f$ is continuous then that essential range is the closure of
   $f(\sigma(T))$, with the closure redundant when $f(\sigma(T))$ is closed.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $H$ be a nonzero complex Hilbert space whose inner product is linear in its first argument. Let $Q\subseteq H$ be a dense linear subspace, and let $q:Q\times Q\to\mathbb C$ be a symmetric sesquilinear form, linear in its first argument. Write $q[u]=q(u,u)$. Assume $q[u]\ge-c\|u\|^2$ for some real $c\ge0$, and assume $Q$ is complete in the form norm $\|u\|_{q,c}^2=q[u]+(c+1)\|u\|^2$; this is the meaning of a closed semibounded form here.

For an integer $n\ge1$, let $\phi_1,\ldots,\phi_n\in Q$ be linearly independent. The exact input matrices are the Gram matrix $G$ and form matrix $A$ with entries

$$G_{ij}=\langle\phi_j,\phi_i\rangle,\qquad A_{ij}=q(\phi_j,\phi_i)\qquad(1\le i,j\le n).$$

For every nonzero coefficient vector $z\in\mathbb C^n$, $z^*Gz=\|\sum_jz_j\phi_j\|^2>0$, so $G$ is positive definite; the symmetry of $q$ makes $A$ Hermitian.

The procedure is:

1. Form $G$ and $A$ from the supplied vectors and form, using exact entries.
2. Diagonalize the positive definite Hermitian matrix $G$ and form its unique positive inverse square root $G^{-1/2}$. Set $B=G^{-1/2}AG^{-1/2}$.
3. Diagonalize the Hermitian matrix $B$, listing its real eigenvalues $\rho_1\le\cdots\le\rho_n$ with multiplicity and selecting an orthonormal eigenbasis $y_1,\ldots,y_n$. For each $j$, set $c_j=G^{-1/2}y_j$ and return $(\rho_j,c_j)$.

Each returned vector satisfies $Ac_j=\rho_jGc_j$ and $c_j^*Gc_k=\delta_{jk}$. Repeated eigenvalues may return any orthonormal basis of the corresponding eigenspace. The procedure uses trial vectors in $Q$ and does not require them to lie in the operator domain of an associated self-adjoint operator. It operates on exact matrix entries: if quadrature or an approximate eigensolver supplies numerical data, this procedure alone supplies no error enclosure or certification for those approximations.

derivations.claim: Fix $V$ with $m=\dim V\ge k$. The algorithm in [F6] gives the eigenvalues $\rho_1\le\cdots\le\rho_m$ of the Hermitian form matrix relative to its positive Gram matrix and coefficient vectors $c_1,\ldots,c_m$. Their linear combinations $e_j:=\sum_{i=1}^m(c_j)_i\phi_i$ form an orthonormal eigenbasis of $V$: Gram normalization gives orthonormality, and the coefficient eigenvalue equation gives $q_A(e_j,e_i)=\rho_j\delta_{ij}$. For any $k$-dimensional $L\subseteq V$, the dimension formula forces $L\cap\operatorname{span}\{e_k,\ldots,e_m\}\ne\{0\}$; a unit vector in this intersection has form value at least $\rho_k$. The subspace $\operatorname{span}\{e_1,\ldots,e_k\}$ has supremum exactly $\rho_k$. Hence $\theta_k(V)=\rho_k$, the $k$th generalized Ritz eigenvalue.

Suppose $\lambda_k(A)<\alpha$. By [F2], $\lambda_1\le\cdots\le\lambda_k=\lambda_k(A)$ are the first $k$ isolated eigenvalues below $\alpha$, counted with multiplicity. Each corresponding eigenspace is finite-dimensional by [F1]. If $x\ne0$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $\lambda$, self-adjointness gives $\lambda\|x\|^2=\langle Ax,x\rangle=\langle x,Ax\rangle=\overline\lambda\|x\|^2$, so $\lambda$ is real. For $x\in\ker(A-\lambda_i I)$ and $y\in\ker(A-\lambda_j I)$ with $\lambda_i\ne\lambda_j$, this reality and self-adjointness give $\lambda_i\langle x,y\rangle=\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle=\lambda_j\langle x,y\rangle$, so the eigenspaces are orthogonal. Within each finite-dimensional eigenspace choose an orthonormal basis and take as many vectors as its multiplicity among $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_k$; concatenating these finite lists gives orthonormal eigenvectors $u_1,\ldots,u_k\in D(A)$ with $Au_j=\lambda_j u_j$.

Every $k$-dimensional subspace of $V$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $Q(A)$, so the infimum defining $\theta_k(V)$ is over a subfamily of the one defining $\lambda_k(A)$. Therefore $\theta_k(V)\ge\lambda_k(A)$.

For $u=\sum_{j=1}^k c_ju_j$ with $\sum_j|c_j|^2=1$, orthonormality gives $\|u\|=1$, while [F3] gives $q_A(u_j,u_i)=\langle Au_j,u_i\rangle=\lambda_j\delta_{ij}$. Hence $q_A[u]=\sum_j\lambda_j|c_j|^2\le\lambda_k(A)$.

For nested $V_n$, every $k$-subspace of $V_n$ is a $k$-subspace of $V_{n+1}$; thus $\theta_k(V_{n+1})\le\theta_k(V_n)$. By step 2.1 this sequence is bounded below by $\lambda_k(A)$, so it has a limit at least $\lambda_k(A)$.

Let $\varepsilon>0$ and put $M=(\sum_{j=1}^k\|u_j\|_{Q(A)}^2)^{1/2}$. For each $j$, density gives an approximation from some $V_{n_j}$; taking $N=\max_jn_j$ and using nesting, choose all $w_j\in V_N$ with $\|w_j-u_j\|_{Q(A)}<\delta$. For coefficients $c$ with $\sum_j|c_j|^2=1$, put $w=\sum_jc_jw_j$ and $u=\sum_jc_ju_j$. Then $\|w-u\|_{Q(A)}\le\sqrt{k}\delta$ and $\|u\|=1$, so $\|w\|\ge1-\sqrt{k}\delta$; taking $\sqrt{k}\delta<1/2$ ensures the $w_j$ are linearly independent. Writing $a(x,y)=q_A(x,y)+(c+1)\langle x,y\rangle$, [F5] and $a[x]\ge\|x\|^2$ give $|q_A(x,y)|\le(c+2)\|x\|_{Q(A)}\|y\|_{Q(A)}$. Since $\|u\|_{Q(A)}\le M$ and $\|w\|_{Q(A)}\le M+\sqrt{k}\delta$, this yields $|q_A[w]-q_A[u]|\le(c+2)\sqrt{k}\delta(2M+\sqrt{k}\delta)$ uniformly in $c$. Also $|\|w\|^2-1|\le\sqrt{k}\delta(2+\sqrt{k}\delta)$ uniformly, so for sufficiently small $\delta$, $\|w\|^2\ge1/2$. The bound just proved for $q_A[w]-q_A[u]$ and the uniform bound $|q_A[u]|\le\max_j|\lambda_j|$ then show that $q_A[w]/\|w\|^2$ converges uniformly to $q_A[u]$. The values $q_A[u]=\sum_j\lambda_j|c_j|^2$ are at most $\lambda_k(A)$ by step 2.2; hence choose $\delta$ small enough that every such $w$ satisfies $q_A[w]/\|w\|^2\le\lambda_k(A)+\varepsilon$.

The span of $w_1,\ldots,w_k$ is a $k$-dimensional subspace of $V_N$, so step 3.2 gives $\theta_k(V_N)\le\lambda_k(A)+\varepsilon$. By monotonicity from step 3.1 the same upper bound holds for all $n\ge N$. As $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, the limit in step 3.1 is at most $\lambda_k(A)$; combined with its lower bound from step 2.1 it equals $\lambda_k(A)$.

reference_flags.evidence: Step 1.1 with k=1 is the minimum Rayleigh quotient on the trial space; step 1.2 gives the ground-state upper bound.
Statement and steps 1.2–2.2 count multiplicities and use the full first-k eigenspace, including repeated eigenvalues.
Statement requires the strict inequality λ_k(A)<α for convergence; the threshold case λ_k(A)=α is outside steps 1.2–4.1.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume AC. Let $T$ be a bounded normal operator on a nonzero complex Hilbert
space $H$, with operator spectrum $\sigma(T)$
([[def-spectrum-and-resolvent-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then:

1. there is a unique regular projection valued measure $E$ on the Borel
   $\sigma$-algebra of the nonempty compact set $\sigma(T)\subseteq\mathbb C$
   such that $\int z\,dE(z)=T$ and, equivalently,
   $$\Phi_E(f)=f(T)\qquad\text{for every continuous }f:\sigma(T)\to\mathbb C,$$
   where $f(T)$ is the continuous functional calculus of
   [[thm-continuous-functional-calculus-for-bounded-normal-operators]] and
   $\Phi_E$ is the bounded Borel integral of the projection valued measure $E$;
   this $E$ is the **spectral projection valued measure** of $T$;
2. conversely, if $\Lambda\subseteq\mathbb C$ is nonempty and compact and $E$ is
   a regular projection valued measure on the Borel $\sigma$-algebra of
   $\Lambda$, then $T_E:=\int z\,dE(z)=\Phi_E(z)$ is a bounded normal operator
   with $\sigma(T_E)\subseteq\Lambda$ and $\|T_E\|\le\max_{z\in\Lambda}|z|$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space
([[def-measurable-space]], [[def-sigma-algebra]]) and let $H$ be a complex
Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]). A **projection valued measure** (PVM) on
$(X,\Sigma)$ is a map

$$E:\Sigma\longrightarrow\mathcal B(H),\qquad B\longmapsto E(B),$$

such that:

1. $E(B)$ is an **orthogonal projection** for every $B\in\Sigma$, that is, a
   bounded operator with $E(B)^2=E(B)=E(B)^*$; there is no finite-dimensional
   restriction;
2. $E(\varnothing)=0$ and $E(X)=I$;
3. $E(B\cap C)=E(B)E(C)$ for all $B,C\in\Sigma$;
4. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(B_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\Sigma$ with
   union $B$ and every $x\in H$, the series $\sum_nE(B_n)x$ converges in norm
   to $E(B)x$, that is
   $$E(B)x=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}E(B_n)x .$$

Clause 4 is **strong countable additivity**. A PVM is called **regular** when
$X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space ([[def-locally-compact-space]]), the
$\sigma$-algebra is the Borel $\sigma$-algebra, and every one of the finite
positive measures

$$E_x(B):=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle,\qquad x\in H,\ B\in\Sigma,$$

is a regular Borel measure ([[def-regular-borel-measure-on-an-lch-space]]). Inner
products are linear in the first variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); this fixed convention is the one
used for every pairing $E_{x,y}(B)=\langle E(B)x,y\rangle$ on this page.

**Well-definedness: the projection clause.** The conditions $P^2=P=P^*$ are
simultaneously meaningful and describe exactly the Hilbert orthogonal
projections, with no hidden finite-dimensional hypothesis. Indeed, for a
bounded $P$ with $P^2=P=P^*$ the range $\operatorname{ran}P$ is a linear
subspace, and for $y=Pw$ one has
$\langle x-Px,y\rangle=\langle P(x-Px),w\rangle=\langle Px-P^2x,w\rangle=0$, so
$x-Px\perp\operatorname{ran}P$; conversely $\langle Pz,Pz\rangle=\langle z,P^*Pz\rangle=\langle z,Pz\rangle=0$
for $z\perp\operatorname{ran}P$, so $z\in\ker P$, while
$\langle z,Px\rangle=\langle Pz,x\rangle=0$ for $z\in\ker P$ gives
$\ker P=(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$
([[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]],
[[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]). Hence
$\operatorname{ran}P=(\ker P)^\perp$ is closed, and the two defining properties
$Px\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $x-Px\in(\operatorname{ran}P)^\perp$ of
[[def-hilbert-orthogonal-projection]] show that $P=P_{\operatorname{ran}P}$ is
the Hilbert orthogonal projection onto a closed subspace, and conversely every
such $P_M$ is idempotent and self-adjoint by
[[lem-orthogonal-projection-is-linear-self-adjoint-contractive]] and
[[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]. Finally $P$ is
contractive: from $\langle Px,x\rangle=\langle Px,Px\rangle=\|Px\|^2$ and
Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|Px\|^2\le\|Px\|\,\|x\|$, so $\|Px\|\le\|x\|$ for all $x$,
and $\langle Px,x\rangle=\|Px\|^2\ge0$ is a nonnegative real number.

**Well-definedness: the regularity clause.** For an orthogonal projection value
the pairing $E_x(B)=\langle E(B)x,x\rangle$ is a nonnegative real number and
$E_x(X)=\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2<+\infty$, so every $E_x$ is a finite
nonnegative set function and the regularity requirement is a meaningful
condition on it; that each $E_x$ is genuinely a countably additive measure of
total mass $\|x\|^2$, and that the polarized pairings $E_{x,y}$ are finite
complex measures, is proved as
[[lem-scalar-and-complex-measures-from-a-pvm]] before either is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and let $f:X\to\mathbb C$ be bounded and $\Sigma$-measurable
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). Then:

1. there is a unique operator $\Phi_E(f)\in\mathcal B(H)$ with
   $$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,y\rangle=\int f\,dE_{x,y}\qquad(x,y\in H),$$
   and for every sequence $(s_n)$ of complex simple functions with
   $\|f-s_n\|_\infty\to0$ one has $\|\Phi_E(f)-\int s_n\,dE\|\to0$: the integral
   is obtained from uniform simple approximations and is independent of the
   approximating sequence;
2. $\|\Phi_E(f)\|\le\|f\|_\infty$, and for every $x\in H$
$$\langle\Phi_E(f)x,x\rangle=\int f\,dE_x,\qquad \|\Phi_E(f)x\|^2=\int|f|^2\,dE_x ;$$
3. the exact norm is the **$E$-essential supremum**
$$\|f\|_{E,\infty}:=\sup\bigl\{\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}:\ x\in H,\ \|x\|=1\bigr\}, \qquad \|\Phi_E(f)\|=\|f\|_{E,\infty},$$
   where $\|f\|_{\infty,E_x}$ denotes the essential supremum of the real measurable function $|f|$ with respect to
   the finite measure $E_x$ ([[def-essential-supremum-with-respect-to-a-measure]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(X,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space, let $H$ be a
nonzero complex Hilbert space, let $E$ be a projection valued measure on
$(X,\Sigma)$, and for a bounded measurable $f$ write $\Phi_E(f)=\int f\,dE$ for
the operator of [[thm-bounded-borel-pvm-integral]]. Then:

1. $\Phi_E$ is linear and unital: $\Phi_E(\mathbf 1_X)=I$ and
   $\Phi_E(af+bg)=a\Phi_E(f)+b\Phi_E(g)$ for bounded measurable $f,g$ and
   $a,b\in\mathbb C$;
2. $\Phi_E$ is multiplicative: $\Phi_E(fg)=\Phi_E(f)\Phi_E(g)$;
3. $\Phi_E$ preserves conjugation: $\Phi_E(\overline f)=\Phi_E(f)^*$;
4. if $(f_n)$ are bounded measurable with $\sup_n\|f_n\|_\infty<\infty$, $f$
   is bounded measurable, and $f_n\to f$ pointwise $E$-almost everywhere,
   meaning $E_x$-almost everywhere for every $x\in H$, then
   $\Phi_E(f_n)\to\Phi_E(f)$ in the strong operator topology.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

derivations.claim: For $u\in D(A)$, [F5] and nonnegativity give $\|(I+A)u\|\,\|u\|\ge|\langle(I+A)u,u\rangle|=\|u\|^2+\langle Au,u\rangle\ge\|u\|^2$. Hence $I+A$ is injective and bounded below by $1$. To prove $A$ is closed, suppose $u_n\in D(A)$, $u_n\to u$, and $Au_n\to v$. For every $w\in D(A)$, self-adjointness gives $\langle Aw,u\rangle=\lim_n\langle Aw,u_n\rangle=\lim_n\langle w,Au_n\rangle=\langle w,v\rangle$; by the defining criterion for the adjoint, $u\in D(A^*)$ and $A^*u=v$. Self-adjointness, including equality of domains, yields $u\in D(A)$ and $Au=v$. Thus $A$ is closed. For $w\in D((I+A)^*)$, subtracting the identity term from the defining adjoint relation gives $w\in D(A^*)$ and $(I+A)^*w=w+A^*w$. Conversely, if $w\in D(A^*)$, then $\langle(I+A)u,w\rangle=\langle u,w+A^*w\rangle$ for every $u\in D(A)$, so $w\in D((I+A)^*)$ with $(I+A)^*w=w+A^*w$. Thus $(I+A)^*=I+A^*=I+A$ with domain $D(A)$, so $I+A$ is self-adjoint. Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra. For $x,y\in \mathfrak g$, let $\operatorname{ad}_x,\operatorname{ad}_y\in \operatorname{End}(\mathfrak g)$ be the adjoint operators. The **Killing form** of $\mathfrak g$ is the symmetric bilinear form

$$B(x,y):=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{ad}_x\operatorname{ad}_y).$$

The trace is taken on the finite-dimensional vector space $\mathfrak g$. This is the invariant form used to define dual bases, the root-theoretic vectors $H_\alpha$, and the quadratic Casimir element on this page.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a finite-dimensional complex semisimple Lie algebra with Killing form $B$. A **Cartan subalgebra** here means a maximal toral subalgebra: a maximal abelian subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ all of whose adjoint operators are diagonalizable. Such subalgebras exist, and every one is self-centralizing. There is a decomposition
$$\mathfrak g=\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha,\qquad \mathfrak g_\alpha=\{x:[h,x]=\alpha(h)x\text{ for all }h\in\mathfrak h\},$$
where the nonzero weights $\Phi$ are finite, span $\mathfrak h^*$, and each root space has dimension one. The form is nondegenerate on $\mathfrak h$, pairs $\mathfrak g_\alpha$ perfectly with $\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}$, and all other weight-space pairings are zero. Define $H_\alpha\in\mathfrak h$ by $B(H_\alpha,h)=\alpha(h)$. Then $c_\alpha=\alpha(H_\alpha)\ne0$, and $h_\alpha=2H_\alpha/c_\alpha$ admits root vectors $e_\alpha,f_\alpha$ with $[e_\alpha,f_\alpha]=h_\alpha$, $[h_\alpha,e_\alpha]=2e_\alpha$, $[h_\alpha,f_\alpha]=-2f_\alpha$.

The real span $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ of the $h_\alpha$ is a real form of $\mathfrak h$ on which $B$ is positive definite. On $E=\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}^*$ with the dual form, $\Phi$ is a finite reduced crystallographic root system and $h_\alpha$ is its coroot. In particular the preceding abstract finite-Weyl conventions apply. For nonproportional roots $\alpha,\beta$, the root spaces with roots $\beta+k\alpha$ form one simple rank-one module: the integers occurring are a consecutive interval, reflection in $\alpha$ reverses it, and raising or lowering between adjacent spaces is nonzero with the positive $fe,ef$ coefficients of $V_m$. The adjoint operators of all root vectors are nilpotent. For any positive system, normalized triples $e_i,f_i,h_i$ of its simple roots generate $\mathfrak g$, and the $h_i$ form a basis of $\mathfrak h$. All assertions include $\mathfrak g=0$ and use no AC.

Let $\mathfrak g$ be a complex semisimple Lie algebra, and let $B$ be the Killing form from [[def-killing-form-of-a-semisimple-lie-algebra]]. Choose dual bases $x_1,\dots,x_n$ and $x^1,\dots,x^n$ with respect to $B$, so $B(x_i,x^j)=\delta_i^j$. The **quadratic Casimir element** is

$$C:=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x^i \in U(\mathfrak g).$$

By [[lem-the-casimir-element-is-independent-of-dual-bases]], this element is independent of the chosen dual bases.

Fix a positive root system $\Phi^+$ as in [[thm-triangular-decomposition-from-a-chosen-positive-root-system]]. The **Weyl vector** for that choice is

$$\rho:=\frac12\sum_{\alpha\in \Phi^+} \alpha \in \mathfrak h^*.$$

This is the shift used in the dot action and in the quadratic Casimir eigenvalue formula on this page.

Let $M$ be a cyclic highest-weight module of highest weight $\lambda$. Then the quadratic Casimir element acts on $M$ by the scalar

$$ (\lambda,\lambda+2\rho), $$

where the pairing on $\mathfrak h^*$ is induced by the Killing form and $\rho$ is the Weyl vector from [[def-weyl-vector-rho-for-a-chosen-positive-system]].

derivations.claim: The adjoint module is irreducible because any invariant subspace of $\mathfrak g$ is an ideal and $\mathfrak g$ is simple. A highest-root vector generates this nonzero module, so [F5] with $\lambda=\theta$ says the Casimir [F3] acts on $\mathfrak g$ by a scalar $\lambda_{\mathrm{ad}}=(\theta,\theta+2\rho)_{\mathrm{Kill}}$. On the other hand, for any Killing-dual bases $(x_a),(x^a)$, its adjoint action is $\sum_a\operatorname{ad}_{x_a}\operatorname{ad}_{x^a}$; its trace is $\sum_a B_{\mathrm{Kill}}(x_a,x^a)=\dim\mathfrak g$ by [F1]. Since the action is scalar on the nonzero space $\mathfrak g$, this trace gives $\lambda_{\mathrm{ad}}=1$.

Since $B_0=B_{\mathrm{Kill}}/c$, the defining equations give $H_{\lambda,0}=cH_{\lambda,\mathrm{Kill}}$ for every $\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*$, and hence $(\lambda,\mu)_0=c(\lambda,\mu)_{\mathrm{Kill}}$. The choice of $c$ gives $(\theta,\theta)_0=2$. By definition, $\theta^\vee=H_{\theta,0}$, and $(\rho,\theta)_0=B_0(H_{\rho,0},H_{\theta,0})=\rho(H_{\theta,0})=\rho(\theta^\vee)=h^\vee-1$. Therefore $\lambda_{\mathrm{ad}}=(\theta,\theta+2\rho)_{\mathrm{Kill}}=c^{-1}(2+2(h^\vee-1))=2h^\vee/c$.
Equating the two expressions for $\lambda_{\mathrm{ad}}$ from steps 1.1 and 2.1 gives $1=2h^\vee/c$, hence $c=2h^\vee$. Substitution into $B_0=B_{\mathrm{Kill}}/c$ proves the asserted form identity.

The Cook condition is
that $t\mapsto\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is norm-$C^1$ on
$[1,\infty)$ and, for constants $C_{\eta,f}\ge0$ and
$\epsilon_{\eta,f}>0$,
$$\left\|\frac{d}{dt}\Psi_t^\eta(f)\right\|\le C_{\eta,f}(1+t)^{-1-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\qquad(t\ge1).$$

The bosonic and fermionic Fock Hilbert spaces are the square-summable direct
sums
$\mathcal F_s(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_s^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$ and
$\mathcal F_a(H)=\{(\Psi_n)_{n\ge0}:\Psi_n\in H_a^{(n)},\
\sum_n\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\}$, with the componentwise inner product.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) for the Lebesgue-measure interfaces. Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space, let $a<b$, and let $f:[a,b]\to X$ be continuous. Differentiation uses the underlying real structure. Then $G(t):=\int_a^t f(s)\,ds$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ and has the corresponding one-sided derivatives at $a,b$, with $G'(t)=f(t)$, and this derivative extends continuously to $[a,b]$. Consequently, if $\varphi:[a,b]\to X$ is continuous, differentiable on $(a,b)$ with $\varphi'$ continuous on $(a,b)$ and extendable to a continuous $X$-valued function on $[a,b]$, then $\int_a^b\varphi'(s)\,ds=\varphi(b)-\varphi(a)$. The Bochner integral here is the one of [[def-bochner-integrable-function]]; the identities also hold for continuous curves on $[0,\infty)$ restricted to compact subintervals.

If $f:\Omega\to X$ is Bochner integrable, then for every measurable $E$,

$$\left\|\int_E f\,d\mu\right\|\leq\int_E\|f\|\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim:
Fix $1\le s\le t$. If $s=t$ the increment inequality is immediate.
If $s<t$, restrict $r\mapsto\Psi_r^\eta(f)$ to $[s,t]$. By [F1] this is a
continuous curve into the Banach space $\mathcal H$, differentiable on $(s,t)$
with derivative extending continuously to $[s,t]$.
The contract's Countable Choice premise satisfies the hypothesis of [F3], so
the Banach-valued fundamental theorem gives
$\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)=\int_s^t\partial_r\Psi_r^\eta(f)\,dr$.
The derivative is continuous and hence Bochner integrable on this compact
interval; [F4] then gives
$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)\|\le\int_s^t
\|\partial_r\Psi_r^\eta(f)\|\,dr$.

Apply the derivative bound in [F1] and integrate the scalar power:
$$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)-\Psi_s^\eta(f)\|\le \frac{C_{\eta,f}}{\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\bigl((1+s)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}-(1+t)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}\bigr)\le \frac{C_{\eta,f}}{\epsilon_{\eta,f}}(1+s)^{-\epsilon_{\eta,f}}.$$
As $s\to\infty$, the last expression tends to zero uniformly for $t\ge s$.
Thus $\Psi_t^\eta(f)$ is Cauchy as $t\to\infty$; completeness gives a limit
$W_\eta f\in\mathcal H$. Taking $t\to\infty$ in the first inequality gives
the claimed rate, and taking $s=1$ gives
$\|\Psi_t^\eta(f)\|\le\|\Psi_1^\eta(f)\|+
C_{\eta,f}/\epsilon_{\eta,f}$ for every $t\ge1$.

For $f,g\in\mathcal D_\sigma$, linearity of each $\Psi_t^\eta$ and norm
convergence from 2.1 imply
$W_\eta(af+bg)=aW_\eta f+bW_\eta g$ for all scalars $a,b\in\mathbb C$:
apply the triangle inequality to the finite linear combination and pass to
the limit. Hence $W_\eta$ is linear on $\mathcal D_\sigma$.

By continuity of the Hilbert inner product and the assumed limit [A1],
$(W_\eta f,W_\eta g)=\lim_{t\to\infty}
(\Psi_t^\eta(f),\Psi_t^\eta(g))=(f,g)_{\mathcal F,1}$.
Setting $g=f$ proves preservation of norm, so $W_\eta$ is an isometry on
$\mathcal D_\sigma$.

If $(f_n)$ in $\mathcal D_\sigma$ converges in its Hilbert-space closure,
then $(W_\eta f_n)$ is Cauchy because
$\|W_\eta f_n-W_\eta f_k\|=\|f_n-f_k\|$. Completeness of $\mathcal H$
defines a limit independent of the approximating sequence; the same equality
passes to the limit. This is the unique isometric extension to
$\overline{\mathcal D_\sigma}$. No surjectivity onto $\mathcal H$ follows.

Fix $d\geq1$. A pair potential is an even Borel function $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. For a finite list of positions $X=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)$, set $U_0=U_1=0$ and
$$U_N(X)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\phi(x_i-x_j).$$
The value $+\infty$ is allowed and represents a forbidden configuration; $-\infty$ is not allowed.

The potential is **stable** if some finite $B\geq0$ satisfies $U_N(X)\geq-BN$ for every $N$ and every $X$. Fix a cell side $\ell>0$ and the half-open cubic tiling $C_k=\ell(k+[0,1)^d)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^d$, and let $n_k(X)$ count the positions of $X$ in $C_k$. The potential is **cell-superstable** if there are constants $A_*>0$ and $B_*\geq0$ such that
$$U_N(X)\geq A_*\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^d}n_k(X)^2-B_*N$$
for every finite configuration; the sum is finite for finite $X$.

For disjoint finite cell-index sets $I,J$, let $W_{I,J}(X)$ be the sum of pair terms with one point in a cell indexed by $I$ and the other in a cell indexed by $J$. The potential is **lower regular** for this tiling if a nonnegative envelope $\Psi:\mathbb Z^d\setminus\{0\}\to[0,\infty)$ exists with $\sum_{k\ne0}\Psi(k)<\infty$ and
$$W_{I,J}(X)\geq-\sum_{k\in I}\sum_{l\in J}\Psi(k-l)n_k(X)n_l(X)$$
for all such $I,J,X$. The ordered-pair convention in this formula is fixed as written.

A **decreasing-integrable tail bound** means that for some $R_0\geq0$ there is a nonnegative nonincreasing function $\psi:[R_0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that $|\phi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|)$ for $|x|\geq R_0$ and $\int_{R_0}^{\infty}\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty$. This explicit envelope condition is stronger than bare Lebesgue integrability of an arbitrary signed tail. Stability, cell-superstability, lower regularity, and a tail bound are separate properties; none is inferred from finite range alone.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in The exponential series converges absolutely for every real argument. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of The factorial $n!$ and the falling factorial $n^{\underline{k}}$, defined by recursion in $\mathbb{N}$, $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field, Canonical naturals are positive and strictly increasing), and powers and series are those of Integer powers $a^m$ and Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series.

This is a real power series centred at $0$ (A real power series about a centre, its interval of convergence, and its radius in $[0,+\infty]$). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space (Topology on a set, open and closed sets, clopen sets, the closed-set axiomatisation, and the coarser/finer comparison). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by Nonempty intersections of sigma-algebras are sigma-algebras, so the generated sigma-algebra exists and is minimal.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space (Measure spaces). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ (The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
(The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space).

A function $f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ is **measurable** when
$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

The **extended real line** is

$$\overline{\mathbb{R}} := \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty,+\infty\}$$

with the total order extending the usual order on $\mathbb{R}$ and satisfying
$-\infty < x < +\infty$ for every real $x$
([[def-extended-reals]]).

Its **Borel sigma-algebra** is the Borel sigma-algebra of that ordered
topological line in the sense of [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]. On this page it is
denoted $\mathcal{B}(\overline{\mathbb{R}})$ and is generated by the rays

$$\{\, (a,+\infty] : a \in \mathbb{R} \,\}.$$

In particular, $\{+\infty\}$ and $\{-\infty\}$ are Borel sets.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of Borel measurable and Lebesgue measurable functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space and let
$f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ be measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra on
the extended real line. Products of functions use
$\odot_X$ from A total pointwise product for extended-real-valued functions, and $cf$
abbreviates $\underline c\odot_X f$ for the constant function $\underline c$.
The magnitude function is $|f|=\max(f,-f)$ as in
The positive and negative parts of a function. Then:

1. $cf$ is measurable for every real scalar $c$;
2. $\max(f,g)$, $\min(f,g)$, $|f|$, $f^+$, and $f^-$ are measurable;
3. if the partial pointwise sum $f+g$ is defined at every point, then it is measurable;
4. the pointwise product $fg:=f\odot_X g$ is measurable.

Let $m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
one has
$$\mathcal B(\mathbb R^m)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n) = \mathcal B(\mathbb R^{m+n}).$$

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
(The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$)). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (The Borel sigma-algebra of a topological space) is Lebesgue
measurable (Lebesgue measurable sets, the family $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, and the restricted set function $\lambda_n$). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (Translation of a subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. If $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ are measurable, then
$$\int(f+g)\,d\mu=\int f\,d\mu+\int g\,d\mu.$$

A **simple graph** is an ordered pair $G=(V,E)$ in which $V$ is a set and

$$E \subseteq [V]^2 := \{\, \{u,v\} \subseteq V : u \ne v \,\}.$$

The elements of $V=V(G)$ are the **vertices** and the elements of $E=E(G)$ are
the **edges**. Thus a simple graph has no loops and no parallel edges.

This is the same incidence convention as [[def-finite-simple-graph]], with the
word "finite" removed from the hypothesis on $V$. Whenever a statement on this
page is made for a simple graph, it allows an arbitrary vertex set unless
finiteness is stated separately.

A **finite simple graph** is an ordered pair $G=(V,E)$ in which $V$ is a finite
set and

$$E\subseteq [V]^2:=\{\,\{u,v\}\subseteq V: u\ne v\,\}.$$

The elements of $V=V(G)$ are the **vertices** and the elements of $E=E(G)$ are
the **edges**. Thus every edge has two distinct endpoints, there are no loops,
and an unordered pair of vertices occurs as at most one edge. Finiteness and the
notation $|V|$ and $|E|$ are those of [[def-finite-cardinality]].

When no qualifier is present, the word **graph** has this meaning.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple graph in the sense of
[[def-simple-graph-without-a-finiteness-hypothesis]].

A **walk**, **closed walk**, **trail**, **path**, and **cycle** in $G$ are
defined exactly as in [[def-graph-walk-trail-path-and-cycle]], with no
finiteness hypothesis on $V$. In particular, a walk is a finite vertex list
$$(v_0,\dots,v_\ell)$$
with $\{v_{i-1},v_i\}\in E$ for each $1 \le i \le \ell$, and a path is a walk
with distinct vertices.

Vertices $u,v \in V$ are **connected** when some path in $G$ has endpoints $u$
and $v$. The graph $G$ is **connected** when $V \ne \emptyset$ and every two
vertices of $G$ are connected.

For $v \in V$, the **connected component** of $v$ is the induced subgraph on
$$C_G(v) := \{\, u \in V : u \text{ is connected to } v \,\}.$$

These are the same notions as in [[def-connected-graph-and-connected-component]],
again with the finiteness hypothesis removed.

Let $G$ be a simple graph.

A **cycle** in $G$ is a cycle in the sense of
[[def-graph-walk-trail-path-and-cycle]], that is, a closed walk of length at
least $3$ whose vertices are distinct except for the repeated endpoint.

The graph $G$ is **acyclic** if it contains no cycle.

A **tree** is a connected acyclic simple graph.

A **forest** is an acyclic simple graph.

Let $G$ be a graph. A **spanning tree** of $G$ is a spanning subgraph $T$ of $G$ that is a tree ([[def-subgraph-induced-subgraph-and-spanning-subgraph]], [[def-tree-forest-and-leaf]]). Equivalently,

$$V(T)=V(G),\qquad E(T)\subseteq E(G),$$

and $T$ is connected and acyclic.

The null graph has no spanning tree under the library convention that a tree is nonempty and connected.
A finite graph $G$ is connected if and only if it has a spanning tree.
Every finite graph has only finitely many spanning trees.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathbb{R}$.

- $m$ is a **maximum** (or *greatest element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $s \le m$
  for every $s \in S$.
- $m$ is a **minimum** (or *least element*) of $S$ if $m \in S$ and $m \le s$
  for every $s \in S$.

A set has at most one maximum: if $m_1$ and $m_2$ are both maxima then
$m_1 \in S$ gives $m_1 \le m_2$ and $m_2 \in S$ gives $m_2 \le m_1$, so
$m_1 = m_2$ by antisymmetry of the order, which is immediate from the trichotomy
axiom of an ordered field (Ordered field, Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)).
The same argument applies to minima, so we may write $\max S$ and $\min S$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: The nonempty finite subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the listable ones proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field). The **absolute value** of
$x \in F$ is

$$|x| \;:=\; \begin{cases} x & \text{if } x \ge 0, \\ -x & \text{if } x < 0. \end{cases}$$

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$, with
$|x|$ the absolute value (Absolute value in an ordered field). Then

$$|x| \ge 0; \quad |x| = 0 \iff x = 0; \quad -|x| \le x \le |x|; \quad |-x| = |x|; \quad |xy| = |x|\,|y|;$$

and, for every $c > 0$, one has $|x| < c \iff -c < x < c$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field (Ordered field) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$|x + y| \le |x| + |y|.$$

Let $S$ be a finite set, $n := \lvert S\rvert$ (The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and
let $a : S \to \mathbb{R}$ or $a : S \to \mathbb{N}$, written $a_i$ for $a(i)$.
Choose a bijection $\varphi : n \to S$, which exists because $S \approx n$
(Equinumerous sets, $A \approx B$ and $A \preceq B$), and set

$$\sum_{i \in S} a_i := \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)}, \qquad \prod_{i \in S} a_i := \prod_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

the right-hand sides being the iterated operations of Finite sums and finite products, by recursion when the
values are real and of Finite sums and finite products of natural numbers, $\sum_{k<n} a_k$ and $\prod_{k<n} a_k$ in $\mathbb{N}$ when they are natural.

**Independence of the enumeration, which is the content of the definition.** Let
$\varphi, \psi : n \to S$ be two bijections. Then $\pi := \varphi^{-1} \circ \psi$
is a bijection $n \to n$ (Injection, surjection, bijection), and
$a_{\psi(k)} = a_{\varphi(\pi(k))}$ for every $k < n$. Applying
A finite sum is unchanged by a permutation of its index range: $\sum_{k<n} a_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} a_k$ for every bijection $\pi : n \to n$ to the list $c_k := a_{\varphi(k)}$
gives

$$\sum_{k<n} a_{\psi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_{\pi(k)} = \sum_{k<n} c_k = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)},$$

and identically for products. So the value does not depend on which bijection is
used, and $\sum_{i \in S} a_i$ is a single well-determined element.

**No choice principle is involved.** The definition does not select an
enumeration: it asserts that all enumerations give the same value, and that value
is what the notation names. Only one bijection is ever produced at a time, from a
set already known to be nonempty.

**Three clauses, recorded here because the page uses them constantly.**

**(a) The bridge to the old notation.** Taking $S = n$ and $\varphi = \mathrm{id}_n$,
which is legitimate since $\lvert n\rvert = n$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in n} a_i = \sum_{k<n} a_k, \qquad \prod_{i \in n} a_i = \prod_{k<n} a_k .$$

So the new notation **extends** the sum over an initial segment rather than
competing with it, and every law proved for the latter is available for the
former whenever the index set is a natural number.

**(b) Reindexing along a bijection.** If $h : T \to S$ is a bijection of finite
sets, then $\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$, and likewise for
products. Indeed $\lvert T\rvert = \lvert S\rvert = n$ by transport
(The cardinality $\lvert A\rvert$ of a finite set), and if $\varphi : n \to S$ is a bijection then
$h^{-1} \circ \varphi : n \to T$ is one, so
$\sum_{j \in T} a_{h(j)} = \sum_{k<n} a_{h(h^{-1}(\varphi(k)))} = \sum_{k<n} a_{\varphi(k)} = \sum_{i \in S} a_i$.

**(c) The empty index set and a constant summand.** $\lvert\varnothing\rvert = 0$,
so $\sum_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 0$ and $\prod_{i \in \varnothing} a_i = 1$ by
the base clause of the recursion. And for a constant $c$, clause (a) together
with the constant clause of Laws of finite sums and products in $\mathbb{N}$, and $\iota\big(\sum_{k<n} a_k\big) = \sum_{k<n} \iota(a_k)$
in $\mathbb{N}$, or clause 2 of Laws of finite sums and finite products in $\mathbb{R}$, gives

$$\sum_{i \in S} c = \lvert S\rvert \cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{N}), \qquad \sum_{i \in S} c = \iota(\lvert S\rvert)\cdot c \quad (c \in \mathbb{R}),$$

the second with $\iota$ written out because $\lvert S\rvert$ is a natural number
and not an element of $\mathbb{R}$ (The canonical natural $\iota(n) = n \cdot 1_F$ of a field).

Let $A$ be a finite set and $n := \lvert A\rvert$. Then the power set
$\mathcal{P}(A)$ is finite and

$$\lvert\mathcal{P}(A)\rvert = 2^{\,n},$$

the power being the $\mathbb{N}$-valued exponentiation of [[def-nat-power]].
Moreover $n < 2^{\,n}$.

The last inequality is the quantitative form, for finite $A$, of Cantor's
theorem $A \prec \mathcal{P}(A)$ ([[thm-cantor-powerset]]), which holds for every
set whatsoever. The two statements are consistent and the proof below derives the
inequality from Cantor's theorem rather than leaving them side by side.

Let $A$ be a finite set ([[def-countable]]) and let $B \subseteq A$. Then:

1. $B$ is finite;
2. $\lvert B\rvert \le \lvert A\rvert$ ([[def-finite-cardinality]]);
3. $\lvert B\rvert = \lvert A\rvert$ if and only if $B = A$;
4. every injection $f : A \to A$ is a bijection, and every surjection
   $f : A \to A$ is a bijection.

Clause 3 is the finite form of the Dedekind statement: a finite set is not
equinumerous with a proper subset of itself. Clause 4 is its working form, and
**finiteness is exactly the hypothesis that fails in general**: the successor map
is an injection of $\mathbb{N}$ into itself that is not surjective, which is the
false statement recorded on this page's companion.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix $n\geq2$ and positions $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, and put $f_{ij}=f_\beta(x_i-x_j)$. For each nonempty label set $I$, let $U_I=\sum_{i<j,\ i,j\in I}v(x_i-x_j)$. If $U_I=+\infty$, the adopted convention gives $e^{-2\beta U_I}=0$; otherwise all pair values in the sum are finite. In either case the exponential definition and addition law [F2], together with evenness of $v$, give $\prod_{i\in I}\prod_{j\in I\setminus\{i\}}|1+f_{ij}|=e^{-2\beta U_I}$. Stability and monotonicity [F1, F2] imply this product is at most $e^{2\beta B|I|}$. Writing $q_i=\prod_{j\in I\setminus\{i\}}|1+f_{ij}|$, all $q_i$ are nonnegative and their product is at most $e^{2\beta B|I|}$; hence some $r\in I$ has $q_r\leq e^{2\beta B}$.

The maps $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\mapsto x_i-x_j$ are continuous and hence Borel under [A1, F4]. Since $v$ is Borel [F1], composition with $v$ is Borel [F4]. The adopted map $u\mapsto e^{-\beta u}$ on $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ is Borel: on $\mathbb R$ it is continuous by [F2], and its value at the Borel singleton $+\infty$ is $0$ by [F4]. Thus $f_\beta$ is Borel, and $U_n$ is a finite sum of finite products of Borel factors [F4]. The same composition and arithmetic facts on $\mathbb R^{dn}$ make each tree weight Borel. Repeated application of the two-factor identity in [F5] identifies the finite product Borel sigma-algebra, and the Borel-to-Lebesgue clause in [F5] makes the tree weight measurable for product Lebesgue measure.

For disjoint label sets $I,J$, define $g(I,J)$ as the finite sum of $\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}f_{ij}$ over simple graphs on $I\cup J$ in which every connected component meets $I$; set $g(\varnothing,\varnothing)=1$ and $g(\varnothing,J)=0$ for nonempty $J$. Evenness in [F1] makes each unordered-edge weight independent of which endpoint is written first. Choose $r\in I$ as in step 1.1 and put $I'=I\setminus\{r\}$. In each graph let $K\subseteq J$ be the neighbors of $r$ in $J$. Edges from $r$ to $I'$ are independently present or absent, and summing their two weights gives $\prod_{j\in I'}(1+f_{rj})$. Deleting $r$ leaves a graph all of whose components meet $I'\cup K$, and conversely any such graph reconstructs exactly one original graph after adjoining the chosen $r$-edges. Thus $g(I,J)=\left(\prod_{j\in I'}(1+f_{rj})\right)\sum_{K\subseteq J}\left(\prod_{k\in K}f_{rk}\right)g(I'\cup K,J\setminus K)$.

Under Countable Choice [A1], the product Lebesgue spaces are sigma-finite by [F3], so Tonelli [F6] applies. Root a labelled tree $T$ at $1$. A finite tree with at least two vertices has at least two leaves: a longest simple path exists in a finite graph, and each endpoint has exactly one incident edge, since another incident edge would either extend the path or create a cycle. At least one of the two leaves differs from the root. Deleting a leaf preserves connectedness and acyclicity on the remaining vertices, so the remaining graph is a tree unless only the root remains. Delete such a leaf and integrate its coordinate first. Translation invariance [F7] and evenness of $f_\beta$ give $\int_{\mathbb R^d}|f_\beta(x_\ell-x_j)|\,dx_\ell=C_\beta$. Repeating after each leaf deletion proves that the pinned tree integral is $C_\beta^{n-1}$.

Let $\mathcal F_I(J)$ be the forests on $I\cup J$ with exactly one vertex from $I$ in each tree, and define $h(I,J)=e^{2\beta B(|I|+|J|)}\sum_{F\in\mathcal F_I(J)}\prod_{\{i,j\}\in E(F)}|f_{ij}|$, with the same empty-root convention as $g$. For nonempty $I$, delete the root $r$ selected in step 1.1. Its component cannot contain another vertex of $I$, and the set $K\subseteq J$ of its neighbors gives exactly the roots of the resulting branches; this is a bijection with forests in $\mathcal F_{I'\cup K}(J\setminus K)$. The exponential addition law [F2] factors the size weight, so $h(I,J)=e^{2\beta B}\sum_{K\subseteq J}(\prod_{k\in K}|f_{rk}|)h(I'\cup K,J\setminus K)$. If $I=\varnothing$, both $g$ and $h$ are $1$ for $J=\varnothing$ and $0$ otherwise. Induct on $|I|+|J|$ from these base cases. Step 1.1 supplies the root bound and step 2.1 supplies the graph recurrence; applying the finite-sum real triangle inequality from [F12, F13] gives $|g(I,J)|\leq q_r\sum_K(\prod_{k\in K}|f_{rk}|)|g(I'\cup K,J\setminus K)|$. The induction hypothesis and $q_r\leq e^{2\beta B}$ bound this by $h(I,J)$. At $I=\{1\}$, $J=\{2,\ldots,n\}$, $g(I,J)=U_n$ and every forest in $\mathcal F_I(J)$ is a spanning tree. This proves the pointwise tree bound.

In the Prüfer encoding, repeatedly delete the least-labelled leaf and record its neighbor; after $n-2$ deletions this gives a word of length $n-2$ over $\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Step 2.2 guarantees a leaf other than the root at every stage with at least two vertices, and deleting a leaf leaves a tree until the final vertex pair. At each stage a vertex occurs in the remaining word exactly once for each incident edge deleted before that vertex; it is recorded when a neighboring leaf is removed, and the vertex itself is deleted once it becomes a leaf, except for the final two vertices. Thus its occurrence count is its current degree minus one, and absence from the word is equivalent to being a current leaf. Conversely, from any such word, repeatedly join the least label absent from the remaining word to its first symbol and delete that label and symbol, then join the last two labels. Adding a new vertex with one edge to a tree makes the new vertex a leaf and preserves connectedness and acyclicity; induction on the word length therefore shows this constructs a tree. In the resulting tree the least absent label is a leaf and the first symbol is its neighbor, so encoding reverses every decoding step. The procedures give a bijection with all $n^{n-2}$ words. Integrating the pointwise tree bound of step 3.1 and using monotonicity, homogeneity and finite additivity [F8, F9] with the tree integral from step 2.2 yields $\int|U_n(0,x_2,\ldots,x_n)|\,dx_2\cdots dx_n\leq e^{2\beta Bn}n^{n-2}C_\beta^{n-1}$.
