Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple graph, so $V$ is finite and $E$ is a set of two-element subsets of $V$. Fix an integer $Q\geq2$, write $[Q]=\{1,\ldots,Q\}$, and assign to each edge $e\in E$ a finite activity $v_e\in[0,\infty)$. A spin configuration is a function $\sigma:V\to[Q]$. Its unnormalized Potts weight and partition function are
$$w_P(\sigma):=\prod_{e=\{u_e,w_e\}\in E}\bigl(1+v_e\mathbf1_{\{\sigma(u_e)=\sigma(w_e)\}}\bigr),\qquad Z_P(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{\sigma:V\to[Q]}w_P(\sigma).$$
For $A\subseteq E$, let $G_A=(V,A)$, and let $k_G(A)$ be its number of connected components, counting isolated vertices; equivalently, these are the equivalence classes generated by the endpoint pairs of edges in $A$. Put $v_A:=\prod_{e\in A}v_e$, with empty product $1$. The unnormalized Fortuin–Kasteleyn (FK) weight and partition function are
$$w_{FK}(A):=Q^{k_G(A)}v_A,\qquad Z_{FK}(Q,\mathbf v):=\sum_{A\subseteq E}w_{FK}(A).$$
Both normalizers are finite and positive: the spin sum is finite with every term at least $1$, while the empty-edge FK term is $Q^{|V|}>0$. These are finite mathematical weights; no physical units or empirical status are assigned.

A **plane graph** is a finite simple graph ([[def-finite-simple-graph]]) together with distinct points of $\mathbb R^2$ for its vertices and a polygonal arc ([[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]]) for each edge, joining its endpoints, such that an edge interior contains no vertex and two edge arcs meet only at a common endpoint. A finite simple graph is **planar** if it is isomorphic to the abstract graph underlying some plane graph.

A **face** is a region of the complement of the drawing ([[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]). The **boundary subgraph** of a face consists of the vertices and whole edges lying in its frontier; this is a subgraph in the sense of [[def-subgraph-induced-subgraph-and-spanning-subgraph]].

For a connected plane graph, walking once around a face with that face locally on the same side gives its **facial boundary walk**. Its **length** is the number of edge traversals, not the number of distinct edges: an edge incident with the same face on both local sides is traversed twice. For a disconnected plane graph a face may have several boundary walks; its boundary length is the sum of their lengths. No boundary walk is assumed to be a cycle unless a later connectivity result proves it.

Let $G$ be a connected plane graph with face set $F(G)$ ([[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]]). Its **dual multigraph** $G^*$ has vertex set $F(G)$ and one edge $e^*$ for every primal edge $e$. If the two local sides of $e$ belong to faces $f$ and $g$, then $e^*$ has endpoints $f,g$.

By [[lem-plane-edge-face-incidence]], a bridge has the same face on both local sides, so its dual edge is a loop. Different primal edges may have the same incident face pair, so their duals may be parallel. These are permitted by [[def-multigraph-loop-and-digraph]]. The definition is attached to the fixed plane embedding: different embeddings of the same abstract planar graph may have nonisomorphic dual multigraphs.

Every connected plane graph $G$ admits a polygonal plane embedding of its dual multigraph [[def-plane-dual-multigraph]] in which each dual edge crosses its corresponding primal edge exactly once and crosses no other primal or dual edge. In this reciprocal embedding, if $G^*$ is itself simple — equivalently, if $G$ has no bridge and no two faces share more than one edge — then $G^*$ is a plane graph in the sense of [[def-plane-graph-face-and-boundary]] and $(G^*)^*$ is isomorphic to $G$ in the sense of [[def-graph-isomorphism-and-complement]]. The simplicity hypothesis is necessary and not a convenience: a plane graph is a finite **simple** graph here, while [[def-plane-dual-multigraph]] may produce loops and parallel edges, so the double dual is otherwise not formed at all. For $G=K_2$ the single edge is a bridge and $G^*$ is one vertex with a loop, which is not a plane graph and has no dual under these definitions. Face finiteness is [[lem-plane-graph-faces-are-finite-with-one-unbounded-face]], local incidence is [[lem-plane-edge-face-incidence]], and polygonal separation is [[thm-polygonal-jordan-curve]].

If a plane graph has $c$ connected components, then

$$|V|-|E|+|F|=1+c.$$

This includes the null graph, for which $c=0$ and the complement is its single face. Component sets and their finite cardinalities are those of [[cor-connected-components-partition-the-vertex-set]] and [[def-finite-cardinality]], and face finiteness is [[lem-plane-graph-faces-are-finite-with-one-unbounded-face]].

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with unit ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) and let $\delta\in R$. The object labels are the nonnegative integers $n=0,1,2,\ldots$. For labels $m,n$, place bottom points $b_1,\ldots,b_m$ and top points $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ along the rectangle from left to right on their respective edges. Their cyclic order is $t_1,\ldots,t_n,b_m,\ldots,b_1$. When $m=n=0$, the empty matching is included.

An $(m,n)$ **diagram** is a perfect matching of these $m+n$ boundary labels which is noncrossing: there are no four labels $a,b,c,d$ in cyclic order whose matched pairs are $\{a,c\}$ and $\{b,d\}$. A picture consists of disjoint arcs realizing the matching; equality is equality of the matching, so planar deformation that fixes the boundary does not change a diagram. If $m+n$ is odd, there are no such diagrams. Write $\mathcal D(m,n)$ for this set and define the $R$-module

$$M_R(m,n):=R^{(\mathcal D(m,n))},$$

the free $R$-module on the set of diagrams ([[def-free-module-on-a-set-and-standard-basis]]). In particular, its diagram basis is empty when $m+n$ is odd.

For basis diagrams $D:m\to n$ and $E:n\to p$, stack $E$ above $D$ and identify the $n$ matching boundary points. The resulting finite graph has degree two at each identified point, where degree means the number of incident arcs. Each component is a path joining two exterior boundary points or a closed cycle. Remove every cycle and multiply the remaining exterior matching by $\delta^c$, where $c$ is the number of removed cycles. Denote this output by $E\circ D$ and extend the rule $R$-bilinearly to a map $M_R(n,p)\times M_R(m,n)\to M_R(m,p)$. A following result proves closure of these operations on the diagram modules and the category axioms.

The matching $1_n:n\to n$ pairs each bottom point to the top point directly above it. Horizontal juxtaposition, with the left diagram placed first, defines $m\otimes m'=m+m'$ on object labels and $D\otimes D'$ on basis diagrams; extend it $R$-bilinearly to the modules. A following result proves that these operations give a strict monoidal category.

For $1\le i<n$, let $d_i\in M_R(n,n)$ be the diagram with a cap joining top points $i,i+1$, a cup joining bottom points $i,i+1$, and vertical through strands at every other position. Define $\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ to be the $R$-module $M_R(n,n)$ with bilinear multiplication $xy:=x\circ y$ and distinguished element $1_n$. A following result proves that it is a unital associative $R$-algebra and identifies it with the endomorphism algebra at object $n$.

The left factor is stacked above the right factor. The loop value is $\delta$; no invertibility or nonzero condition on $\delta$ is part of these data.

For every commutative ring $R$, loop value $\delta\in R$, and objects $m,n,p,q\ge0$, the raw diagram data of [[def-temperley-lieb-diagram-category]] form a strict monoidal category $\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)$ with hom-modules $M_R(m,n)$ and the stated $R$-bilinear stacking composition. Composition is associative, the identity diagrams are two-sided identities, and horizontal juxtaposition is a strict monoidal bifunctor with unit object $0$. Consequently $\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal{TL}_R(\delta)}(n)=\mathrm{TL}_n(R,\delta)$ is a unital associative $R$-algebra whose underlying $R$-module is free on its noncrossing pairing diagrams.
Every connected component of an open subset $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is open in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and polygonally connected.

derivations.claim: Fix $A\subseteq E$. The drawing of $G_A$ is a finite union of points and closed line segments, hence is closed in $\mathbb R^2$. Its complement is open, so each of its face components is open and polygonally connected by [F7]. The original faces are vertices of $G^*$. Two such faces lie in the same face of $G_A$ exactly when they are connected by dual edges corresponding to $E\setminus A$. A dual path crosses only absent primal edges and therefore stays in the complement of $G_A$. Conversely, a path between two original face points inside one face of $G_A$ can be chosen polygonal; perturb its finitely many segments to avoid primal vertices and to cross edge interiors transversely. Because it avoids $G_A$, every crossed edge lies in $E\setminus A$, so the crossed dual edges form a path in $(F(G),A^*)$. Thus the faces of $G_A$ correspond bijectively to the components counted by $k^*(A)$.

Apply [F4] to the spanning plane subgraph $G_A$. Its vertex set is $V$, its edge set is $A$, its component count is $k(A)$, and by step 1.1 its face count is $k^*(A)$. Therefore $|V|-|A|+k^*(A)=1+k(A)$, or $k(A)-k^*(A)=|V|-|A|-1$.

View the fixed embedding on the sphere $S^2$ by adding the point at infinity. By [F4] the plane subgraph $G_A$ has finitely many faces; choose one point in each. For every vertex $x\in V$, including each vertex isolated in $G_A$, choose a closed polygonal disk $D_x$ so that the disks are pairwise disjoint and avoid all the chosen face points. Choose pairwise disjoint attachment intervals on each $\partial D_x$, one for each edge incident to $x$ and in the cyclic order of the embedding. For each $e\in A$, choose a closed polygonal rectangular band around the part of its polygonal arc outside its endpoint disks; make the bands pairwise disjoint, disjoint from all nonendpoint disks, and attach them to the corresponding intervals. These choices are possible with sufficiently small radii and widths because the graph is finite and edge arcs meet only at shared endpoints. Let $N_A$ be the union of these disks and bands. Each band joins exactly its two endpoint disks, and distinct bands otherwise remain disjoint, so the connected components of $N_A$ correspond exactly to those of $G_A$, including isolated-vertex disks; hence there are $k(A)$. Its boundary is a finite disjoint union of simple polygonal circles. In particular, the one-vertex graph with no edges gives one disk and one boundary loop. At a primal-dual crossing, the two sides of an occupied-edge band join the medial half-edges as $(h_4,h_1)$ and $(h_2,h_3)$; when the edge is absent, there is no band there and the two face-side sectors join as $(h_1,h_2)$ and $(h_3,h_4)$. The cyclic ordering of the attachment intervals fixes these local continuations, so $\partial N_A$ gives exactly the smoothings in the Statement and has $\ell(A)$ loops. Inside each face $U$ of $G_A$, the disk-and-band pieces form collars along the facial boundary side occurrences: each band side is a polygonal strip, and intervening vertex-disk sectors join consecutive strips in cyclic order. Repeated vertices or edges in a facial boundary walk are treated as separate side occurrences, so a bridge's two sides remain distinct; an isolated vertex gives a punctured-disk collar in its unique incident face. Choose all radii and widths small enough that distinct collars meet only at their prescribed continuations within the same face. Trimming them leaves a nonempty core $U_A=U\setminus N_A$, since the selected point of $U$ lies outside $N_A$. The core is connected: for finite points use the polygonal path in the plane face $U$ supplied by [F7], perturb the path to meet the finitely many polygonal collar sides transversely, and replace each excursion into a collar by a parallel path just outside $N_A$ along that collar's connected $U$-facing boundary, with the vertex-disk sector prescribing the continuation at each turn. For the unbounded face, $N_A$ is bounded; outside a sufficiently large disk its complement contains the whole exterior, and a ray there joins finite points to the point at infinity in the one-point compactification. Thus the same connected core includes infinity. Each face therefore leaves exactly one nonempty component of $S^2\setminus N_A$. Since $N_A$ contains $G_A$, these trimmed faces are all the components of $S^2\setminus N_A$; by step 1.1 their number is $k^*(A)$. The regions of $S^2\setminus\partial N_A$ are the interiors of the $k(A)$ components of $N_A$ together with those $k^*(A)$ complementary components, so there are $k(A)+k^*(A)$ regions.

Subdivide each of the disjoint polygonal boundary loops from step 2.2 at at least three distinct points and regard the result as a finite simple plane graph $H_A$, with one cycle component per loop. Each cycle has the same number of vertices and edges, so $|V(H_A)|=|E(H_A)|$, and $H_A$ has $\ell(A)$ connected components. By [F4], its complement therefore has $|F(H_A)|=1+\ell(A)$ regions. These are the regions counted in step 2.2, hence $k(A)+k^*(A)=1+\ell(A)$ and $\ell(A)=k(A)+k^*(A)-1$.

Adding the identities in steps 2.1 and 3.1 yields $2k(A)=|V|-|A|+\ell(A)$. Since $Q\geq2$, its positive square root $\delta=\sqrt Q$ is nonzero, and $Q^{k(A)}\prod_{e\in A}v_e=Q^{|V|/2}(\sqrt Q)^{\ell(A)}\prod_{e\in A}\frac{v_e}{\sqrt Q}$. This equality also holds when an activity is zero, because both corresponding terms vanish.

Each subset $A$ selects exactly one of the two noncrossing smoothings at every medial vertex, so summing the termwise identity of step 4.1 over $A\subseteq E$ gives the displayed loop formula. In any fixed rectangular decomposition, the local smoothings are Temperley–Lieb diagrams; [F5] fixes the left-above-right and $\delta$ conventions, and [F6] makes the stacked product independent of parentheses. Thus the local loop weight is exactly $\delta=\sqrt Q$, without invoking a trace or any representation-theoretic property.

derivations.claim: For the coordinate observables, the generator gives $L\eta_1=\alpha+\eta_2-2\eta_1$ and $L\eta_2=\beta+\eta_1-2\eta_2$. If $\pi$ is stationary and $m_i:=\mathbb E_\pi\eta_i$, then $\mathbb E_\pi L\eta_i=0$, so $2m_1-m_2=\alpha$ and $2m_2-m_1=\beta$. Solving gives $m_1=(2\alpha+\beta)/3$ and $m_2=(\alpha+2\beta)/3$.

Let $q:=\mathbb E_\pi(\eta_1\eta_2)$. The swap does not change $\eta_1\eta_2$, and the two reservoir flips give $L(\eta_1\eta_2)=\alpha\eta_2+\beta\eta_1-2\eta_1\eta_2$. Stationarity therefore yields $2q=\alpha m_2+\beta m_1$, hence $q=(\alpha^2+4\alpha\beta+\beta^2)/6$.

Substituting the moments from steps 1.1 and 2.1 gives $q-m_1m_2=\frac{\alpha^2+4\alpha\beta+\beta^2}{6}-\frac{(2\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+2\beta)}{9}=-\frac{(\alpha-\beta)^2}{18}$. If $\alpha\ne\beta$, this covariance is nonzero, whereas two independent Bernoulli occupations have zero covariance; thus $\pi$ is not a product law.

Define probabilities by $\pi_{11}=q$, $\pi_{10}=m_1-q$, $\pi_{01}=m_2-q$, and $\pi_{00}=1-m_1-m_2+q$. They sum to one; $\pi_{11}>0$ and $\pi_{00}=[(1-\alpha)^2+4(1-\alpha)(1-\beta)+(1-\beta)^2]/6>0$. For fixed $\beta$, $6\pi_{10}=g(\alpha)$ where $g(a)=a(4-4\beta-a)+\beta(2-\beta)$ is concave on $[0,1]$ and has positive endpoint values $g(0)=\beta(2-\beta)$ and $g(1)=(1-\beta)(3+\beta)$; hence $\pi_{10}>0$. By interchanging $\alpha$ and $\beta$ the same argument gives $\pi_{01}>0$.

The probabilities in step 3.2 have the moments in steps 1.1 and 2.1, so their expectation of $L$ vanishes on $1,\eta_1,\eta_2,\eta_1\eta_2$. These four functions form a basis of all real functions on $\Omega$, hence the probability vector is stationary. Conversely, every stationary law must satisfy the same three moment equations, which determine $m_1,m_2,q$ uniquely and then determine all four atom probabilities; therefore this stationary law is unique. If $\alpha=\beta=r$, the same probabilities reduce to $\pi_{00}=(1-r)^2$, $\pi_{10}=\pi_{01}=r(1-r)$, and $\pi_{11}=r^2$, the product Bernoulli law. Step 3.1 gives the claimed covariance.

Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $k\ge1$, let $w:X\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive reference weight, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$. Use the Euclidean inner product $\theta\cdot T(x):=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_jT_j(x)$. For $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, define the partition sum and log-partition function by
$$Z(\theta):=\sum_{x\in X}w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)},\qquad A(\theta):=\log Z(\theta),$$
and define the finite exponential Gibbs family by
$$\pi_\theta(x):=w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)-A(\theta)}\quad(x\in X).$$
All objects here are mathematical; $\theta\cdot T(x)$ is a real number. The representation is called minimal when there is no nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^k$ for which $a\cdot T(x)$ is constant over all $x\in X$.

For a finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, its convex hull is the set of sums $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s s$ with $\lambda_s\ge0$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s=1$. Its affine hull is the set of sums of the same form with real coefficients $\lambda_s$ whose sum is $1$. The relative interior of a convex set is its interior in its affine hull with the Euclidean subspace topology. These definitions will be used for the sufficient-statistic support $T(X)$.

For the finite exponential family of the preceding Definition, write $\mu_	heta:=\sum_{x\in X}\pi_	heta(x)T(x)$. Define $\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_	heta}(T)$ by entries
$\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_	heta}(T)_{ab}:=\sum_{x\in X}\pi_	heta(x)(T_a(x)-\mu_{	heta,a})(T_b(x)-\mu_{	heta,b})$.
The gradient and Hessian mean $
abla A(	heta):=(\partial_jA(	heta))_{j=1}^k$ and $
abla^2A(	heta):=(\partial_i\partial_jA(	heta))_{i,j=1}^k$. A symmetric matrix is positive definite when its quadratic form is positive on every nonzero vector. The map $	heta\mapsto\pi_	heta$ is injective when $\pi_	heta(x)=\pi_\varphi(x)$ for every $x$ implies $	heta=\varphi$. The following conditions are equivalent: the representation is minimal; no nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^k$ makes $a\cdot T(x)$ constant on $X$; the affine hull of $T(X)$ is $\mathbb R^k$; $
abla^2 A(	heta)$ is positive definite for every $	heta$; and the map $	heta\mapsto\pi_	heta$ is injective.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a sigma-finite measure space, let $w\ge0$ be
measurable with $m(\{w>0\})>0$, let $r\ge1$ and let
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_r):\Omega\to\mathbb R^r$ be measurable and finite, and let
$\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For
each compact $K\subset\Theta$, assume an integrable $G_K$ satisfies
$$w(x)e^{\theta\cdot X(x)}\left(1+\sum_a|X_a(x)|^2\right)\le G_K(x)\quad(\theta\in K).$$
Then $Z(\theta)=\int w e^{\theta\cdot X}\,dm$ is finite, strictly positive
and $C^2$, and the probability density $\rho_\theta=Z(\theta)^{-1}we^{\theta\cdot X}$
defines $dP_\theta=\rho_\theta\,dm$ as in [[def-measure-with-density]].
For any integrable real $A$, write $\langle A\rangle_\theta:=\int A\,dP_\theta$;
for square-integrable real $A,B$, define
$\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(A,B):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_\theta)(B-\langle B\rangle_\theta)\,dP_\theta$.
These extend the phase-space conventions of
[[def-csm-statistical-state-observable]] to the present measure space.
Then
$$\partial_a\log Z=\langle X_a\rangle_\theta,\qquad \partial_a\partial_b\log Z=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b).$$
In particular, the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite.

Let $X=\{x_1,\dots,x_m\}$ be finite and nonempty, let $k\ge1$, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$ have full affine hull, meaning that the affine combinations $\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_jT(x_j)$ with $\sum_ja_j=1$ fill $\mathbb R^k$. Define the finite convex hull

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,

inner product and the Euclidean norm as in The Euclidean inner product $\langle x,y\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k y_k$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**

   it induces is $d_2$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**

Since every $\pi_\theta(x_i)>0$, the likelihood is positive. Repeated application of the logarithm product law [F8], followed by $\log(\exp t)=t$ [F7], gives the log likelihood
$$\ell(\theta)=\log\prod_{i=1}^n\pi_\theta(x_i)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log w(x_i)+n\bigl(\theta\cdot\bar T-A(\theta)\bigr).$$
Because $\log$ is strictly increasing [F8], maximizing this log likelihood is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood. Also $\bar T$ is the convex combination with weights $1/n$ of $T(x_i)$, so $\bar T\in K$.

Let $\theta\ne\varphi$ and put $v=\varphi-\theta$ and $g(s)=\ell(\theta+sv)$ for $s\in[0,1]$. By $A\in C^2$ [F3], $g$ is twice continuously differentiable; by [F2] its second derivative is $g''(s)=-n\,v^\mathsf T\nabla^2A(\theta+sv)v<0$. Thus $g'$ is strictly decreasing: for $0\le a<b\le1$, the mean value theorem [F9] applied to $g'$ gives $g'(b)-g'(a)=g''(c)(b-a)<0$ for some $c\in(a,b)$. Fix $t\in(0,1)$. Applying [F9] to $g$ on $[0,t]$ and $[t,1]$ gives $\alpha\in(0,t)$ and $\beta\in(t,1)$ such that
$$\frac{g(t)-g(0)}{t}=g'(\alpha)>g'(\beta)=\frac{g(1)-g(t)}{1-t}.$$
Rearranging yields $g(t)>(1-t)g(0)+tg(1)$. By [F12], $\ell$ is strictly concave on $\mathbb R^k$.

Suppose $\bar T\in\operatorname{ri}K$. Minimality makes $K$ full-dimensional, so there is $\epsilon>0$ such that the open ball of radius $\epsilon$ about $\bar T$ lies in $K$; set $\delta=\epsilon/2$, so the closed ball of radius $\delta$ lies in that open ball and hence in $K$. For every unit $u$, $\bar T+\delta u$ is a convex combination of the vectors $T(x)$; since $u\cdot u=1$ by [F11], at least one $x$ satisfies $u\cdot(T(x)-\bar T)\ge\delta$. Put $w_{\min}=\min_{x\in X}w(x)>0$. If $\theta\ne0$, write $r=\|\theta\|_2$ and $u=\theta/r$; [F10] gives $r>0$ and $\|u\|_2=1$. For some $x$ as above, $\theta\cdot(T(x)-\bar T)\ge r\delta$. Since the $x$th summand is part of $Z(\theta)$ and is positive by [F13], monotonicity and the product law of $\log$ [F8], together with [F7], give
$$A(\theta)=\log Z(\theta)\ge\log\bigl(w_{\min}e^{\theta\cdot T(x)}\bigr)=\log w_{\min}+\theta\cdot T(x),$$
and hence $A(\theta)-\theta\cdot\bar T\ge r\delta+\log w_{\min}$. Thus $\theta\mapsto A(\theta)-\theta\cdot\bar T$ tends to $+\infty$ as $\|\theta\|_2\to\infty$.

The function $\Phi(\theta):=A(\theta)-\theta\cdot\bar T$ is continuous: $A$ is continuous by [F3], and the linear form is continuous by the Cauchy–Schwarz bound [F10]. It tends to $+\infty$ by step 1.3. Choose $R>0$ large enough that $\Phi(\theta)>\Phi(0)$ whenever $\|\theta\|_2>R$. The closed ball $\overline B_2(0,R)$ is nonempty and compact by [F6], so [F5] gives a minimizer $\hat\theta$ on it. Since $0$ lies in the ball and every point outside has value greater than $\Phi(0)$, $\hat\theta$ is a global minimizer on $\mathbb R^k$. The log-likelihood formula in step 1.1 and $n\ge1$ show that it is a finite MLE. If two distinct finite MLEs existed, their midpoint would have a strictly larger log likelihood by step 1.2, a contradiction; hence it is unique.

Suppose $\bar T\notin\operatorname{ri}K$. Since $\bar T\in K$ by step 1.1 and $K$ is full-dimensional, $\bar T$ is a boundary point. By [F4] choose a unit $u$ with $u\cdot(T(x)-\bar T)\le0$ for every $x$. Full affine span implies at least one of these inequalities is strict; otherwise $u\cdot T$ would be constant on $X$. Every $\pi_\theta(x)$ is positive, so
$u\cdot(\nabla A(\theta)-\bar T)=\sum_x\pi_\theta(x)u\cdot(T(x)-\bar T)<0$
for every finite $\theta$. Therefore the directional derivative of $\ell$ along $u$ is
$n\,u\cdot(\bar T-\nabla A(\theta))>0$ at every finite $\theta$. By the definition of a positive derivative, a sufficiently small positive step along $u$ increases $\ell$, and therefore increases the likelihood by [F8]. No finite MLE exists. This proves both directions.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $X$ be a finite nonempty set, let $k\ge1$, let $w:X\to(0,\infty)$ be a positive reference weight, and let $T:X\to\mathbb R^k$. Use the Euclidean inner product $\theta\cdot T(x):=\sum_{j=1}^k\theta_jT_j(x)$. For $\theta\in\mathbb R^k$, define the partition sum and log-partition function by
$$Z(\theta):=\sum_{x\in X}w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)},\qquad A(\theta):=\log Z(\theta),$$
and define the finite exponential Gibbs family by
$$\pi_\theta(x):=w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)-A(\theta)}\quad(x\in X).$$
All objects here are mathematical; $\theta\cdot T(x)$ is a real number. The representation is called minimal when there is no nonzero $a\in\mathbb R^k$ for which $a\cdot T(x)$ is constant over all $x\in X$.

For a finite set $S\subseteq\mathbb R^k$, its convex hull is the set of sums $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s s$ with $\lambda_s\ge0$ and $\sum_{s\in S}\lambda_s=1$. Its affine hull is the set of sums of the same form with real coefficients $\lambda_s$ whose sum is $1$. The relative interior of a convex set is its interior in its affine hull with the Euclidean subspace topology. These definitions will be used for the sufficient-statistic support $T(X)$.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [F1] [[def-csm-frontier-inverse-finite-exponential]]: $\pi_\theta(x)=w(x)e^{\theta\cdot T(x)-A(\theta)}$ with $w(x)>0$; its proof verifies $0<Z(\theta)<\infty$, normalization and full support, and $K$ is the finite convex hull of $T(X)$.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,m)$ be a sigma-finite measure space, let $w\ge0$ be
measurable with $m(\{w>0\})>0$, let $r\ge1$ and let
$X=(X_1,\ldots,X_r):\Omega\to\mathbb R^r$ be measurable and finite, and let
$\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^r$ be open. For
each compact $K\subset\Theta$, assume an integrable $G_K$ satisfies
$$w(x)e^{\theta\cdot X(x)}\left(1+\sum_a|X_a(x)|^2\right)\le G_K(x)\quad(\theta\in K).$$
Then $Z(\theta)=\int w e^{\theta\cdot X}\,dm$ is finite, strictly positive
and $C^2$, and the probability density $\rho_\theta=Z(\theta)^{-1}we^{\theta\cdot X}$
defines $dP_\theta=\rho_\theta\,dm$ as in [[def-measure-with-density]].
For any integrable real $A$, write $\langle A\rangle_\theta:=\int A\,dP_\theta$;
for square-integrable real $A,B$, define
$\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(A,B):=\int(A-\langle A\rangle_\theta)(B-\langle B\rangle_\theta)\,dP_\theta$.
These extend the phase-space conventions of
[[def-csm-statistical-state-observable]] to the present measure space.
Then
$$\partial_a\log Z=\langle X_a\rangle_\theta,\qquad \partial_a\partial_b\log Z=\operatorname{Cov}_\theta(X_a,X_b).$$
In particular, the Hessian of $\log Z$ is positive semidefinite.
supplier_excerpts.relevant_hypotheses_and_conventions: [F3] [[thm-csm-exponential-normalization-covariance]]: for the finite family, $\nabla A(\theta)=\mathbb E_{\pi_\theta}T$ and $\nabla^2A(\theta)=\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi_\theta}(T)$; its compact-envelope hypothesis is verified in the finite-family Definition.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space,
Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
(Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below (Lower bound, bounded below, bounded set), and it has a
maximum and a minimum (Maximum and minimum of a set): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property), Greatest lower bound (infimum)).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

citations.quote:
For every finite undirected multigraph $G=(V,E,\partial)$, boundary set $B\subseteq V$, boundary partition $\xi$ on $B$, $q\geq1$, and $p\in(0,1)$, the finite FK law defined by the stated finite weights is strictly positive and log-supermodular on the Boolean lattice $2^E$: for $A,C\subseteq E$,

$$\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cup C)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A\cap C)\geq\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(A)\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}(C).$$

Consequently it is positively associated: $\phi(fg)\geq\phi(f)\phi(g)$ for increasing real functions $f,g:2^E\to\mathbb R$. Conditioning on the states of all edges outside a finite edge set $F$ gives a finite FK law on $F$ whose boundary partition wires exactly the vertices joined by the fixed exterior open edges and the original partition $\xi$. Given all other edge states, an edge is open with conditional probability $p$ if its endpoints are already connected, and $p/(p+q(1-p))$ otherwise. If $p_1\leq p_2$ and $\xi_1$ refines $\xi_2$ (each $\xi_1$-class lies in a $\xi_2$-class), then $\phi_{p_1,q}^{\xi_1}\leq_{st}\phi_{p_2,q}^{\xi_2}$.

Let $q\geq1$ be a finite real number. On the nearest-neighbor square lattice let $\Lambda_n=\{-n,\ldots,n\}^2$, let $E_n$ consist of edges with both endpoints in $\Lambda_n$, and let $B_n=\{x\in\Lambda_n:\|x\|_\infty=n\}$. For $p\in(0,1)$ and a partition $\xi$ of $B_n$, give $A\subseteq E_n$ probability proportional to $p^{|A|}(1-p)^{|E_n\setminus A|}q^{k_\xi(A)}$, where $k_\xi$ counts components after the partition classes are identified. Write $\phi^b_{n,p,q}$ for the free partition when $b=0$ and the one-class wired partition when $b=1$.

For every event $C$ determined by finitely many edge coordinates, the numerical limits
$$\pi^b_{p,q}(C):=\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^b_{n,p,q}(C),\qquad b\in\{0,1\},$$
exist. They are consistent, nonnegative normalized finite-coordinate probability families, invariant under translations and quarter-turns. On increasing cylinder events they are increasing in $p$, with $\pi^0\leq\pi^1$. Every cylinder-probability limit of arbitrary boundary partitions lies between these two families on increasing cylinder events. There is an at most countable set $D_q\subset(0,1)$ such that $\pi^0_{p,q}(C)=\pi^1_{p,q}(C)$ for every cylinder event $C$ whenever $p\notin D_q$.

Let $D_r$ be the event that actual open edges inside $\Lambda_r$ join $0$ to $B_r$, and define the real numbers
$$\Theta_b(p,q)=\inf_{r\geq1}\pi^b_{p,q}(D_r).$$
Then $\Theta_1(p,q)\leq\Theta_0(p',q)$ for $0<p<p'<1$, and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\phi^1_{n,p,q}(0\leftrightarrow B_n)=\Theta_1(p,q).$$
Connections here use actual edges, not artificial boundary-identification paths. These are statements about real limits and finite probability tables; existence of a countably additive probability on the infinite configuration space is not asserted.

For each $q\geq1$ and aspect ratio $\alpha>1$, there is a constant $c(\alpha,q)>0$ such that the following holds. Let $n,m$ be positive integers with $m>\lceil\alpha n\rceil$, let $T_m=(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^2$ with its nearest-neighbor horizontal and vertical edges and periodic boundary conditions, and give its edges the FK law with no boundary wiring, parameter $q$, and $p_{\rm sd}(q)=\sqrt q/(1+\sqrt q)$. The probability of a horizontal open crossing of the vertex rectangle $\{0,\ldots,\lceil\alpha n\rceil\}\times\{0,\ldots,n\}$ is at least $c(\alpha,q)$, uniformly in $n$ and $m$.

Let $G=(V,E,\partial)$ be a finite undirected multigraph, let $B\subseteq V$ have boundary partition $\xi$, fix $q\geq1$, $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$, and $p\in[\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon]$, and let $\phi=\phi_{G,p,q}^{\xi}$ be the finite FK law. For every increasing event $A\subseteq2^E$ with $0<\phi(A)<1$ and $|E|\geq2$, define the conditional influence of edge $e$ by

$$I_A(e):=\phi(A\mid \omega_e=1)-\phi(A\mid\omega_e=0).$$

There is a constant $c(q,\varepsilon)>0$ such that

$$\max_{e\in E}I_A(e)\geq c(q,\varepsilon)\,\phi(A)(1-\phi(A))\frac{\log|E|}{|E|}.$$

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite connected plane graph with a fixed embedding and $|V|\geq1$. Use the free partition on all primal vertices, $B=V$. Its plane dual multigraph $G^*$ has one vertex for each face, including the unbounded face, and one dual edge $e^*$ crossing each primal edge $e$; use the identity partition on the dual face-vertices. The unbounded face is one dual vertex, so this convention retains the exterior-face connection in the dual. For a primal open set $A\subseteq E$, let $A^*:=\{e^*:e\in E\setminus A\}$, so a dual edge is open exactly when its crossing primal edge is closed. For $q\geq1$ and $p\in(0,1)$ define $p^*\in(0,1)$ by

$$\frac{p^*}{1-p^*}=q\frac{1-p}{p}.$$

Then complementing the primal edges sends the finite FK law $\phi_{G,p,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$ to the dual FK law $\phi_{G^*,p^*,q}^{\mathrm{free}}$: the random dual edge set $A^*$ has exactly that distribution. The unnormalized weight ratio is the configuration-independent factor $q^{|V|-1}((1-p)/p^*)^{|E|}$; the exponent $|V|-1$ includes the exterior-face contribution under this identity-partition convention.

Let $a,b\geq1$ be integers and let $Q_{a,b}=\{0,\ldots,a\}\times\{0,\ldots,b\}$ have its nearest-neighbor square-grid edges, drawn as unit horizontal and vertical segments. A left-to-right path is a finite edge path whose endpoints lie on the sides $x=0$ and $x=a$; a bottom-to-top path is defined analogously using $y=0$ and $y=b$. Every left-to-right path and every bottom-to-top path in $Q_{a,b}$ share a vertex.

If $P\subseteq\mathbb R^2$ is a polygon, then $\mathbb R^2\setminus P$ has exactly two regions, one bounded and one unbounded, and

$$\operatorname{Fr}(U)=P$$

for each of them. Regions and frontiers are from [[def-plane-region-and-frontier]]. The proof uses the finite simple edge cycle of [[def-polygonal-arc-and-polygon]] and polygonal crossing parity from [[lem-polygonal-crossing-parity-is-locally-constant]].

derivations.claim: For an increasing event $B$ on a finite graph, differentiation of its finite FK weights gives $\phi'_p(B)=\operatorname{Cov}_p(\mathbf1_B,|\omega|)/[p(1-p)]$. Writing $u_e=\phi_p(e\text{ open})$ and $I_B(e)=\phi_p(B\mid e\text{ open})-\phi_p(B\mid e\text{ closed})$ yields $\phi'_p(B)=\sum_e u_e(1-u_e)I_B(e)/[p(1-p)]$. By [F1] the coefficients have a positive lower bound on a compact parameter interval inside $(0,1)$. On an $L$-torus a translation-invariant $B$ has equal influences on each of the two edge orbits, each of size $L^2$. Thus [F4] implies $\phi'_p(B)\geq c\phi_p(B)(1-\phi_p(B))\log L$. Integrating its logistic derivative between $p_s$ and fixed $p>p_s$ shows that $\phi_{p_s}(B)\geq b>0$ implies $1-\phi_p(B)\leq C L^{-\eta}$, with constants independent of $L$.

We specify the finite stopping operation used for an outer circuit. In a finite ambient box list all simple circuits disjoint from $\Lambda_{r_{k+1}}$, strictly inside $\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$, and surrounding the inner square. For a candidate $\gamma$, let $I(\gamma)$ be the edges whose relative interiors lie in its bounded component, including edges entering that component from circuit vertices. Let $O(\gamma)$ contain all other ambient edges, including circuit edges. The event selecting $\Gamma=\gamma$ is: every edge of $\gamma$ is open and there is no surrounding open circuit in $O(\gamma)$ whose bounded interior strictly contains that of $\gamma$. These tests involve only $O(\gamma)$. To verify that exactly one candidate is selected whenever a surrounding circuit exists, splice any exterior excursion of another surrounding circuit with the outer arcs of $\gamma$, keeping the unbounded face on the outside, and erase subloops not surrounding the inner square. This gives a surrounding circuit in the union, on or outside $\gamma$, with strictly larger interior if that excursion protrudes. Applying this finite operation to all candidates yields an outermost circuit; two different maximal circuits would enlarge each other by the same surgery. Equal interiors have the same Jordan boundary. Thus the selected candidate is unique. For each output $(\gamma,\tau)$, where $\tau$ is the full assignment on $O(\gamma)$, the output fiber is precisely the fixed-exterior cylinder $\{\omega|_{O(\gamma)}=\tau\}$ if $\tau$ passes the tests, and is empty otherwise. Every interior assignment is admitted. This fiber identity, rather than a claim about a particular probing order, certifies that conditioning on the output never conditions an interior edge.

For $m\geq r$, reaching $\partial\Lambda_m$ entails $D_r$, and wired domain comparison gives $a_m\leq\phi^1_{m,p,q}(D_r)\leq a_r$. In particular $a_n$ decreases, so $\Theta^1=\inf_n a_n$ exists. Taking $m\to\infty$ in the displayed inequalities gives $\Theta^1\leq\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r)\leq a_r$. Infimizing over $r$ proves $\Theta^1=\inf_r\pi^1_{p,q}(D_r)$. This is a pair of real inequalities, not an exchange of two limits.

On a finite edge set and for an increasing event $D$, its Hamming distance $H_D$ is the minimum number of closed edges to open to enter $D$. Opening one coordinate lowers it by zero or one; hence $|\omega|+H_D$ is increasing, $H_D$ is decreasing, and $H_D\mathbf1_D=0$. Finite differentiation and FKG give $\frac{d}{dp}\phi_p(D)=\{\operatorname{Cov}_p(\mathbf1_D,|\omega|+H_D)+\phi_p(D)\mathbb E_pH_D\}/[p(1-p)]\geq4\phi_p(D)\mathbb E_pH_D$. Integrate from $p$ to $t>p$ and use monotonicity of the decreasing $H_D$ to obtain $\phi_p(D)\leq\exp\{-4(t-p)\mathbb E_tH_D\}$. Apply this to $D_n$ in wired $\Lambda_m$ with $m>n$ and take $m\to\infty$. Both sides involve only fixed finite cylinder sums, proving the claimed Hamming inequality.

We derive the exact numerical free/wired duality from a concrete free plane graph. Let $H_m$ be the free rectangular grid on the $(2m)^2$ unit-cell centers of $\Lambda_m$. Each bounded face of $H_m$ surrounds one interior vertex of $\Lambda_m$; its one unbounded face represents all vertices of $B_m$ identified together. A dual edge of $H_m$ crosses exactly one nonperimeter edge of $\Lambda_m$, with precisely those interior-vertex or boundary-class endpoints. Thus $H_m^*$ is the wired quotient graph with the perimeter edge labels omitted. Each omitted perimeter edge is a loop after wiring, so its open/closed weight sums to $p+(1-p)=1$ independently and changes no retained-edge law. Apply [F5] to the connected free plane graph $H_m$ at parameter $t^*$, whose dual parameter is $t$. The inverse complement bijection sends the wired retained-edge law at $t$ to the free law on $H_m$ at $t^*$. This proves the finite identity before taking any limit; the exterior face is one of the wired-quotient vertices, not an additional cell-center vertex. The cell-center grids exhaust the translated dual lattice, and, after its fixed half-unit identification with $\mathbb Z^2$, lie between centered boxes with radii differing by a fixed constant. Finite domain comparison and [F2] therefore give, for every dual cylinder $E$, $\pi^1_{t,q}(\text{dual-complement }E)=\pi^0_{t^*,q}(E)$. This is a numerical cylinder identity, not a claim of an unconstructed infinite law.

To turn this estimate into a bound for one specified rectangle, first take width $2u$, height $2bu$ with integer $b\geq1$, and torus side $L=16b^2u$. Let $B$ mean that some translate of a width-$u$, height-$L/2$ rectangle has a vertical crossing. It is translation invariant and has self-dual probability bounded below by [F3], since its fixed aspect is $8b^2$ and its height is strictly less than $L$. Every such narrow strip is contained horizontally in one of the width-$2u$ strips starting on the $u$-grid, and its height interval contains a full height-$2bu$ band starting on the $2bu$-grid. Its crossing therefore crosses one of $M=(L/u)(L/(2bu))$ fixed translates of the target rectangle. Wrapping translates are lifted to the plane for this containment. If their crossing events are $B_i$, positive association of their decreasing complements gives $(1-\phi_p(B_1))^M\leq\phi_p(\bigcap_iB_i^c)\leq\phi_p(B^c)$. Step 1.1 proves $\phi_p(B_1)\geq1-Cu^{-\eta/M}$. The number $M$ is independent of $u$.

For a rectangle of width $w$ and height $h$ with $1\leq h/w\leq\beta$, take $u=\lfloor w/2\rfloor$ and a fixed integer $b$ depending only on $\beta$ with $2bu\geq h$. A crossing of the narrower, taller rectangle restricts to a crossing of the target. Rotating handles the other orientations. A fixed enlargement of $L/u$ in step 2.1 preserves the proof and accommodates any surrounding planar box of size comparable to $w$. Condition that torus law on all edges outside the box; its induced partition is bounded above by the wired partition. Hence the wired box gives the specified rectangle a crossing probability at least $1-Cw^{-\delta}$. The finitely many small widths are absorbed into $C$.

Fix $\alpha>1$. For large $k$ put $a=r_k+2$, $b=r_{k+1}-2$, $R=r_{k+2}$. Use vertical crossings of $[a,b]\times[-b,b]$ and $[-b,-a]\times[-b,b]$, horizontal crossings of $[-b,b]\times[a,b]$ and $[-b,b]\times[-b,-a]$, and a horizontal crossing of $[-R,R]\times[-b,b]$. In each corner square the adjacent side crossings intersect by [F6]; their union contains a surrounding closed walk, from which erasing nonsurrounding loops gives a simple circuit. The last crossing intersects the two vertical sides and connects that circuit to the outer boundary. All widths are comparable to $\alpha^k$ and all aspects are fixed. Step 3.1 and a union bound give $\phi^1_{r_{k+2},p,q}(A_k)\geq1-d_k$ with $d_k=C e^{-\varepsilon k}$. Enlarge $K$ until $b>a$ and $d_k<1/2$ for $k\geq K$.

Suppose $A_{k+1},\ldots,A_n$ hold. Apply step 1.2 to the next annulus. The selected $\Gamma$ has an outgoing open connection to $\partial\Lambda_{r_{k+3}}$: an outgoing path from any surrounding circuit meets $\Gamma$. These outer events are measurable in its returned exterior data. For $A_{k+1}$ one may use $\Gamma$ itself, and any path excursion inside it can be replaced by an open circuit arc; circuits of $A_j$ for $j\geq k+2$ are outside it. On each output fiber, [F1] gives the interior FK law with all vertices of $\Gamma$ wired together by its actual open edges. Let $G_k(\Gamma)$ mean that a circuit of the inner annulus connects to $\Gamma$ inside its bounded domain. Its connection then follows the already exposed outgoing path through $\Gamma$ to $\partial\Lambda_{r_{k+2}}$, giving $A_k$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ be a densely defined closable antilinear operator.
Its graph closure $\overline S$ is closed and has the polar decomposition
$$\overline S=J|\overline S|,\qquad |\overline S|=(\overline S^{\,*}\overline S)^{1/2}.$$
Here $J$ is antilinear, vanishes on $\ker\overline S$, and is isometric on
$(\ker\overline S)^\perp$; if $\overline S$ is injective and has dense range,
$J$ is antiunitary.

For a concrete von Neumann algebra $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ and a vector
$\Omega$ cyclic and separating for $M$, define
$D(S_0)=M\Omega$ and $S_0(x\Omega)=x^*\Omega$ for $x\in M$. Then $S_0$ is
well defined, densely defined, antilinear, and closable.

Assume Countable Choice. All inner products are linear in their first
argument. If $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, its **conjugate Hilbert space**
$\overline H$ consists of symbols $\overline x$ for $x\in H$, with
$\overline x+\overline y=\overline{x+y}$,
$a\,\overline x=\overline{\overline a\,x}$ for $a\in\mathbb C$, and
$$\langle\overline x,\overline y\rangle_{\overline H} :=\overline{\langle x,y\rangle_H}.$$
The canonical map $c_H:H\to\overline H$, $c_Hx=\overline x$, is a
conjugate-linear surjective isometry.

For complex Hilbert spaces $H_1,H_2$, a linear operator $A$ is a linear map
$A:D(A)\to H_2$ on a linear domain $D(A)\subseteq H_1$. Its graph is
$\Gamma(A)=\{(x,Ax):x\in D(A)\}\subseteq H_1\oplus H_2$, with the direct-sum
Hilbert norm. It is densely defined when $D(A)$ is dense in $H_1$, and closed
when $\Gamma(A)$ is closed.

For a densely defined linear operator $A:D(A)\subseteq H_1\to H_2$, define
$D(A^*)$ to consist of those $y\in H_2$ for which
$x\mapsto\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}$ is bounded on $D(A)$ in the $H_1$ norm.
The bounded functional extends uniquely to $H_1$; its Riesz vector
$A^*y\in H_1$ is specified by
$$\langle Ax,y\rangle_{H_2}=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_{H_1} \qquad(x\in D(A)).$$
This defines the linear adjoint $A^*:D(A^*)\subseteq H_2\to H_1$.

An operator $S:D(S)\subseteq H\to H$ is **antilinear** when
$S(ax+by)=\overline a\,Sx+\overline b\,Sy$. Its associated linear operator
$\widetilde S:D(\widetilde S)\subseteq\overline H\to H$ is
$D(\widetilde S)=c_H(D(S))$ and
$\widetilde S(\overline x)=Sx$. For densely defined antilinear $S$, define
$$S^*:=c_H^{-1}\widetilde S^*,$$
on the domain $D(S^*)=D(\widetilde S^*)$. Thus $S^*$ is antilinear and
$$\langle Sx,y\rangle_H=\langle S^*y,x\rangle_H \qquad(x\in D(S),\ y\in D(S^*)).$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and let
$R\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ be a unital star subalgebra. Its strong-operator
closure is $R''$. If $M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ is a concrete von Neumann
algebra and $\Omega\in H$, then $\Omega$ is cyclic for $M$ exactly when it is
separating for $M'$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and
$\mathcal B(H)$ the space of bounded linear operators on $H$
([[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For a set
$\mathcal S\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$, write

$$\mathcal S':=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):Ts=sT\text{ for every }s\in\mathcal S\}, \qquad \mathcal S'':=(\mathcal S')'.$$

The strong operator topology on $\mathcal B(H)$ is the topology of pointwise
norm convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$ strongly exactly when
$\|(T_\alpha-T)\xi\|\to0$ for every $\xi\in H$. The weak operator topology is
the topology of pointwise matrix-coefficient convergence: $T_\alpha\to T$
weakly exactly when $\langle T_\alpha\xi,\eta\rangle\to\langle T\xi,\eta\rangle$
for every $\xi,\eta\in H$. Use the linear-first inner-product convention.

A **concrete von Neumann algebra** on $H$ is a unital star subalgebra
$M\subseteq\mathcal B(H)$ satisfying $M=M''$. Under Choice, the double
commutant theorem makes this equivalent to being closed in the weak operator
topology.

An operator $a\in\mathcal B(H)$ is **positive** when $a=a^*$ and
$\langle a\xi,\xi\rangle\ge0$ for every $\xi\in H$, using the bounded
adjoint convention of [[thm-hilbert-adjoint-properties]]. Write $M_+$ for the
positive operators in $M$ and $a\le b$ when $b-a$ is positive.

A vector $\Omega\in H$ is **cyclic** for $M$ when
$\overline{M\Omega}=H$, and is **separating** for $M$ when
$x\Omega=0$ for $x\in M$ implies $x=0$. For a unit vector $\Omega$, define its
vector functional by $\omega_\Omega(x)=\langle x\Omega,\Omega\rangle$.
It is **faithful** when $\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=0$ implies $x=0$; this is
equivalent to $\Omega$ being separating because
$\omega_\Omega(x^*x)=\|x\Omega\|^2$.

For a bounded linear functional $\varphi:M\to\mathbb C$, **positive** means
$\varphi(a)\ge0$ for every $a\in M_+$. A positive functional is **normal**
when $\varphi(\sup_\alpha x_\alpha)=\sup_\alpha\varphi(x_\alpha)$ for each
bounded increasing net $(x_\alpha)$ in $M_+$ whose supremum is taken in $M$.

derivations.claim: If $x\Omega=y\Omega$ for $x,y\in M$, then $(x-y)\Omega=0$ and separatingness gives $x=y$. Thus $S_0$ is well defined; it is antilinear by $(ax+by)^*=\bar a x^*+\bar b y^*$, and its domain is dense by cyclicity. The same reasoning makes $F_0$ well defined; [F4] makes $M'\Omega$ dense. Also $S_0^2(x\Omega)=x\Omega$ and $F_0^2(x'\Omega)=x'\Omega$.

By [F4], $\Omega$ is cyclic for $M'$ because it is separating for $M$, and separating for $M'$ because it is cyclic for $M$. Applying [F2] to the Tomita operator $F_0$ of $M'$ therefore proves directly that $F_0$ is closable; applying [F2] to $M$ proves that $S_0$ is closable. For $x\in M$ and $x'\in M'$, the adjoint identity and commutation give $$(x'\Omega|S_0x\Omega)=(x'\Omega|x^*\Omega)=(x\Omega|x'^*\Omega)=(x\Omega|F_0x'\Omega).$$ By [F3] this says $F_0\subseteq S_0^*$ and $S_0\subseteq F_0^*$.

Let $\xi\in D(S)$ and choose $\xi_n\in M\Omega$ with $\xi_n\to\xi$ and $S_0\xi_n\to S\xi$, using the definition of graph closure. Since $S_0^2\xi_n=\xi_n$, the graph points $(S\xi_n,S(S\xi_n))=(S_0\xi_n,\xi_n)$ converge to $(S\xi,\xi)$. Closedness of $S$ implies $S\xi\in D(S)$ and $S^2\xi=\xi$. Hence $S$ is an involution, so it is injective and its range is the dense domain $D(S)$.

Apply the closed-antilinear polar result [F2] to $S$. Injectivity and dense range make its partial anti-isometry $J$ antiunitary. The inverse of $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$ is $\Delta^{-1/2}J^*=J^*(J\Delta^{-1/2}J^*)$, whose second factor is positive self-adjoint. Since $S^{-1}=S$, uniqueness of the polar decomposition gives $J=J^*$ and $\Delta^{1/2}=J\Delta^{-1/2}J$. Thus $J^2=I$ and $J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1}$. For antiunitary conjugation the functional-calculus rule is $Jf(\Delta)J=\overline f(J\Delta J)$. Taking $f(s)=s^{it}$ gives $J\Delta^{it}J=(\Delta^{-1})^{-it}=\Delta^{it}$, so $J$ commutes with every $\Delta^{it}$.

Because $S$ is the graph closure of $S_0$, their adjoints agree: the adjoint identity for $S_0$ extends along convergent graph pairs to $S$, and restriction gives the converse. Hence $F=S^*=S_0^*$ and $F_0\subseteq F$. From $S=J\Delta^{1/2}$, the antilinear adjoint identity [F3] and self-adjointness of $\Delta^{1/2}$ give $F=\Delta^{1/2}J$. Functional calculus applied to $J\Delta J=\Delta^{-1}$ gives $\Delta^{1/2}J=J\Delta^{-1/2}$ on their common domain.

Since $S_0\Omega=F_0\Omega=\Omega$ and $F_0\subseteq F$, steps 3.1 and 4.1 give $\Delta^{1/2}\Omega=J\Omega=\Delta^{-1/2}\Omega$. For the spectral measure of $\Delta$, this equality has squared norm difference $\int_{(0,\infty)}|\lambda^{1/2}-\lambda^{-1/2}|^2\,d\mu_\Omega(\lambda)=0$. The integrand vanishes only at $\lambda=1$, so $\Delta\Omega=\Omega$ and then $J\Omega=\Omega$.

derivations.claim: The operators $A_v,B_f$ are commuting self-adjoint involutions by [F1], so $\Pi=\prod_{v\in V}(I+A_v)/2\prod_{f\in F}(I+B_f)/2$ is the orthogonal projection onto their common $+1$ eigenspace. Expand this finite product. Each term is a tensor-product Pauli $X(a)Z(b)$ with coefficient $+1$: factors of the same type multiply without phases, and every vertex operator commutes with every face operator. For the ordinary matrix trace on $\mathcal H_K$, the trace of a tensor product is the product of the factor traces. A nonidentity Pauli therefore has trace zero because at least one edge factor is $X$, $Z$, or $XZ$, each of which has trace zero; an identity term has trace $2^{|E|}$. The empty subset contributes one identity term and no term contributes negative trace, so $\operatorname{Tr}\Pi\ge 2^{|E|-|V|-|F|}>0$. Thus $\Pi\ne0$. Since each $A_v,B_f$ is a self-adjoint involution, each penalty factor $(I-A_v)/2$ or $(I-B_f)/2$ is an orthogonal projection. The positive coefficients make $H_K$ positive semidefinite, with kernel exactly the common $+1$ eigenspace; hence a nonzero ground vector exists and has $H_K$-eigenvalue zero.

Let $b\in\mathbb F_2^E$ be the edge chain of the primal path $\gamma$. Because the path visits no vertex twice and has distinct endpoints, each internal vertex has even path incidence and the endpoints have odd incidence, so $\partial_1b=v_1+v_2$. For each vertex $v$, $Z(b)A_v=(-1)^{\langle b,\partial_1^Tv\rangle}A_vZ(b)=(-1)^{(\partial_1b)_v}A_vZ(b)$; $Z(b)$ commutes with every $B_f$. Hence applying $Z(b)$ to any ground vector flips exactly $A_{v_1}$ and $A_{v_2}$ from $+1$ to $-1$ and leaves every other stabilizer eigenvalue unchanged.

Regard the dual path $\gamma^*$ as a path in the dual graph whose vertices are faces, and let $a\in\mathbb F_2^E$ indicate the primal edges crossed by its dual edges. By the definition of the dual incidence map as $\partial_2^T$, the no-repeated-face hypothesis and distinct endpoint faces give $\partial_2^Ta=f_1+f_2$. For each face $f$, $X(a)B_f=(-1)^{\langle a,\partial_2f\rangle}B_fX(a)=(-1)^{(\partial_2^Ta)_f}B_fX(a)$; $X(a)$ commutes with every $A_v$. Hence applying $X(a)$ to any ground vector flips exactly $B_{f_1}$ and $B_{f_2}$ and leaves every other stabilizer eigenvalue unchanged.

By step 1.2, the vector $Z(b)\psi$ has eigenvalue $-1$ precisely for the two vertex stabilizers at $v_1,v_2$ and eigenvalue $+1$ for every other stabilizer, when $\psi$ is a ground vector. Thus the only nonzero terms in $H_K Z(b)\psi$ are the penalties $J_{v_i}(I-A_{v_i})/2$, each acting as multiplication by $J_{v_i}$; its $H_K$-eigenvalue, and hence its energy increase from the ground eigenvalue zero, is $J_{v_1}+J_{v_2}$.

By step 1.3, the vector $X(a)\psi$ has eigenvalue $-1$ precisely for $B_{f_1},B_{f_2}$ and eigenvalue $+1$ for every other stabilizer, when $\psi$ is a ground vector. Therefore only the two penalties $K_{f_i}(I-B_{f_i})/2$ contribute, and its $H_K$-eigenvalue, hence energy increase from zero, is $K_{f_1}+K_{f_2}$.

Write $S^+=E$, $S^-=F$, and $S^z=H/2$.

$$ E=x\partial_y,\qquad F=y\partial_x,\qquad H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y. $$

derivations.claim:
In the ordered tensor basis, define
$v_{++}=|\uparrow\uparrow\rangle$,
$v_0=(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle+|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)/\sqrt2$,
$v_{--}=|\downarrow\downarrow\rangle$, and
$v_s=(|\uparrow\downarrow\rangle-|\downarrow\uparrow\rangle)/\sqrt2$.
These four vectors are pairwise orthonormal by the tensor-product inner
product, and they span the four-dimensional space. The swap $P$ fixes the first
three and sends $v_s$ to $-v_s$, so the same space decomposes into the
symmetric eigenspace $W_+=\ker(P-I)$ of dimension three and the antisymmetric
eigenspace $W_-=\ker(P+I)$ of dimension one. The swap is an involutive
permutation of an orthonormal basis, so $P=P^*$. By [F2], it commutes with
$\rho(X)$ for every $X\in\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$; hence both eigenspaces
are invariant under the action.

Let $A_0=0$ and $A_1=JP$. Both are self-adjoint because $J$ is real
and $P=P^*$, and both belong to $\mathscr H_\rho$: the zero map commutes
with every endomorphism and [F2] gives the required commutation for $P$.
The spectrum of $A_0$ is $0$ with multiplicity four; that of $A_1$ is $J$
with multiplicity three and $-J$ with multiplicity one. Therefore, by [F4]
and [F5],
$$Z_{A_0}(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}_W(\exp(-\beta A_0))=4,\qquad Z_{A_1}(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}_W(\exp(-\beta A_1))=3e^{-\beta J}+e^{\beta J}.$$

Since $\beta J=\ln2$, the second trace is
$3/2+2=7/2$, which differs from $4$. Hence the same spin representation
decomposition admits distinct symmetry-preserving spectra and Gibbs traces.

The Hall data in [F1] and the KLR Grothendieck isomorphism in [F3] are
fixed for both $A_0$ and $A_1$; neither specifies a selected endomorphism of
$W$. Since both operators lie in the quantified class but have different
spectra and different partition traces, they refute the stated uniqueness
claim.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

the standard two-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$.

$\mathcal H_{N,m}=\ker(S_N^z-mI)$. These are dimensionless matrices in the
algebraic spin convention.

For each integer $r\geq0$, define $V(r)$ to be the vector space
$\mathbb C[x,y]_r$ of homogeneous polynomials of degree $r$, with
$\mathfrak{sl}_2$ action
$$ E=x\partial_y,\qquad F=y\partial_x,\qquad H=x\partial_x-y\partial_y. $$
The ordered monomials $x^{r-k}y^k$ for $0\leq k\leq r$ form its basis.
Under $x\mapsto|\uparrow\rangle$ and $y\mapsto|\downarrow\rangle$,
$V(1)$ is the representation on $V$ above. A tensor power $V(1)^{\otimes N}$
uses the diagonal action defined by the sums $S_N^+,S_N^-,2S_N^z$.

Let $q_H>1$ be a prime power and fix a finite field $\mathbb F_{q_H}$ of that
cardinality. Put $\nu=\sqrt{q_H}>1$ and $K=\mathbb Q(\nu)$. The representation category of
the one-vertex, no-arrow quiver over $\mathbb F_{q_H}$ is the category of
finite-dimensional $\mathbb F_{q_H}$-vector spaces, with unique simple object
$S=\mathbb F_{q_H}$. Its Hall composition algebra is the subalgebra generated
by the class $[S]$ in the twisted Hall algebra with the normalization of the

$U_\nu^+(\mathfrak{sl}_2)=K[E]$. The canonical Ringel map $E\mapsto[S]$
identifies this positive half with the composition algebra; the finite-Dynkin
criterion identifies it with the full Hall algebra in this one-vertex case.

supplier_excerpts.exact_statement:
Let $\mathcal H$ be a complex Hilbert space of finite dimension $d\ge1$, $H=H^*$ with energy unit J, $\hbar>0$ with unit J s, $\beta>0$ with unit J$^{-1}$, and let $\sigma=Z_\beta^{-1}e^{-\beta H}$ be the stationary Gibbs density from [[thm-qsm-dt-finite-unitary]]. Let $A=A^*$ and $B=B^*$ be matrices, let $T>0$ be finite in s, let $h:[0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $\epsilon\in\mathbb R$ be dimensionless; $h(t)B$ has unit J. Put $U_0(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ for time $t$ in s, $\alpha_t(A)=U_0(t)^*AU_0(t)$, and $B_t=\alpha_t(B)$. Let $W_\epsilon$ solve
$$W_\epsilon'(t)=\frac{i\epsilon h(t)}{\hbar}B_tW_\epsilon(t),\qquad W_\epsilon(0)=I,$$
and set $U_\epsilon(t)=U_0(t)W_\epsilon(t)$ and $\rho_I(t)=W_\epsilon(t)\sigma W_\epsilon(t)^*$. Then $U_\epsilon$ solves $i\hbar U_\epsilon'(t)=(H-\epsilon h(t)B)U_\epsilon(t)$, $U_\epsilon(0)=I$, and $\rho_\epsilon(t):=U_\epsilon(t)\sigma U_\epsilon(t)^*$ satisfies $\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_\epsilon(t)A)=\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_I(t)\alpha_t(A))$. Define
$$R_{AB}(u)=\frac{i}{\hbar}\operatorname{Tr}\!\left(\sigma[\alpha_u(A),B]\right),\qquad C_T=\frac{2}{\hbar}\int_0^T|h(s)|\,\|B\|\,ds.$$
Then $W_\epsilon(t)$ is unitary and, for $0\le t\le T$,
$$\operatorname{Tr}(\rho_I(t)\alpha_t(A))=\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\alpha_t(A))+\epsilon\int_0^t h(s)R_{AB}(t-s)\,ds+r_\epsilon(t),\qquad |r_\epsilon(t)|\le\|A\|\frac{(|\epsilon|C_T)^2e^{|\epsilon|C_T}}2.$$
The initial Gibbs matrix is fixed as $\epsilon$ varies. The result is an exact finite-time first variation with a controlled remainder, not a static derivative of a re-prepared Gibbs family. $C_T$ and $\epsilon$ are dimensionless, and $R_{AB}$ has units $[A][B]/(\mathrm J\,\mathrm s)$.

citations.quote:
Let $n\ge2$, let $M$ be an oriented, time-oriented smooth $n$-manifold, and let $g$ be a smooth Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. Write $\boldsymbol\epsilon_g$ for its oriented metric volume form. Let $\nabla$ be its Levi-Civita connection, the unique torsion-free, metric-compatible connection. Let $\phi=(g,\psi)$ denote a smooth section of a specified field bundle $\pi:E\to M$, including the metric and any other dynamical fields $\psi$ that are smooth tensor fields with the pullback action of spacetime diffeomorphisms. An admitted field family is a smooth map $\Phi:P\times M\to E$ with $\pi(\Phi(p,x))=x$, where $P$ is a finite-dimensional smooth parameter manifold; for $v\in T_pP$, $\delta_v\phi$ is the derivative of $\Phi$ along any smooth parameter curve with initial velocity $v$. A **finite-jet Lagrangian $n$-form** is a smooth spacetime $n$-form $\mathcal L(\phi)$ whose coordinate coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many spacetime derivatives. It is **diffeomorphism-covariant** when pullback by every admitted local diffeomorphism $\Psi$ satisfies $\mathcal L(\Psi^*\phi)=\Psi^*\mathcal L(\phi)$.

A **chosen covariant first-variation decomposition** is data consisting of an Euler–Lagrange expression $E_\phi[\eta]$, the $n$-form linear in a field variation $\eta$ left after spacetime derivatives have been moved off $\eta$ by integration by parts, and a covariant $(n-1)$-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, also linear in $\eta$, such that
$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)$$
for every admitted smooth finite-dimensional family of fields. Here covariance means that for every admitted local diffeomorphism $\Psi$ and field variation $\eta$,
$$E_{\Psi^*\phi}[\Psi^*\eta]=\Psi^*E_\phi[\eta],\qquad \theta(\Psi^*\phi;\Psi^*\eta)=\Psi^*\theta(\phi;\eta).$$
The choice of $\theta$ is part of the data and need not be unique. A solution has $E_\phi=0$; a linearized solution $\delta\phi$ at $\phi$ has $\delta E_\phi[\delta\phi]=0$.

A **stationary solution with generator $\xi$** is a solution $\phi$ and a fixed smooth spacetime vector field $\xi$ such that $\mathcal L_\xi\phi=0$. Thus $\mathcal L_\xi g=0$, so $\xi$ is a Killing field of $g$. A **bifurcate Killing horizon** is a pair of smooth null hypersurfaces generated by this Killing flow: $\xi$ is nonzero, null, tangent and normal on each hypersurface away from their transverse intersection $B$, and $\xi=0$ on $B$. Fix a compact, oriented, boundaryless, spacelike embedded codimension-two submanifold $B\subset M$. Choose a future-directed unit timelike normal $u$ and a chosen unit spacelike normal $n_B$ along $B$, orthogonal to each other, and define the binormal $\epsilon_{ab}=2u_{[a}(n_B)_{b]}$, so $\epsilon_{ab}\epsilon^{ab}=-2$. Orient $B$ compatibly with the spacetime orientation and this normal frame so that, on $B$, $(\boldsymbol\epsilon_g)_{ab a_3\ldots a_n}=\epsilon_{ab}(dA_B)_{a_3\ldots a_n}$; here $dA_B$ is the positive volume form of the induced metric with that orientation. The horizon is **nondegenerate** when the fixed normalization of $\xi$ gives a constant $\kappa>0$ on $B$ with $\nabla_a\xi_b=\kappa\epsilon_{ab}$ there; $\kappa$ is its surface gravity. Variations keep $\xi$ and the embedded surface $B$ fixed.

For such data define the **Noether current** $(n-1)$-form
$$J_\xi:=\theta(\phi;\mathcal L_\xi\phi)-\iota_\xi\mathcal L.$$
Choose a smooth covariant $(n-2)$-form $Q_\xi$ on a neighborhood of the admitted field data and define the residual constraint form $C_\xi:=J_\xi-dQ_\xi$. Require $C_\xi=0$ on the selected solution and, for each admitted linearized perturbation used below, require its fixed-$\xi$ variation $\delta C_\xi=0$. These are explicit on-shell and linearized-constraint conditions; no existence or global exactness of $Q_\xi$ follows merely from closure of a presymplectic current. The pullback of $Q_\xi$ is required to be globally compatible on the integration region.

Boundary data consist of a specified smooth solution space $\mathcal S$, with specified falloff, a family of closed codimension-two surfaces $S_R$ approaching the asymptotic boundary, and finite oriented smooth singular hypersurface chains $C_R$ with $\partial C_R=S_R-B$. With a fixed boundary-term convention, define the charge-variation one-form by
$$\alpha_\xi(\delta\phi):=\lim_{R\to\infty}\int_{S_R}\bigl(\delta Q_\xi-\iota_\xi\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)\bigr).$$
Require this limit to exist and be globally integrable: there is a smooth Hamiltonian charge $H_\xi$ on the specified solution space with $d_{\mathcal S}H_\xi=\alpha_\xi$, where $d_{\mathcal S}$ is the exterior derivative on that solution space. This exactness, and the chosen boundary formula itself, are hypotheses. Other boundary actions or falloff conditions can add terms and require a separately stated charge formula.

Adopt the $c=1$ action-unit convention: time is measured as length, $[\hbar]=\text{action}$, and $[k_B]=\text{energy}/\text{temperature}$; neither $\hbar$ nor $k_B$ is set to $1$. Normalize the flow parameter of the fixed generator $\xi$ in length units. Then its Lie action and $\nabla\xi$ have units $L^{-1}$, and the surface gravity $\kappa$ in $\nabla_a\xi_b=\kappa\epsilon_{ab}$ has units $L^{-1}$. The spacetime integral of $\mathcal L$ has units of action, so if $\mathcal L=\ell\boldsymbol\epsilon_g$, then $[\ell]=\text{action}\,L^{-n}$. Since curvature has units $L^{-2}$, the Einstein--Hilbert normalization $\ell_{\rm EH}=R/(16\pi G)$ in $n$ spacetime dimensions has $[G]=L^{n-2}\,\text{action}^{-1}$. Thus the curvature derivative $P^{abcd}$ used below has units $[P]=\text{action}\,L^{2-n}$, and the downstream functional $-(2\pi k_B/\hbar)\int_B P^{abcd}\epsilon_{ab}\epsilon_{cd}\,dA_B$ has entropy units $k_B$. The integrated Noether charge and $H_\xi$ have energy units, consistent with $\hbar\kappa\,\delta S_W/k_B$.

When SI units are restored for the $n$-dimensional Einstein--Hilbert normalization $c^3R/(16\pi G)$, $[G]={\rm m}^{n-1}{\rm kg}^{-1}{\rm s}^{-2}$ and $[A_B]={\rm m}^{n-2}$, so the area expression is $S_W=k_Bc^3A_B/(4G\hbar)$. In four spacetime dimensions this is the usual SI Newton constant in ${\rm m}^3{\rm kg}^{-1}{\rm s}^{-2}$ and horizon area in ${\rm m}^2$; the SI acceleration surface gravity is $\kappa_{\rm acc}=c^2\kappa_{\rm geom}$.

If $X$ has local flow $\Phi_t$ and $T$ is a smooth tensor field of type $(r,s)$, its Lie derivative is $$\mathcal L_XT=\left.\frac d{dt}\right|_{t=0}\Phi_t^*T,$$ on every local flow domain where this derivative is defined. Here the pullback by the local diffeomorphism $\Phi_t$ acts by $d\Phi_{-t}$ on each contravariant slot and by $d\Phi_t$ on each covariant slot.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$.  For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$,
$\mathcal L_X\omega$ is the Lie derivative of $\omega$ regarded as an
alternating covariant tensor.
For every vector field $X$ and differential form $\omega$, $$\mathcal L_X\omega=d(\iota_X\omega)+\iota_X(d\omega).$$

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Use the metric, tensor fields, covariant first-variation decomposition, and
Noether current of [[def-tgrx-noether-horizon-data]]. Suppose the Lagrangian is
$$\mathcal L=\ell(g_{ab},R_{abcd},\psi,\nabla\psi,\ldots,\nabla_{(a_1}\cdots\nabla_{a_m)}\psi)\,\boldsymbol\epsilon_g,$$
where $m<\infty$, all fields and coefficients are smooth, and the curvature
argument is algebraic (there are no covariant derivatives of $R_{abcd}$).
Use the curvature convention
$$R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z,$$
and write $R_{abcd}:=g(R(e_c,e_d)e_b,e_a)$ in any local frame. Square
brackets denote weight-one antisymmetrization.
Define the Riemann-symmetric derivative $P^{abcd}$ by
$$\delta\ell\big|_{g,\psi,\nabla\psi,\ldots}=P^{abcd}\delta R_{abcd},$$
with $P^{abcd}=-P^{bacd}=-P^{abdc}=P^{cdab}$ and $P^{a[bcd]}=0$.

Use the covariant first-variation potential produced by the finite covariant
integration-by-parts construction on the field jets, up to the stated
potential ambiguities. For each smooth vector field $\zeta$, use the local
Noether potential obtained by covariantly integrating the derivatives of
$\zeta$ in $J_\zeta=\theta(\phi;\mathcal L_\zeta\phi)-\iota_\zeta\mathcal L$
by parts.
Call this the **canonical local representative**: it is defined on a
neighborhood of the fields and generators, is a local covariant primitive of
$J_\zeta$ on shell, and has no independent closed-form addition. The permitted
representative changes are exactly those induced by
$$\mathcal L\mapsto\mathcal L+d\mu,\qquad \theta\mapsto\theta+\delta\mu+d\mathbf Y,$$
and by an exact charge change; here $\mu$ is a covariant $(n-1)$-form and
$\mathbf Y(\phi;\eta)$ is a covariant $(n-2)$-form linear in $\eta$.
Assume the chosen representative is globally compatible on the integration
region. Then it has the form
$$Q_\zeta=W^c\zeta_c+X^{cd}\nabla_{[c}\zeta_{d]} +\mathbf Y(\phi;\mathcal L_\zeta\phi)+dZ,$$
where $W^c$ and $X^{cd}$ are local covariant form-valued coefficients,
$Z$ is a local covariant $(n-3)$-form (the exact term is absent when $n=2$),
and
$$(X^{cd})_{a_3\ldots a_n} =-P^{abcd}(\boldsymbol\epsilon_g)_{ab a_3\ldots a_n}.$$
For the canonical representative before the permitted changes one may take
$\mathbf Y=0$ and $Z=0$.

derivations.claim: By [F4], the selected charge has the stated $W^c\xi_c$, $X^{cd}\nabla_{[c}\xi_{d]}$, $\mathbf Y(\mathcal L_\xi\phi)$, and exact-form decomposition. On $B$, $\xi=0$ and $\mathcal L_\xi\phi=0$. The $W^c\xi_c$ and $\mathbf Y$ terms and their field variations vanish there except for $\mathbf Y(\phi;\mathcal L_\xi\delta\phi)$. Covariance identifies this term with $\mathcal L_\xi\mathbf Y(\phi;\delta\phi)$; Cartan's formula [F2] writes it as $\iota_\xi d\mathbf Y+d(\iota_\xi\mathbf Y)$, whose pullback integrates to zero because $\xi=0$ on $B$ and $B$ has no boundary. The $dZ$ variation integrates to zero by Stokes [F3]. The Lagrangian ambiguity $\iota_\xi\mu$ vanishes on $B$, and the exact charge ambiguity also integrates to zero. Therefore $\delta\int_BQ_\xi=\delta\int_BX^{cd}\nabla_{[c}\xi_{d]}$.

Define $w_{cd}:=
abla_{[c}\xi_{d]}-\kappa\epsilon_{cd}$ along $B$. It vanishes on the background. Since $\xi$ and $B$ are fixed and $\xi=0$ on $B$, $\delta(
abla_c\xi^a)=\delta\Gamma^a_{ce}\xi^e=0$ there. Lowering the index and using $
abla_c\xi^a=\kappa\epsilon_c{}^a$ gives $\delta w_{cd}=-\kappa g_{a[d}\delta\epsilon_{c]}{}^a$. The binormal annihilates tangent vectors, so its variation has no tangent-tangent block; its fixed normalization $\epsilon^a{}_b\epsilon^b{}_a=2$ removes the normal-normal antisymmetric block in $g_{a[d}\delta\epsilon_{c]}{}^a$. Thus $\delta w_{cd}$ has only normal-tangent components. The coefficient $X^{cd}$, including its form slots, is local and covariant in the fields, so stationarity gives $\mathcal L_\xi X=0$. At $p\in B$, define $A^a{}_b:=
abla_b\xi^a|_p$. It annihilates tangent vectors and is a Lorentz-boost generator on the normal plane with opposite nonzero eigenvalues $+\kappa$ and $-\kappa$. Choose null normal eigenvectors $l,k$ with $g(l,k)=-1$ and a tangent basis $e_A$. After choosing the sign of the flow parameter $s$, the induced linear action sends $l\mapsto e^{\kappa s}l$, $k\mapsto e^{-\kappa s}k$, and fixes every $e_A$. Since $\xi(p)=0$, $\mathcal L_\xi X=0$ is invariance of each component under this pointwise action. In the pullback of $X$ to $B$, all form slots are tangent and have boost weight zero. A component with exactly one of the indices $c,d$ normal and the other tangent has nonzero weight $+\kappa$ or $-\kappa$, so invariance for every $s$ forces that component to vanish. These are precisely the components that could contract with the normal-tangent $\delta w_{cd}$. Hence the pullback of $X^{cd}\delta w_{cd}$ to $B$ vanishes.

On the background, $\nabla_a\xi_b=\kappa\epsilon_{ab}$ and [F4] gives $X^{cd}\epsilon_{cd}=-P^{abcd}\epsilon_{ab}\epsilon_{cd}\,dA_B$. Write the charge term as $X^{cd}(\kappa\epsilon_{cd}+w_{cd})$. Since $w=0$ on the background, its variation is $\kappa\delta(X^{cd}\epsilon_{cd})+X^{cd}\delta w_{cd}$. The second term integrates to zero by step 1.2; the first includes the variations of $P$, the binormal, and the induced area form. Hence $\delta\int_BQ_\xi=\kappa\,\delta\int_BX^{cd}\epsilon_{cd}=-\kappa\,\delta\int_BP^{abcd}\epsilon_{ab}\epsilon_{cd}\,dA_B=(\hbar\kappa/(2\pi k_B))\,\delta S_W$. The coefficient $\kappa$ is the fixed background surface gravity, so no $\delta\kappa$ term appears.
